## gestureKeyframes.kt { #gesturekeyframes-kt }

Gesture takes and keyframe lanes, in both directions: `bakeGesture` turns a take recorded on a
pad into two editable lanes, and `lanesToTake` renders lanes back into a take a pad accepts.

A take recorded by `gesture(...)` is a run of (t, x, y) samples that `GestureHandle.at` joins with
straight lines. Baking keeps the fewest of those samples that stay within a tolerance of the
take, as `linear` keys in two lanes that share their key times. Because the keys are a subset of
the samples and both are joined by straight lines, the largest difference anywhere in time is the
largest difference at a sample, so the tolerance holds at every t, not only at the samples.

## keyframeInterpolants.kt { #keyframeinterpolants-kt }

Custom key types for the keyframe editor that `keyframes(...)` opens: a named segment shape,
written as a Kotlin lambda.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
interpolant("overshoot") { v0 + (v1 - v0) * (1 + 2.7 * (u - 1).pow(3) + 1.7 * (u - 1).pow(2)) }
```

The name becomes a key type, offered in the key menu, and a key of that type shapes the segment
that leaves it. The `interpolant` macro (`macro_interpolant`) keeps the lambda's source beside
the live lambda and saves it with the box, in its `keyframeInterpolants` property. Compiling
that source again is what keeps a curve's shape while the definition has not run: when the box
defines the type only after it calls `keyframes`, and when the definition has been deleted.

## keyframeCodeBlend.kt { #keyframecodeblend-kt }

Blending two *code* keyframes by finding the structure they share and interpolating the numbers
they do not.

A [`KeyframeScope`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keyframescope) can snapshot code as well as values: a `stack.auto` StackSL program through
[`KeyframeScope.stackAuto`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--stackauto), and a Kotlin expression through the `sourceBlock { }` macro. Two such
snapshots have no midpoint in general — half a program is not a program — so
[`KeyframeScope.interpolate`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--interpolate) steps them, taking the right-hand source once `t >= 1`. That is all
that is available when the two programs disagree about what they do.

When they *agree* about what they do and differ only in numbers, there is a real midpoint, and
this file finds it. Both sources are lexed, the two token streams are aligned, and every place
where the alignment pairs a number with a number becomes a [`CodeBlendSite`](graphics.md#keyframecodeblend-kt-codeblendsite). Anything the
alignment cannot pair is a [`CodeBlendDivergence`](graphics.md#keyframecodeblend-kt-codeblenddivergence), and one divergence is enough to put the whole
slot back on the stepping path: a program built from the left structure with the right numbers,
where the two structures differ, is neither keyframe at either end.

### The two ways to spend the blend

`CodeBlendMode.STATIC` writes the interpolated numbers into the source and hands back a new
program, which the slot then compiles. It reaches every site — including StackSL's modifier chains
and random ranges, whose grammar demands literals — and it costs a shader compile (or, for Kotlin,
a K2 compile) per value of `t`. Scrubbing a timeline or stepping between two looks is what it is
for; sixty times a second is not.

`CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME` emits *one* program in which each moving site reads the blend from
outside. The program is then invariant in `t`, so it compiles once and animates for free. StackSL
gets there by rewriting `0.5` as `0.2 0.9 ?pc.keyframeBlend .x mix` — a push of each endpoint and
the builtin `mix`, which leaves one value on the stack exactly as the literal it replaced did, so
the surrounding stack arithmetic is untouched. Kotlin gets there by rewriting `0.5f` as
`afield.animation.keyframes.kfMix(0.2f, 0.9f, ...)`. Sites a mix expression cannot reach — see
`StackSLNumericFormKind` — make the plan report [`CodeBlendPlan.runtimeCapable`](graphics.md#keyframecodeblend-kt--codeblendplan--runtimecapable) false, and a
RUNTIME request over one of those falls back to STATIC and says so.

### The push-constant convention

A StackSL program can only read what the host has already put in the shader, and a `stack.auto`
slot cannot declare a uniform of its own. So the blend parameter arrives by convention: declare a
`vec4` called `keyframeBlend` in the shader's push-constant block, and register the matching
keyframe lane so the scope can write it.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
layout(push_constant) uniform Controls {
    vec4 keyframeBlend;
} pc;
```
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
scope.target("keyframeBlend") { module.current.liveUniformStructures["pc"] }
scope.codeBlend = CodeBlendOptions(mode = CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME)
```

[`KeyframeScope.interpolate`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--interpolate) then fills that lane with [`keyframeBlendVector`](graphics.md#keyframecodeblend-kt--keyframeblendvector) on every blend, and
the four components are four shapes of the same parameter — see [`CodeBlendLane`](graphics.md#keyframecodeblend-kt-codeblendlane). A vec4 rather
than a float because a push-constant block is padded to vec4 boundaries anyway, and because a
program that wants the eased blend for one number and the raw one for another should not need a
second uniform to say so.

The names are defaults ([`keyframeBlendPushConstant`](graphics.md#keyframecodeblend-kt--keyframeblendpushconstant), [`keyframeBlendKey`](graphics.md#keyframecodeblend-kt--keyframeblendkey)); a shader whose block
instance is called something other than `pc` sets [`CodeBlendOptions.stackSLRead`](graphics.md#keyframecodeblend-kt--codeblendoptions--stackslread) to match.

## keyframeSweep.kt { #keyframesweep-kt }

Overnight exploration of a keyframe space: a directory of saved keys in, an archive of renders out.

A [`KeyframeScope`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keyframescope) gives you one look at a time — capture it, edit it, put it back. A directory of
saved keys is something else: a *space*, whose interesting points are mostly the ones nobody has
visited. [`KeyframeSweep`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt-keyframesweep) visits them while you sleep. Each pass draws a few keys from the pool,
blends them at random weights (sometimes past either end of the hull), applies the blend to the
live scope, makes a directory, and hands that directory to a `suspend` callback of yours which
runs to completion before the next pass starts. What the callback writes there is its business —
a still, a clip, a mesh, a CSV. What the sweep writes there is the provenance: the blended key as
ordinary key JSON, and a manifest saying which keys went in at which weights.

The point of the archive is what happens to it afterwards. A night of this is a few thousand
directories to categorise, cluster, score or hand to a model, and the sweep's job is to make that
second pass possible: every render is self-describing, `index.jsonl` is one line per render for a
reader that does not want to walk the tree, and `renders/` is itself a valid keyframe pool — so
tonight's output is a legitimate input for tomorrow night.

### The blend is a fold, not new maths

[`KeyframeScope.interpolate`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--interpolate) already knows how every lane type blends — numbers and vectors lerp,
quaternions slerp, `CameraPose` sclerp, code blends or steps. So an N-way blend here is a
*pairwise fold* over it rather than a second type table that would immediately drift from the
first: with weights sorted descending and running sums `S`, folding `t = w / S` at each step
yields exactly the affine weighted mean for every linear lane, and inherits the rest for free.

Sorting descending is what makes it safe rather than merely neat. Weights sum to 1, so the running
sums start at the largest weight and end at 1, rising while the terms are positive and falling
once they go negative — the minimum is therefore `min(w_max, 1)`, which is always positive. No
division ever approaches zero, including under extrapolation, where some weights *are* negative.

Three things the fold alone gets wrong, and this file handles — see [`DiscreteBlend`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt-discreteblend),
[`MissingSlots`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt-missingslots) and [`SweepConfig.preserveNumericKind`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt--sweepconfig--preservenumerickind). All three are recorded per render rather
than assumed, so a later pass over the archive can see which of them applied to any given render.

### What a night survives

Nothing here trusts the run to finish. A render's manifest is written *before* its callback and
rewritten after, atomically, so a crashed pass is identifiable as one; [`SweepConfig.resume`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt--sweepconfig--resume) picks
up where the process died and re-derives each render's randomness from `seed + index`, so skipping
completed work cannot change what the unfinished work would have drawn. A throwing callback is
one failed render, not a lost night — until [`SweepConfig.maxConsecutiveFailures`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt--sweepconfig--maxconsecutivefailures) of them in a row
says the night is broken. And [`SweepConfig.minFreeBytes`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt--sweepconfig--minfreebytes) stops the sweep before the disk does.

| <a id="keyframesweep-kt--sweepconfig--resume"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">resume</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Skip renders a previous process already finished. See [`KeyframeSweep.run`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt--keyframesweep--run). |
| <a id="keyframesweep-kt--sweepconfig--keepfailedrenders"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">keepFailedRenders</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Keep the directory of a failed render, with its manifest and partial output, for forensics. |
| <a id="keyframesweep-kt--sweepconfig--draws"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">draws</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">SweepDraw</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Renders to make exactly as written, instead of drawing them at random. |
| <a id="keyframesweep-kt--sweepconfig--renders"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">renders</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframeSweep/#L360) | How many renders the run attempts: [`count`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt--sweepconfig--count), or the number of [`draws`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt--sweepconfig--draws) when there are any. |
| <a id="keyframesweep-kt--sweepconfig--arity"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">arity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">IntRange</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframeSweep/#L363) | [`minArity`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt--sweepconfig--minarity)`..`[`maxArity`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt--sweepconfig--maxarity), for reading. |

## keyframeSweepCapture.kt { #keyframesweepcapture-kt }

The GPU half of a keyframe sweep: turning one blended look into the still and the short clip that
a night's archive is actually made of.

[`KeyframeSweep`](graphics.md#keyframesweep-kt-keyframesweep) is renderer-free: it blends, it records, it calls your callback. But
*most* callbacks do the same two things, and they are the two things with traps in them: an
offscreen readback that can come back empty, and a frame sequence that has to be muxed by a tool
which may not be installed. So they live here once rather than in every sweep.

Both helpers follow the pattern the RectSL and StackSL gallery harnesses established: **one**
renderer and one [`RenderToTexture`](graphics.md#rendertotexture-kt-rendertotexture) for the whole run, reused across thousands of renders, with
only the uniforms changing. Building a target per render is what makes an overnight sweep run out
of device memory at 3am.

Neither helper will invent a file. A readback that comes back empty and a missing `ffmpeg` are
both recorded as an artifact with a null path and a stated reason, and the frame PNGs are left on
disk so the clip can be muxed later. An archive that says what it is missing can be analysed; one
with a plausible-looking wrong file in it cannot.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframeSweepCapture.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframeSweepCapture/)

**Used in:** [Sweeping saved keyframes overnight](../keyframe_autosweep.md)

## keyframeTypeLibrary.kt { #keyframetypelibrary-kt }

The key types every keyframe editor offers beyond its five built-in ones: the easing family,
splines that look past the segment to the keys either side, shapes, and shaped noise. Each is a
[`KeySegment`](graphics.md#keyframeinterpolants-kt-keysegment) lambda like the ones a box defines with `interpolant(...)`, evaluated in Kotlin and
drawn by the editor from samples of the segment.

## keyframer.kt { #keyframer-kt }

Snapshot, interpolate and persist the live state of a running sketch. A [`KeyframeScope`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keyframescope) is a set
of named targets — typed Kotlin locals, keyframe-aware `controlGroup` controls, contributors such
as a score object, uniform `Structure` bindings, the uniform structures of a `ModulePointer` /
`ComputeModulePointer` / `MeshModulePointer`, a stackAuto shader-source slot via
[`KeyframeScope.stackAuto`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--stackauto), or a `Camera` pose via [`KeyframeScope.camera`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--camera). `capture()` reads them
all into a [`KeyframeScope.Key`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--key); invoking that `Key` writes them all back.

[`KeyframeScope.interpolate`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--interpolate) blends two keys per value type: numbers and vectors lerp, quaternions
slerp, dual quaternions and `CameraPose` sclerp, and strings / [`StackSLString`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-stackslstring) /
`SourceBackedBlock` step to the right-hand value at `t >= 1`. `remap` can re-time an individual
key's `t`. The two code types can do better than stepping when the two sources differ only in
numbers — see [`KeyframeScope.codeBlend`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--codeblend) and `keyframeCodeBlend.kt`.

Persistence goes through the [`KValue`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-kvalue) serial union, so only the types `KValue.fromAny` recognises
survive a save — numbers (a `Long` exactly), Booleans, vec2/3/4, quaternion, dual quaternion,
camera pose, string, StackSL source and source-backed block; anything else is left out and reported
on `error,keyframer`. Every `saveKey` also writes a
numbered copy into a `<file>.versions` directory with a manifest, which
[`KeyframeScope.keyVersions`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--keyversions) lists and [`KeyframeScope.loadLatestKey`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--loadlatestkey) follows. [`KeyframeScope.missingKey`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--missingkey) supplies defaults for
keys absent from an older file, optionally per schema version.

Keys render themselves as HTML for box output ([`KeyDiff`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keydiff), `diffHtml`), and
`copyUpdateCodeToClipboard` emits pasteable Kotlin — that one goes through the AWT clipboard, and on a headless JVM it logs and just returns the string.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/)

**Used in:** [Keyframes: capturing, persisting and replaying live state](../keyframer_examples.md), [Values over time: interpolants & keyframes](../interpolants_examples.md)

### NumKind { #keyframer-kt-numkind }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">NumKind</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L167)

Which Kotlin numeric type a saved number came from, so that [`KValue.toAny`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--kvalue--toany) can hand back a `Byte`/`Short`/`Int`/`Long`/`Float`/`Double` rather than always a `Double` — a uniform bound to an `Int` has to come back as an `Int`.

Constants: `BYTE`, `SHORT`, `INT`, `LONG`, `FLOAT`, `DOUBLE`.

### KValue { #keyframer-kt-kvalue }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">sealed</span> <span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L188)

The closed set of value types a [`KeyframeScope.Key`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--key) can *persist*: numbers, vec2/3/4, quaternion, dual quaternion, camera pose, string, StackSL source and source-backed block. A key in memory holds plain Kotlin values; this is the serial union they are converted to on the way to disk and back.

| <a id="keyframer-kt--kvalue--toany"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toAny</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L277) | Rebuild the live Kotlin value this entry stands for — the load half of the round trip. A [`DualQuat`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--kvalue--dualquat) and a [`CameraPoseValue`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--kvalue--cameraposevalue) are re-normalised on the way out, because a rigid transform that has drifted is a broken transform; a plain [`Quat`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--kvalue--quat) is **not** (see its own note — it may be standing in for something that is not a rotation). Numbers regain their [`NumKind`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-numkind) type, and a [`SourceBlock`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--kvalue--sourceblock) becomes a `SourceBackedBlock` that has not compiled anything yet. |

### KeyDTO { #keyframer-kt-keydto }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">KeyDTO</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">schemaVersion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Map</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L369)

| --- | --- |
| <a id="keyframer-kt--keydto--schemaversion"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">schemaVersion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | The owning scope's `schemaVersion` at the moment of saving. Nothing validates it on load: a mismatch is not an error, it only selects which [`KeyframeScope.missingKey`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--missingkey) defaults apply. |

### KeyVersionInfo { #keyframer-kt-keyversioninfo }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">KeyVersionInfo</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">index</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">timestamp</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">note</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">file</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L388)

One row of a key file's version history, as recorded in the `<file>.versions/manifest.json` that every `saveKey` appends to. [`KeyframeScope.keyVersions`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--keyversions) hands these back, sorted by [`index`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyversioninfo--index).

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="keyframer-kt--keyversioninfo--index"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">index</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Monotonic version number, starting at 0 and simply "highest so far plus one" — a save counter, not a schema version and not related to [`KeyDTO.schemaVersion`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keydto--schemaversion). |
| <a id="keyframer-kt--keyversioninfo--timestamp"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">timestamp</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | When the version was written, as an ISO-8601 `Instant.now()` string in UTC — or, for a row rebuilt from the file alone, that file's last-modified time. |
| <a id="keyframer-kt--keyversioninfo--note"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">note</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Whatever note was passed to `saveKey`, for telling two snapshots apart later. A row rebuilt from the file alone says `"(recovered from disk; the manifest row for this version was lost)"` here instead, since the real note lived only in the manifest that went missing. |
| <a id="keyframer-kt--keyversioninfo--file"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">file</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | File name inside the `.versions` directory, `"%06d.json"` of [`index`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyversioninfo--index). |

### KeyDiffKind { #keyframer-kt-keydiffkind }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">KeyDiffKind</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframer/#L1740)

How one name differs between two keys, always read left-to-right: `ADDED` means the right key has it and the left does not, `REMOVED` the other way round, `CHANGED` that both have it with unequal values. There is no "same" kind — unchanged names are left out of a diff entirely.

Constants: `ADDED`, `REMOVED`, `CHANGED`.

## keyframes.kt { #keyframes-kt }

Keyframe curves edited by hand in a box's output panel and read back by code as a number at any
time.

`keyframes(name = "x")` opens a curve editor in the box's output area and returns a
[`KeyframeEvaluator`](graphics.md#keyframes-kt-keyframeevaluator); the curve the user draws is saved on the box under that name, so it
survives a re-run and a reload. Seed a new curve with times, `(time, value)` pairs, or
[`Keyframe`](graphics.md#keyframes-kt-keyframe)s carrying their segment types:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val x = keyframes(name = "x", defaults = listOf(Vec2(0.0, 0.0), Vec2(5.0, 1.0), Vec2(10.0, 0.0)))
val now = x.evaluateValueAt(2.5)
```

The evaluator also edits the curve from code (`add`, `remove`, `edit`, `simplify`, `smooth`),
moves the editor's playhead with `setTime`, and draws reference overlays with `setOverlay`.
Tests: `KeyframeEvaluatorTest`, `KeyframerTest`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframes.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframes/)

**Used in:** [The keyframe editor: drawing a value over time](../keyframe_editor.md), [Agent transcript gallery](../agent_transcripts.md)

## PatchyWeb.kt { #patchyweb-kt }

Drive the browser build of the Patchy editor from box code: [`Box.patchyWeb`](graphics.md#patchyweb-kt--patchyweb) shows Patchy in an
output channel and returns a [`PatchyWebSession`](graphics.md#patchyweb-kt-patchywebsession).

The session's suspend methods ([`PatchyWebSession.state`](graphics.md#patchyweb-kt--patchywebsession--state), [`PatchyWebSession.script`](graphics.md#patchyweb-kt--patchywebsession--script),
[`PatchyWebSession.newDocument`](graphics.md#patchyweb-kt--patchywebsession--newdocument), [`PatchyWebSession.addLayer`](graphics.md#patchyweb-kt--patchywebsession--addlayer), [`PatchyWebSession.fillRect`](graphics.md#patchyweb-kt--patchywebsession--fillrect),
[`PatchyWebSession.undo`](graphics.md#patchyweb-kt--patchywebsession--undo), [`PatchyWebSession.redo`](graphics.md#patchyweb-kt--patchywebsession--redo)) send tool calls to the Patchy page and wait
for its replies, so call them inside `go { ... }`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/app/server/PatchyWeb.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/app/server/PatchyWeb/)

## fline_graph_connectivity.kt { #fline-graph-connectivity-kt }

Bridge from drawn geometry to the graph algorithms: turns one or more `FLine`s into a welded
point graph.

[`flineGraph`](graphics.md#fline-graph-connectivity-kt--flinegraph), or the `toFLineGraph` extensions on `FLine` and `Iterable<FLine>`, adaptively
subdivides cubics down to `cubicFlatness`, samples every node, then welds samples closer than
`epsilon` using a uniform grid plus union-find (`epsilon = 0` welds only bit-identical
positions). A welded vertex is the mean of the samples that reached it, and
[`FLineGraph.vertexSources`](graphics.md#fline-graph-connectivity-kt--flinegraph--vertexsources) records which line index and node instruction each of those samples
came from. Edges join consecutive samples, `close()` joins back to the subpath start,
self-edges are dropped and duplicates collapse to the shortest.

The result carries a `PointGraph` of `GraphEdge`s — the same types as `graph_connectivity.kt` —
so the search, spanning-tree and analysis functions there apply directly to a drawing.

## graph_connectivity.kt { #graph-connectivity-kt }

Self-contained graph / computational-geometry library over 2D and 3D point sets
(`Vec2`/`Vec3`). Every algorithm has a `vec2*` and (where meaningful) a `vec3*` entry point
returning a [`PointGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt-pointgraph); see each function's own KDoc for its definition and complexity.

Proximity / neighbourhood families: KNN ([`vec2KnnGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2knngraph)), Orthant ([`vec2OrthantGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2orthantgraph)),
Relative Neighborhood ([`vec2RelativeNeighborhoodGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2relativeneighborhoodgraph)), Gabriel ([`vec2GabrielGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2gabrielgraph)),
Beta-Skeleton ([`vec2BetaSkeleton`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2betaskeleton)), Nearest-Neighbor ([`vec2NearestNeighborGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2nearestneighborgraph)),
Minimum Spanning Tree ([`vec2MinimumSpanningTree`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2minimumspanningtree)), Maximum-Diameter/radius
([`vec2MaximumDiameterGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2maximumdiametergraph)), Maximum-Cut ([`vec2MaximumCutGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2maximumcutgraph)) and Complete
([`vec2CompleteGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2completegraph)) graphs.

JTS-backed (2D only): full Delaunay triangulation ([`vec2DelaunayGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2delaunaygraph), [`vec2DelaunayTriangles`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2delaunaytriangles)),
Urquhart ([`vec2UrquhartGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2urquhartgraph), a real Urquhart graph built by removing the longest edge of each
Delaunay triangle; there is no 3D one, because Field has no 3D Delaunay of a point set), Voronoi diagram/dual ([`vec2VoronoiDiagram`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2voronoidiagram), [`vec2VoronoiDualGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2voronoidualgraph)) and convex
hull ([`vec2ConvexHull`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2convexhull), [`vec2ConvexHullGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2convexhullgraph), [`vec2HullProjectionGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2hullprojectiongraph)).

Traversal / analysis: BFS/DFS/A* path search, [`GraphEdgeVisitState`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt-graphedgevisitstate) greedy walks and
graph-diameter path decomposition (see the search/path functions below), plus FLine rendering
integration in `fline_graph_connectivity.kt`.

Custom distance metrics: pass [`GraphConnectivityOptions.customDistanceMetric`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--graphconnectivityoptions--customdistancemetric). It is honoured by
the distance-driven algorithms (KNN, MST, RNG, Gabriel, Beta-Skeleton, Delaunay/Urquhart edge
weights, etc.). This includes [`vec2OrthantGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec2orthantgraph)/[`vec3OrthantGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt--vec3orthantgraph), whose nearest-neighbour
ranking within each orthant honours `customDistanceMetric` when supplied (Euclidean otherwise).

Smoke tests: `afield.examples.stdlib.GraphConnectivitySmokeTest` (its `runTests()` drives 35
checks, covering path search, edge-visit-state and FLine rendering as well as the core graphs).
Live rendered examples: `public/docs/graph_connectivity_examples.md`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/data/graph/graph_connectivity.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/data/graph/graph_connectivity/)

**Used in:** [Neighbours and graphs on a point cloud](../graph_connectivity_examples.md), [Points into structure — Voronoi, Apollonius, contours and clusters](../spatial_geometry_examples.md)

## PrincipalCurves.kt { #principalcurves-kt }

Elastic principal graphs: smooth curves, trees and forests fitted through a 2-D or 3-D point
cloud, as a port of ElPiGraph.

[`PrincipalCurves`](graphics.md#principalcurves-kt-principalcurves) is the entry point, and what it hands back is not a finished answer but an
optimisation state. A [`PrincipalForest`](graphics.md#principalcurves-kt-principalforest) can be fitted again, grown with more nodes under one of
the graph grammars [`Growth`](graphics.md#principalcurves-kt-growth) offers, have nodes moved and pinned, and be read back at any point
along the way: as node positions and edges, as FLines, or as a [`GeometryNetwork`](graphics.md#geometrynetwork-kt-geometrynetwork) whose channels
carry the per-node measurements. So pinning a node, replacing the points under a fitted graph, or
adding nodes to it continues from where the fit had reached rather than starting over.

[`ElasticParameters`](graphics.md#principalcurves-kt-elasticparameters) holds the energy the fit minimises, [`ElasticEnergy`](graphics.md#principalcurves-kt-elasticenergy) its value split by term,
[`PointAssignments`](graphics.md#principalcurves-kt-pointassignments) which node and edge each point ended up on, and [`NodeStatistics`](graphics.md#principalcurves-kt-nodestatistics) the spread
of the points around each node, which is what the ribbon widths are drawn from.

The solver is the optional native library `field_principal_curves`
([`PrincipalCurvesLibrary`](graphics.md#principalcurvesnative-kt-principalcurveslibrary)), so a forest holds native memory, is closed by the box's next run,
and `PrincipalCurves.isAvailable` reports whether the library loaded at all. The worked account
is `public/docs/principal_curves.md`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/curves/principal/PrincipalCurves.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/curves/principal/PrincipalCurves/)

**Used in:** [Principal curves: smooth curves through point clouds](../principal_curves.md), [Chaining the geometry extensions](../geometry_chains.md)

### ElasticParameters { #principalcurves-kt-elasticparameters }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">ElasticParameters</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">lambda</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.01</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">mu</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.1</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">trimmingRadius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">branchPenalty</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxIterations</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">30</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">eps</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1e</span><span class="p">-</span><span class="mi">3</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">candidateSample</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">5000</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">threads</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/curves/principal/PrincipalCurves/#L47)

The weights of the elastic energy and the solver's controls.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="principalcurves-kt--elasticparameters--lambda"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">lambda</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Penalises stretching — the squared length of every edge, and so total length. |
| <a id="principalcurves-kt--elasticparameters--mu"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">mu</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Penalises bending: how far each node of degree two or more sits from the mean of its neighbours. |
| <a id="principalcurves-kt--elasticparameters--trimmingradius"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">trimmingRadius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Makes the fit robust: points farther than this from every node stop pulling. 0 turns it off. |
| <a id="principalcurves-kt--elasticparameters--branchpenalty"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">branchPenalty</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Added per unit of excess degree at branch points when choosing how to grow, so a branch must reduce the energy by more than this to be kept. |
| <a id="principalcurves-kt--elasticparameters--maxiterations"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxIterations</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | EM iterations per fit. |

| <a id="principalcurves-kt--elasticparameters--candidatesample"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">candidateSample</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How many points are sampled to score growth candidates; 0 scores against all of them. |
| <a id="principalcurves-kt--elasticparameters--threads"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">threads</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Worker threads; 0 uses the hardware concurrency. |

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">PointAssignments</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">node</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">IntArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">edge</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">IntArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">t</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">distance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/curves/principal/PrincipalCurves/#L94)

## PrincipalCurvesNative.kt { #principalcurvesnative-kt }

Finding `field_principal_curves` on this machine, and calling into it once found.

[`PrincipalCurvesLibrary`](graphics.md#principalcurvesnative-kt-principalcurveslibrary) is the half that answers without loading anything: the library's file
name on this OS, the paths it is looked for in, whether one of them exists, and the Gradle task
and per-OS shell commands that build it. `NativeGeometry` registers it as a
[`NativeGeometryCapability`](graphics.md#nativegeometry-kt-nativegeometrycapability), so the welcome page's Geometry extensions panel can report on the
library whether or not it is installed. The path is resolved afresh on every read, so a library
built during a live session is picked up by the next box run.

The other half, internal to the package, binds the C ABI declared in
`native/field-principal-curves/src/field_principal_curves.h` with java.lang.foreign: one lazy
downcall handle per `fpc_` entry point, the solver's parameter struct laid out by hand with its
padding, and a 512-byte buffer that each call which can fail carries down and reads a message out
of when it reports failure. Reading the fit back out (the node and edge arrays, the energies, the
per-point assignments, the per-node statistics) takes no error buffer. The first symbol lookup
checks `fpc_abi_version` against the version this binding expects and refuses a library that
disagrees, naming the task that rebuilds it.

[`PrincipalCurves`](graphics.md#principalcurves-kt-principalcurves) is the API over it, and its only caller.

## Elements.kt { #elements-kt }

Propositions from Euclid's *Elements*, constructed with compass and straightedge in the manner of
Oliver Byrne's coloured edition (1847).

Each proposition takes geometry in and returns a [`Construction`](graphics.md#elements-kt-construction): its `Construction.result` (the
triangle, segment, line or circle the proposition asks for) and the numbered `Construction.steps`
that build it, each holding the coloured circles, lines and lettered points it draws. A
proposition that cites an earlier one carries that one's steps inside its own, prefixed with the
citation, just as the text says "by I.1".

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val c = Elements.prop1(Segment2(point2(100, 200), point2(220, 200)))
val triangle = c.result
lines(c.toFLines(width = 520.0, height = 400.0), w = 520.0, h = 400.0)  // the plate, fitted to the output
```

`toFLines(upTo = 2)` draws only the first two steps, for stepping through a proof, and
`toFLines(style = ByrneStyle.WORKING)` shows the working of the propositions this one cites.

Every step is built only from the intersections of circles and straight lines in `Euclid.kt`;
nothing is placed by a formula the proposition does not use. Where Euclid says "take any point",
the choice here is fixed, so the same input always draws the same figure; [`Elements.solutions`](graphics.md#elements-kt--elements--solutions)
enumerates the others.

## Euclid.kt { #euclid-kt }

Plane geometry in the classical sense: points, lines, rays, segments, circles, arcs and polygons,
with every pairwise intersection, closest point and distance, and the standard constructions
(perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors, circumcircles, incircles, tangents).

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val c = Circle2(point2(0, 0), 50.0)
val s = Segment2(point2(-80, 10), point2(80, 30))
val hits = s.intersect(c).points           // the two places the segment crosses the circle
val (onS, onC) = s.closestPoints(Circle2(point2(0, 200), 20.0))
lines(c.toFLine(), s.toFLine())
```

Everything is immutable and computed in `Double`. `Vec2` converts in and out with
`Vec2.toPoint2()` / `Point2.toVec2()`. Every shape implements [`Shape2`](graphics.md#euclid-kt-shape2), so `intersect`,
`closestPoints` and `distanceTo` work for any pair, including a shape with itself.

Robustness: comparisons use a distance tolerance of [`Euclid.epsilon`](graphics.md#euclid-kt--euclid--epsilon) times the size of the inputs
(one plus the largest coordinate involved, and any radius), so tangencies, touching endpoints and
collinear or co-circular overlaps are reported as such rather than lost to rounding.
Overlaps come back as shapes in `Intersection2.overlaps` (a shared piece of a line or of a
circle), not as a single point. Degenerate inputs are treated as what they are: a zero-length
segment or zero-radius circle behaves as a point.

Arcs run from `Arc2.start` through a signed `Arc2.sweep` in radians: positive is
counter-clockwise in a y-up frame (clockwise on a y-down screen).

The result of intersecting two shapes: isolated crossing or touching `points`, and any stretch the shapes share in `overlaps` (a [`Segment2`](graphics.md#euclid-kt-segment2), [`Ray2`](graphics.md#euclid-kt-ray2), [`Line2`](graphics.md#euclid-kt-line2), [`Arc2`](graphics.md#euclid-kt-arc2) or [`Circle2`](graphics.md#euclid-kt-circle2)).

## GeometryBuilder.kt { #geometrybuilder-kt }

A recipe language for triangle meshes: emit triangles through a transform stack with a current
colour and a current material, and get back a scene of named, shaded parts.

[`GeometryBuilder`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt-geometrybuilder) is the language and [`GeometryScene`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt-geometryscene) is what a recipe builds: [`GeometryPart`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt-geometrypart)s,
each an unindexed [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) with its own [`GeometryMaterial`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt-geometrymaterial) and a normal per triangle, plus the
[`GeometryView`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt-geometryview) that says how the scene asks to be shown. The usual way to run a recipe is
[`afield.graphics.three.geometry`](graphics.md#geometryview-kt--geometry), which draws it in a studio-lit `three` view in a box output,
or [`afield.graphics.three.animateGeometry`](graphics.md#geometryview-kt--animategeometry), which runs it again every frame with the recipe's
`t` moving. [`geometryScene`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt--geometryscene) builds the same scene with no viewer, for code that wants the mesh
rather than the picture.

From there, [`GeometryScene.toTriMesh`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt--geometryscene--totrimesh) joins the parts into one mesh for the rest of
`afield.geometry.mesh`, [`writeGlb`](graphics.md#geometryglb-kt--writeglb) writes a still as glTF, and [`writeGlbAnimation`](graphics.md#geometryglb-kt--writeglbanimation) records a
recipe played over time, which needs every frame to emit the same parts with the same vertex
counts.

A part's material: what [`GeometryBuilder.mat`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt--geometrybuilder--mat) set. `color` and [`emissive`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt--geometrymaterial--emissive) are sRGB, as written; [`linearColor`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt--geometrymaterial--linearcolor) and [`linearEmissive`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt--geometrymaterial--linearemissive) are what a renderer shades with.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="geometrybuilder-kt--geometrymaterial--color"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">color</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FloatArray</span></code> | The base colour as sRGB `r, g, b` in `0..1`; the part's vertex colours multiply it. |
| <a id="geometrybuilder-kt--geometrymaterial--roughness"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">roughness</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | 0 is a mirror, 1 is chalk. |
| <a id="geometrybuilder-kt--geometrymaterial--metalness"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">metalness</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | 0 is a dielectric (plastic, clay, wood), 1 is a metal. |
| <a id="geometrybuilder-kt--geometrymaterial--emissive"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">emissive</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FloatArray</span></code> | A colour the surface glows with, sRGB, scaled by [`emissiveIntensity`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt--geometrymaterial--emissiveintensity). |
| <a id="geometrybuilder-kt--geometrymaterial--emissiveintensity"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">emissiveIntensity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | How strongly [`emissive`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt--geometrymaterial--emissive) glows. 0 leaves the surface unlit from within. |
| <a id="geometrybuilder-kt--geometrymaterial--opacity"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">opacity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Below 1 is see-through. |
| <a id="geometrybuilder-kt--geometrymaterial--side"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">side</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">GeometrySide</span></code> | Which faces draw; double-sided by default, as in the toolbox. |
| <a id="geometrybuilder-kt--geometrymaterial--wireframe"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">wireframe</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Draw the triangle edges over the surface. |

## GeometryGlb.kt { #geometryglb-kt }

The exit from [`GeometryBuilder`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt-geometrybuilder) to a file every other tool can open.

A [`GeometryScene`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt-geometryscene) becomes one `.glb` with a node per part; a recipe whose vertices move becomes an
animated one. [`toGlb`](graphics.md#geometryglb-kt--toglb) returns the bytes and [`writeGlb`](graphics.md#geometryglb-kt--writeglb) puts them in a file; [`geometryAnimationGlb`](graphics.md#geometryglb-kt--geometryanimationglb)
and [`writeGlbAnimation`](graphics.md#geometryglb-kt--writeglbanimation) do the same for a run of frames. Both writers compress by default, through
[`Gltfpack`](graphics.md#gltfpack-kt-gltfpack) when it is installed.

The animation is stored as morph targets rather than a skeleton: one target per frame after the
first, played by a weights animation. That needs no rig, which is what makes it open anywhere, and
it is why every frame must emit the same parts with the same vertex counts. A morph target is a
vertex-for-vertex delta against frame 0, so there is nowhere to put a triangle that appeared
halfway through.

A part carries its positions, face normals, linear vertex colours and a metallic-roughness material
built from its [`GeometryMaterial`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt-geometrymaterial). `KHR_materials_emissive_strength` is declared only when some
channel of a part's emissive colour, times its intensity, exceeds 1.

## Gltfpack.kt { #gltfpack-kt }

The optional gltfpack step between a GLB and the disk.

Field writes binary glTF in two places, and both offer the bytes here first: [`writeGlb`](graphics.md#geometryglb-kt--writeglb), for a
geometry recipe, and the three viewer's **Export GLB**, which posts to `POST /three-gltfpack`. The
object below is all there is to it: where to find a gltfpack, whether there is one, and two
ways to run it.

Nothing breaks without the tool. [`compressIfSmaller`](graphics.md#gltfpack-kt--gltfpack--compressifsmaller), which the file writers use, returns the GLB
it was handed when gltfpack is missing, fails, or saves nothing, and the route answers 404 so the
viewer keeps its uncompressed export. [`compress`](graphics.md#gltfpack-kt--gltfpack--compress) is the strict version, for a caller that would
rather hear about the failure.

## mesh.kt { #mesh-kt }

[`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) — the CPU triangle mesh Field's 3D geometry family is built on, plus the builder that
makes one and the whole-mesh transforms that move one around.

A [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) is *not* a renderer buffer (that is Field 4's
[`afield.graphics.render.Mesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-src-jvmmain-kotlin-afield-graphics-render-mesh)) and *not* a graph of vertex objects. It is flat
`FloatArray` attribute storage plus an `IntArray` of triangle indices: the layout every algorithm
in this family wants, the layout a GPU upload wants, and cheap to copy. Positions are required;
normals, uvs and per-vertex colours are optional and either absent or complete.

The reason the vertices are floats-in-an-array rather than `List<Vec3>` is that [`Vec3`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec3) is a
*mutable* `Vector3f`. A mesh holding shared mutable vectors is a mesh where `mesh.position(0).y +=
1` silently edits the mesh — or worse, edits three triangles because the vector was shared. So
every accessor here ([`position`](graphics.md#mesh-kt--trimesh--position), [`normal`](graphics.md#mesh-kt--trimesh--normal), [`uv`](graphics.md#mesh-kt--trimesh--uv), [`color`](graphics.md#mesh-kt--trimesh--color)) returns a **fresh** vector you own, and
the `…Into` variants let a hot loop reuse one.

### The family

| file | what it adds |
|---|---|
| `mesh.kt` | this: the type, [`TriMeshBuilder`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimeshbuilder) / [`triMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt--trimesh), transforms, concatenation |
| `mesh_topology.kt` | [`MeshTopology`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt-meshtopology) — adjacency, boundary loops, components, manifoldness, Euler characteristic / genus, [`TriMesh.weld`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt--weld), [`TriMesh.fixWinding`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt--fixwinding) |
| `mesh_generate.kt` | [`boxMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--boxmesh), [`uvSphereMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--uvspheremesh), [`icosphereMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--icospheremesh), [`torusMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--torusmesh), [`cylinderMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--cylindermesh), [`extrudeMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--extrudemesh), [`revolveMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--revolvemesh), `tubeMesh`, [`heightfieldMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--heightfieldmesh), [`reliefMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--reliefmesh) |
| `mesh_sdf.kt` | [`ScalarField3D`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d), the SDF primitives / combinators, and [`marchingCubes`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt--marchingcubes) |
| `mesh_process.kt` | [`TriMesh.loopSubdivide`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--loopsubdivide), [`TriMesh.laplacianSmooth`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--laplaciansmooth), [`TriMesh.taubinSmooth`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--taubinsmooth), [`TriMesh.withVertexNormals`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--withvertexnormals), [`TriMesh.decimate`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--decimate) |
| `mesh_measure.kt` | [`TriMesh.surfaceArea`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt--surfacearea), [`TriMesh.signedVolume`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt--signedvolume), curvature, [`MeshBvh`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt-meshbvh) (rays, closest point, inside test) |
| `mesh_io.kt` | OBJ and STL, read and write |
| `mesh_field.kt` | the bridges: [`TriMesh.toFLines`](graphics.md#mesh-field-kt--toflines), [`VoronoiCell3.toTriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-field-kt--totrimesh), `Box.showMesh` |

### Conventions

- **Winding is counter-clockwise seen from outside**, so [`faceNormal`](graphics.md#mesh-kt--trimesh--facenormal) points out of a closed
  solid and [`signedVolume`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt--signedvolume) of one is positive. Everything in the family agrees on this, and
  [`TriMesh.fixWinding`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt--fixwinding) repairs a mesh that does not.
- Nothing here mutates: every operation returns a new [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh). The arrays are `val`s and are
  not copied on construction, so do not hand a builder's scratch array to the constructor and
  then keep writing to it — use [`TriMeshBuilder.build`](graphics.md#mesh-kt--trimeshbuilder--build).
- No dependencies beyond the Kotlin stdlib and Field's own generated linalg. No GPU, no AWT, no
  model-format libraries.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val ball = icosphereMesh(subdivisions = 3, radius = 1.0)
val shell = ball.scaled(1.0, 0.6, 1.0).withVertexNormals()
println("${shell.triangleCount} tris, volume ${shell.signedVolume()}")
display(shell.toFLines())            // draw its wireframe
```

## mesh_field.kt { #mesh-field-kt }

What makes the mesh family *Field's* rather than a generic geometry library: the bridges out of
[`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) and into the things Field already draws, renders and displays.

Four bridges:

 1. **Mesh → [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline).** [`TriMesh.toFLines`](graphics.md#mesh-field-kt--toflines) gives you the wireframe, the silhouette-free edge set,
    the open boundary loops or the normals as drawable lines, so a marched iso-surface goes
    straight into the same drawing / animation / export machinery as anything hand-drawn — and is
    visible in a Field document *today*, with no renderer set up.
 2. **Mesh → pixels.** [`TriMesh.renderPng`](graphics.md#mesh-field-kt--renderpng) rasterises the mesh — perspective, z-buffer,
    perspective-correct attributes, two-light lambert, depth-tested wireframe — by packing it for
    [`VisionGeometryPreview`](graphics.md#visiongeometrypreview-kt-visiongeometrypreview)'s renderer, which already had all of that. [`Box.showMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-field-kt--showmesh) pushes the
    result to a box output and [`TriMesh.toHTML`](graphics.md#mesh-kt--trimesh--tohtml) uses it for the inline value thumbnail, so
    evaluating a mesh in a box shows the shape.
 3. **3D Voronoi → mesh.** [`VoronoiCell3.toTriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-field-kt--totrimesh) and [`VoronoiLattice.toTriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-field-kt--totrimesh) triangulate the
    polygonal cells `voronoi.kt` already computes by half-space clipping. Field could compute a 3D
    Voronoi diagram and not turn it into geometry; now it can.
 4. **Field lines → mesh.** [`tubeMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-field-kt--tubemesh) on an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline), so a drawn stroke becomes a solid.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val cells = voronoi3d(List(24) { vec(rand(-1, 1), rand(-1, 1), rand(-1, 1)) })
val solid = cells.toTriMesh(shrink = 0.9)   // every cell, shrunk toward its own site
showMesh(solid, caption = "${solid.triangleCount} triangles from 24 sites")
```

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_field.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_field/)

**Used in:** [Geometry from disk](../geometry_from_disk.md), [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md), [Three.js scenes with `three { … }`](../three_output.md)

## mesh_generate.kt { #mesh-generate-kt }

Where a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) comes from: the primitives ([`boxMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--boxmesh), [`uvSphereMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--uvspheremesh), [`icosphereMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--icospheremesh),
[`torusMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--torusmesh), [`cylinderMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--cylindermesh), [`coneMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--conemesh), [`capsuleMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--capsulemesh), the five platonics) and the *derived*
generators that build one out of something you already have ([`extrudeMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--extrudemesh), [`revolveMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--revolvemesh),
[`tubeMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--tubemesh), [`heightfieldMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--heightfieldmesh), [`reliefMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--reliefmesh), [`polygonMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--polygonmesh)).

### Welding and normals

**Everything here is welded and watertight where it can be.** A generator returns the minimal
vertex set, so [`MeshTopology.eulerCharacteristic`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt--meshtopology--eulercharacteristic) of a box, a sphere, a cone or a capped cylinder
is exactly `2`, of a torus exactly `0`, and [`TriMesh.isWatertight`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt--iswatertight) is true. The volume, curvature
and decimation code all need that; a mesh that merely renders is not enough for any of them.

**Normals are only attached where they are unambiguous.** A sphere, icosphere, torus and capsule
are smooth everywhere, so they carry per-vertex normals. A box, cylinder, cone, extrusion or
platonic solid has *creases*: the two faces meeting at an edge want different normals at the same
vertex, and you cannot have both a shared vertex and two normals. Duplicating the vertex would
break watertightness and averaging across the crease would round it off, so these ship with
**no** normals and you pick:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
boxMesh().flatShaded()          // one normal per triangle: hard edges, 3 verts per tri
boxMesh().shadedNormals(35.0)   // split only where faces disagree by > 35 degrees
boxMesh().withVertexNormals()   // one averaged normal per shared vertex: rounded corners
```

The preview / render bridges in `mesh_field.kt` call [`TriMesh.shadedNormals`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--shadednormals) for you when a mesh
arrives without normals, so a bare `boxMesh()` still looks like a box.

### Orientation

`+y` is up, matching the preview camera. Radial generators sweep `x = r cos u, z = -r sin u`, which
is the handedness that makes counter-clockwise-from-outside windings come out right. [`planeMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--planemesh)
and [`polygonMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--polygonmesh) live in the `xy` plane facing `+z`; [`heightfieldMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--heightfieldmesh) lives in the `xz` plane
facing `+y`: a plane is a wall and a heightfield is a landscape.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_generate.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_generate/)

**Used in:** [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md), [Three.js scenes with `three { … }`](../three_output.md), [A photograph, closed and mounted](../chain_photo_to_solid.md)

Which axis [`revolveMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-generate-kt--revolvemesh) sweeps a `(radius, height)` profile around.

Constants: `Y`, `Z`.

## mesh_io.kt { #mesh-io-kt }

Getting a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) in and out of the two formats every 3D tool on the machine can already read:
**OBJ** (text, indexed, carries normals and uvs) and **STL** (ASCII or binary, triangle soup, the
lingua franca of 3D printing).

Both directions, in pure Kotlin, and what each format carries is different:

 - [`TriMesh.toObj`](graphics.md#mesh-io-kt--toobj) / [`objToTriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-io-kt--objtotrimesh) keep the index structure, so a watertight mesh round-trips as a
   watertight mesh. Normals and uvs survive; per-vertex colours do not (OBJ has no standard for
   them). Faces with more than three corners are fan-triangulated on read, so a quad-mesh OBJ from
   a modeller loads fine.
 - [`TriMesh.toStlAscii`](graphics.md#mesh-io-kt--tostlascii) / [`TriMesh.toStlBinary`](graphics.md#mesh-io-kt--tostlbinary) / [`stlToTriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-io-kt--stltotrimesh) are *triangle soup*, because STL
   has no vertex sharing at all: a mesh written to STL and read back has `3 * triangleCount`
   vertices and reports every edge as a boundary. `stlToTriMesh(bytes).weld()` gives you the mesh
   back. The read path does not weld for you, because welding needs a tolerance, and a tolerance
   guessed on your behalf is what loses a hairline feature.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val mesh = icosphereMesh(3)
File("/tmp/ball.obj").writeText(mesh.toObj())
File("/tmp/ball.stl").writeBytes(mesh.toStlBinary())
val back = objToTriMesh(File("/tmp/ball.obj").readText())
```

These two formats, and no others — see [`meshFromFile`](graphics.md#mesh-io-kt--meshfromfile) for where to go for PLY, glTF and GLB, and
`public/docs/geometry_from_disk.md` for the measured account of what each format loses.

## mesh_measure.kt { #mesh-measure-kt }

Asking a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) questions: how big is it, where is its middle, how curved is it — and, through
[`MeshBvh`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt-meshbvh), what does this ray hit, what is the nearest point on the surface, and is this point
inside.

The measurements ([`TriMesh.surfaceArea`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt--surfacearea), [`TriMesh.signedVolume`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt--signedvolume), [`TriMesh.centroid`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt--centroid)) are exact for
the polyhedron, computed in double precision, and cheap. [`TriMesh.signedVolume`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt--signedvolume) is the one to keep
in mind: it is the divergence-theorem tetrahedron sum, so it is exact for any closed mesh, it is
**positive for outward winding and negative for inward**, and comparing it against an analytic
answer (`4/3 π` for a marched unit sphere) is the single most informative test a geometry pipeline
can have.

The curvatures are the standard discrete operators — angle deficit for Gaussian, the
cotangent-Laplacian's magnitude for mean, both divided by the mixed Voronoi area. They satisfy
Gauss-Bonnet (`Σ K_v A_v = 2π χ`) to float precision on a closed mesh, which is how they are tested.

[`MeshBvh`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt-meshbvh) exists because the useful queries are all `O(n)` without it and `O(log n)` with it. It is
a plain median-split bounding-volume hierarchy over triangles, built once, then:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val bvh = mesh.bvh()
bvh.raycast(vec(0, 0, -5), vec(0, 0, 1))?.let { println("hit at ${it.point}") }
bvh.closestPoint(vec(2, 0, 0))                 // nearest surface point + distance
bvh.contains(vec(0, 0, 0))                     // inside test, by parity of crossings
bvh.signedDistance(vec(0.5f, 0, 0))            // negative inside
```

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_measure.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_measure/)

**Used in:** [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md), [Three.js scenes with `three { … }`](../three_output.md)

## mesh_process.kt { #mesh-process-kt }

Changing a mesh's *sampling* without changing the shape it stands for: normals, subdivision,
smoothing and decimation.

These are the four operations that make the difference between a mesh you generated and a mesh you
can use. In rough order of how often you will reach for them:

 - [`TriMesh.withVertexNormals`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--withvertexnormals) / [`TriMesh.flatShaded`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--flatshaded) / [`TriMesh.shadedNormals`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--shadednormals) — shading.
   [`TriMesh.shadedNormals`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--shadednormals) splits a vertex only where the faces meeting there genuinely
   disagree, so a cylinder comes out smooth around its side and hard at its rim, from one call.
 - [`TriMesh.loopSubdivide`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--loopsubdivide) — four triangles for one, converging on the Loop limit surface. Refines
   *and* smooths, and preserves the Euler characteristic exactly.
 - [`TriMesh.laplacianSmooth`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--laplaciansmooth) / [`TriMesh.taubinSmooth`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--taubinsmooth) — noise removal. Laplacian shrinks the shape
   (that is what a diffusion does); Taubin's λ/μ pair alternates a shrink with an expand and so
   does not, which is why it is the one to default to. Both offer cotangent weights, which are
   scale- and shape-independent where the uniform ones are not.
 - [`TriMesh.decimate`](graphics.md#mesh-process-kt--decimate) — quadric error metric edge collapse down to a triangle budget. The dual of
   subdivision, and the one that has to work hardest: it maintains per-vertex quadrics, a
   cost-ordered queue with lazy invalidation, the link condition (so a collapse cannot make the
   mesh non-manifold) and a normal-flip veto (so it cannot turn the mesh inside out locally).

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val fine = icosphereMesh(4)                       // 5120 triangles
val coarse = fine.decimate(400)                   // 400, and still a sphere
val smooth = coarse.taubinSmooth(iterations = 20) // volume preserved to within ~1%
```

Catmull-Clark is absent: it is a quad scheme, [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) is triangles-only, and
running it on a triangulated quad mesh gives a different (worse) surface than running it on the
quads. Loop is the triangle scheme, and it is the one here.

## mesh_repair.kt { #mesh-repair-kt }

Why a mesh is not a solid, and what can be done about it — the paved road between "I loaded a file"
and `toSolid()`.

[`TriMesh.diagnose`](graphics.md#mesh-repair-kt--diagnose) answers *why*, in terms a person can act on: which loops are open and how big,
which edges have the wrong number of faces, which faces are duplicated, whether the winding is
consistent and whether it points out. [`TriMesh.repairToSolid`](graphics.md#mesh-repair-kt--repairtosolid) then attempts the fixes in a
defensible order and hands back a [`MeshRepairResult`](graphics.md#mesh-repair-kt-meshrepairresult) that says **what it did and what it could
not do** — a repair that silently drops half your model is worse than one that refuses, so nothing
here returns a bare mesh.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val mesh = meshFromAnyFile("scan.glb")
println(mesh.diagnose().report())     // why it is not a solid, worst first
val fixed = mesh.repairToSolid()
println(fixed.report())               // what was done, and what was not
if (fixed.isSolid) display(fixed.mesh.toSolid() - drill)
```

### What actually blocks `toSolid`

Every severity below was established by feeding Manifold a mesh damaged in exactly one named way
(see `MeshDamage` in the tests) and asking whether it accepted the result. Three of the answers
change how a diagnosis should be read:

 - **A mesh with several disjoint components is fine.** Manifold accepts it and reports the sum of
   the volumes. "Split into parts" is not a defect; it is `MeshDefectKind.MULTIPLE_COMPONENTS`, and
   it is informational.
 - **Zero-area triangles are fine.** Manifold accepts them and the volume is unchanged.
 - **An inside-out mesh is fine, and that is the dangerous one.** Manifold accepts a consistently
   but inwardly wound closed surface and reports a **negative volume** — so the boolean you do next
   silently computes the wrong thing rather than throwing (`toSolid()` refuses it on Manifold's
   behalf when the total comes out negative). That is
   `MeshDefectKind.INVERTED_ORIENTATION`, and it is the reason this file reports severity
   `MeshDefectSeverity.SUSPICIOUS` at all instead of just a pass/fail.

What Manifold genuinely rejects is a short list: a non-finite position, an edge with other than two
incident faces (which a duplicated face also produces, on all three of its edges), an open boundary,
and inconsistent winding.

### Which repair handles which defect

[`TriMesh.repairToSolid`](graphics.md#mesh-repair-kt--repairtosolid) runs [`TriMesh.repaired`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt--repaired) first —
`weld → removeDegenerateTriangles → removeUnusedVertices → fixWinding` — which handles an
unwelded seam (welding is what turns an STL's pile of triangles into a surface) and inconsistent
winding. Of the twelve damaged meshes in `MeshRepairTest`'s table that Manifold rejects, that
alone fixes six.

Two families of damage need the repairs in this file:

 1. **Open boundaries** — [`fillHoles`](graphics.md#mesh-repair-kt--fillholes).
 2. **Non-manifold edges** — [`removeDuplicateFaces`](graphics.md#mesh-repair-kt--removeduplicatefaces) for a duplicated face,
    [`removeNonManifoldFins`](graphics.md#mesh-repair-kt--removenonmanifoldfins) for a dangling fin.

### MeshDefectSeverity { #mesh-repair-kt-meshdefectseverity }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">MeshDefectSeverity</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_repair/#L134)

How much a defect matters — the distinction between "Manifold will refuse this" and "Manifold will accept this and give you a wrong answer without saying so".

Constants: `BLOCKING`, `SUSPICIOUS`, `INFORMATIONAL`.

### MeshDefectKind { #mesh-repair-kt-meshdefectkind }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">MeshDefectKind</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_repair/#L153)

The kinds of thing that can be wrong with a mesh, **declared in the order worth fixing them**.

Constants: `NON_FINITE_POSITION`, `UNWELDED_VERTICES`, `DEGENERATE_FACE`, `DUPLICATE_FACE`, `NON_MANIFOLD_EDGE`, `NON_MANIFOLD_VERTEX`, `OPEN_BOUNDARY`, `UNWALKABLE_BOUNDARY`, `INCONSISTENT_WINDING`, `INVERTED_ORIENTATION`, `MULTIPLE_COMPONENTS`, `UNREFERENCED_VERTEX`.

## mesh_sdf.kt { #mesh-sdf-kt }

Modelling with functions: a [`ScalarField3D`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d) is `(Vec3) -> Float`, the signed-distance primitives
and combinators that let you write a shape as an expression, and [`marchingCubes`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt--marchingcubes), which turns any
such expression into a watertight [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh).

This is the 3D counterpart of `contours.kt`. There, a [`ScalarField2D`](graphics.md#contours-kt-scalarfield2d) is marched by
[`generateIsoContours`](graphics.md#contours-kt--generateisocontours) into `FLine` polylines; here a [`ScalarField3D`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d) is marched into triangles.
The two files are parallel, and reading the 2D one first is the fastest way to
understand this one.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val body = sdfSmoothUnion(
    sdfSphere(0.8),
    sdfBox(vec(1.4, 0.25, 0.25)),
    k = 0.25,
)
val drilled = sdfSubtract(body, sdfCylinder(0.22, 3.0))
val mesh = marchingCubes(drilled, boundsOf(vec(-1.6, -1.6, -1.6), vec(1.6, 1.6, 1.6)), resolution = 96)
println("${mesh.triangleCount} tris, watertight ${mesh.isWatertight()}")
```

### What [`marchingCubes`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt--marchingcubes) here actually does

It is a **topologically consistent** marching cubes, not the 1987 lookup table:

 - The field is sampled once per grid corner, so the cost is `(n+1)^3` evaluations however many
   triangles come out.
 - Every crossing sits on a grid *edge*, and edges are keyed globally, so a vertex is created once
   and **shared** by all the cubes that touch it. That is what makes the output watertight
   (`χ = 2` for a marched sphere) rather than a soup of unwelded triangles needing [`TriMesh.weld`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt--weld).
 - Instead of a 256-entry triangle table, each cube's crossings are joined into closed loops on the
   cube's own boundary and each loop is triangulated. On a face where four edges cross — the
   ambiguous case the classic table resolves arbitrarily — the pairing is chosen by the
   **asymptotic decider** (the sign of the bilinear saddle value). Because that decision is a pure
   function of the face's four corner values, the two cubes sharing the face always agree, which is
   exactly the property the classic table lacks and the reason plain marching cubes leaks.
 - Winding comes from the field itself: each triangle is oriented against the gradient of the
   trilinear interpolant, so normals point toward increasing field value — outward, for the
   signed-distance convention where outside is positive.

Known limits, stated rather than hidden: a cube containing two separate sheets of surface can be
oriented from one gradient and get the other sheet backwards, so a field with structure much finer
than the grid wants more resolution; and the loop triangulation reproduces the *sign pattern*
faithfully but is not guaranteed to reproduce the trilinear interpolant's exact topology in the
rarest configurations.

### A note on mutation

[`Vec3`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec3) is mutable and the march reuses one sample vector for speed. A [`ScalarField3D`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d) must
therefore **read** the vector it is handed and not write to it. Every combinator below copies
before transforming, so composing them is safe; a hand-written field that does `p.mul(2f)` will
corrupt the march.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_sdf.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/mesh/mesh_sdf/)

**Used in:** [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md), [Three.js scenes with `three { … }`](../three_output.md), [Typography as geometry — a string becomes contours](../typography_examples.md)

## mesh_topology.kt { #mesh-topology-kt }

What a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) *is*, as opposed to where it is: adjacency, boundaries, components,
manifoldness, orientation, and the Euler characteristic those add up to — plus the repairs
([`TriMesh.weld`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt--weld), [`TriMesh.fixWinding`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt--fixwinding), [`TriMesh.removeDegenerateTriangles`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt--removedegeneratetriangles)) that turn a mesh
which fails those checks into one that passes.

[`MeshTopology`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt-meshtopology) is a **derived, cached** view: building one costs one pass over the triangles, and
everything after that is a lookup. Build it once and ask it many questions; the convenience
properties on [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh) ([`TriMesh.isWatertight`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt--iswatertight) and friends) build a throwaway one each time,
which is fine interactively and wasteful in a loop.

The invariant the tests lean on: for a closed orientable surface, `V - E + F = 2 - 2g`. So a cube,
a sphere and an icosphere all report [`MeshTopology.eulerCharacteristic`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt--meshtopology--eulercharacteristic) `2` and
[`MeshTopology.genus`](graphics.md#mesh-topology-kt--meshtopology--genus) `0`, a torus reports `0` and `1`, and a two-holed shape reports `-2` and `2`.
A duplicated seam, a missing cap and an unwelded march all change that number, so it is the
cheapest single check on a generator.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val t = torusMesh(48, 24)
val topo = t.topology()
println("${topo.eulerCharacteristic} χ, genus ${topo.genus}, watertight ${topo.isWatertight}")
// 0 χ, genus 1, watertight true
```

**Used in:** [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md), [Geometry from disk](../geometry_from_disk.md), [Solids that cannot fail: Manifold in Field](../manifold.md)

## pointing_mesh.kt { #pointing-mesh-kt }

Pointing a [`Ray`](graphics.md#pointing-kt-ray) at a mesh and asking what it hits.

One extension lives here, because the two halves of this question are in different packages.
Rays are made in `afield.graphics.interaction`: [`Pointer`](graphics.md#pointing-pointer-kt-pointer) is what a person points with, and the
unprojection behind [`RayCamera`](graphics.md#pointing-kt-raycamera) turns the pixel or the pose it reports into a [`Ray`](graphics.md#pointing-kt-ray). The
structure that answers which triangle a ray meets is [`MeshBvh`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt-meshbvh), which belongs with the meshes and
takes an origin and a direction as two separate `Vec3` arguments. The overload below unpacks a
[`Ray`](graphics.md#pointing-kt-ray) into them.

Two things follow from that hop and are easier to state here than at the call site. A [`Ray`](graphics.md#pointing-kt-ray)
normalises its direction when it is constructed, so the distance in the [`RayHit`](graphics.md#mesh-measure-kt-rayhit) that comes back
is in world units however the caller built the ray. And a [`Ray`](graphics.md#pointing-kt-ray) holds its origin and direction in
double precision while `Vec3` is float, so both narrow at this call before the intersection test
widens them again and runs in double.

For ray to *named part* rather than ray to triangle, see [`PickScene`](graphics.md#pointing-pick-kt-pickscene).

## GeometryNetwork.kt { #geometrynetwork-kt }

The answer Field's geometry-extraction modules share: named points, the curves that join them,
and typed channels holding whatever each module measured along the way.

[`MorseSmale`](graphics.md#morsesmale-kt-morsesmale), [`Polyvector`](graphics.md#polyvector-kt-polyvector), [`PrincipalCurves`](graphics.md#principalcurves-kt-principalcurves), [`Mapper`](graphics.md#mapper-kt-mapper), [`ContourTrees`](graphics.md#contourtrees-kt-contourtrees), [`VectorFieldTopology`](graphics.md#vectorfieldtopology-kt-vectorfieldtopology)
and the feature tracker all return a [`GeometryNetwork`](graphics.md#geometrynetwork-kt-geometrynetwork), so code that filters, counts or draws
one does not need to know which of them produced it, and `metadata` says which did.

The three parts divide the work. [`GeometryNodes`](graphics.md#geometrynetwork-kt-geometrynodes) holds the points a module considers meaningful,
each under an identity it keeps stable across recomputation where it can, so a downstream object
stays attached to the same feature. A [`GeometryCurve`](graphics.md#geometrynetwork-kt-geometrycurve) is a polyline that names the nodes at its
ends, which is why two curves crossing at a position are still unconnected: connectivity is
stated, never inferred from proximity. A [`Channel`](graphics.md#geometrynetwork-kt-channel) packs a scalar, a direction or a covariance
for every node or every vertex into one array, so a large network costs no per-element objects.

[`GeometryNetwork.toFLines`](graphics.md#geometrynetwork-kt--geometrynetwork--toflines) turns a network into drawable lines and leaves the network itself on
each of them, so whatever the lines cannot carry is still reachable from them.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/network/GeometryNetwork.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/network/GeometryNetwork/)

## NativeGeometry.kt { #nativegeometry-kt }

Which of Field's optional native geometry libraries are installed, and what the welcome page
says about the rest.

Morse–Smale complexes, principal curves and polyvector vectorization each need a native library
that Field does not build by default. [`NativeGeometry`](graphics.md#nativegeometry-kt-nativegeometry) holds one [`NativeGeometryCapability`](graphics.md#nativegeometry-kt-nativegeometrycapability) per
module, registered by that module's own library object, and answers [`NativeGeometry.available`](graphics.md#nativegeometry-kt--nativegeometry--available)
and [`NativeGeometry.describe`](graphics.md#nativegeometry-kt--nativegeometry--describe) without loading any of them, so asking never fails. Field runs
without any of them, and calling into one that is absent throws an error naming the Gradle task
that builds it.

[`NativeGeometry.status`](graphics.md#nativegeometry-kt--nativegeometry--status) reports every module as a [`NativeGeometryStatus`](graphics.md#nativegeometry-kt-nativegeometrystatus), which
`GET /api/native-geometry-status` serves to the welcome page's Geometry extensions panel:
whether the library loaded, its docs page, its build task, and the shell commands that install
its prerequisites on macOS, Linux and Windows.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/network/NativeGeometry.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/network/NativeGeometry/)
