## FLine.kt { #fline-kt }

[`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) is Field's drawn path: a list of move, line and cubic segments with per-node
and per-line properties, built with `moveTo` / `lineTo` / `cubicTo` and drawn by `Box.lines(...)`.

Also here are the operators that translate, scale and rotate a `List<FLine>` (or a map of
them) as a group.

## FLineEditing.kt { #flineediting-kt }

The server side of an editable `Box.lines(..., editable = true)` drawing: an edit session per
widget that applies the browser's point drags and new strokes to the live [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline)s.

`Box.lines` returns an [`EditableFLineViewState`](graphics.md#flineediting-kt-editableflineviewstate) when `editable = true` (null otherwise); call
[`EditableFLineViewState.currentLines`](graphics.md#flineediting-kt--editableflineviewstate--currentlines) to read the lines as they are after the user's edits.

## FLineExact.kt { #flineexact-kt }

Curve-preserving boolean operations and cubic offsets for [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline), in the manner of Paper.js.

Booleans: every segment of both operands is cut at its exact crossings with every other segment
(Bézier–Bézier by bounding-box subdivision refined by Newton, plus endpoint-on-curve projection
for coincident edges and T-junctions). Each resulting piece is a sub-curve of an original
segment, so cubics stay cubics and straight segments stay [`FLine.LineTo`](graphics.md#fline-kt--fline--lineto). A piece is kept when
the operation's answer differs a hair to its left and to its right (winding numbers of both
operands, non-zero rule), oriented with the result on its left, and the kept pieces are chained
into closed contours. The result is checked against the java.awt.geom.Area answer by area; on
any failure the Area answer is returned instead (`FLineBooleanResult.exact` says which).

Offsets: each cubic is approximated by a cubic whose end tangents are the original's and whose
handle lengths are fitted to the true offset at the midpoint (Tiller–Hanson curvature scaling
where that fit is ill-conditioned), subdivided until the sampled error is within tolerance.
Corners get round, miter or bevel joins; closed results are resolved through the boolean engine
with a positive-winding rule, which removes the swallowtails at concave corners.

All arithmetic is in doubles over the xy plane; z is dropped.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/FLineExact.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/FLineExact/)

## FLineGaussianProcess.kt { #flinegaussianprocess-kt }

Gaussian-process curves: fit a GP to an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) or to points, then draw its mean, samples and uncertainty as lines.

[`FLine.gaussianProcess`](graphics.md#flinegaussianprocess-kt--gaussianprocess) and [`gpCurve`](graphics.md#flinegaussianprocess-kt--gpcurve) return an [`FLineGaussianProcess`](graphics.md#flinegaussianprocess-kt-flinegaussianprocess), which gives the mean,
covariance, velocity and moving frames along the curve; [`FLineGaussianProcess.posterior`](graphics.md#flinegaussianprocess-kt--flinegaussianprocess--posterior) gives an
[`FLineGpJoint`](graphics.md#flinegaussianprocess-kt-flinegpjoint) for coherent samples. For scalar GPs, [`meanFLine`](graphics.md#flinegaussianprocess-kt--meanfline), [`sampleFLine`](graphics.md#flinegaussianprocess-kt--samplefline) and
[`intervalFLines`](graphics.md#flinegaussianprocess-kt--intervalflines) turn a joint into plottable lines. Tests: `FLineGaussianProcessTest`,
`FLineGpGeometryTest`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/FLineGaussianProcess.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/FLineGaussianProcess/)

| <a id="flinegaussianprocess-kt--flinegaussianprocess--frames"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">frames</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">parameters</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">step</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">defaultStep</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">parameters</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">GpCurveFrame</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/FLineGaussianProcess/#L96) | A moving frame along the mean curve, with how uncertain its tangent is. The normal of a planar curve is the tangent turned a quarter to the left; a spatial curve's is the Frenet normal, taken from the mean velocity `step` either side, and is null where the curve is straight. |
| <a id="flinegaussianprocess-kt--flinegaussianprocess--curvature"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">curvature</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">parameters</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">samples</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">256</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0L</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">step</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">defaultStep</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">parameters</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">GpCurvature</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/FLineGaussianProcess/#L138) | Curvature with uncertainty, by drawing `samples` whole velocity fields and differencing each `step` either side. [`GpCurvature.ofMean`](graphics.md#flinegaussianprocess-kt--gpcurvature--ofmean) is the curvature of the mean curve, which is not the mean curvature of the draws: wiggly draws curve more than their average does. Planar curvature is signed (positive turns left); spatial curvature is unsigned. Costs a joint of 3 × parameters × dimensions values, so keep parameters to a few hundred. `step` defaults to a thousandth of the parameter span (at least 0.001); much smaller and the sampler can no longer resolve the difference between neighbouring velocities, understating the uncertainty. The same floor applies to a curve pinned so tightly that its velocity variance nears the [`GpNumerics`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt-gpnumerics) tolerances; if [`GpCurvature.std`](graphics.md#flinegaussianprocess-kt--gpcurvature--std) changes with `step`, it is at that floor. |

## FLineGeometry.kt { #flinegeometry-kt }

Comprehensive computational geometry utilities for FLine operations implemented as extension functions.
Provides transformations, projections, intersections, decompositions, curvature analyses,
tangents, osculating planes, offsets, and a rich set of 2D and 3D geometric algorithms.

Functions that return new FLine instances use a "by" prefix to indicate non-mutating operations:
- `byWaving()` instead of `wave()`
- `byOffsetting()` instead of `offset()`

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/FLineGeometry.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/FLineGeometry/)

**Used in:** [FLine examples (Field graphics)](../fline_examples.md), [Vectorizing line drawings: polyvector fields](../polyvector.md), [Euclid's Elements](../euclid_elements.md)

## FLineGeometrySmile.kt { #flinegeometrysmile-kt }

Resamples an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) through a fitted curve: [`bySmileSplineInterpolating`](graphics.md#flinegeometrysmile-kt--bysmilesplineinterpolating) (Smile cubic spline),
[`bySmileGaussianProcessInterpolating`](graphics.md#flinegeometrysmile-kt--bysmilegaussianprocessinterpolating) (Gaussian process) and [`byAkimaInterpolating`](graphics.md#flinegeometrysmile-kt--byakimainterpolating).

Each one samples the line, fits X, Y and Z separately against normalised arc length, and returns
a new line of `samples` points, mixed with the original by `dryWet`.

## FLineHyperbezier.kt { #flinehyperbezier-kt }

Fits ordinary cubics to [`Hyperbezier`](graphics.md#hyperbezier-kt-hyperbezier) curves, so that family is usable everywhere an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline)
already accepts a cubic.

A hyperbezier is specified exactly the way a cubic Bezier is: a start, two control points, an end.
It is a different curve through that polygon, one whose curvature varies smoothly, and it is an
exact circular arc or Euler spiral when the arms are "circle-like" (see [`circleArm`](graphics.md#hyperbezier-kt--circlearm)). Push the
arms out past that and the curve tightens into a corner instead of bulging. What it will not do is
the cubic's double inflection: a hyperbezier has at most one.

Nothing downstream of an FLine needs to know any of that. [`fitHyperbezierCubics`](graphics.md#flinehyperbezier-kt--fithyperbeziercubics) hands back a
handful of ordinary cubics, G1-continuous by construction because every join is pinned to the
hyperbezier's own tangent there. To draw one, use [`FLine.hyperbezierTo`](graphics.md#flinehyperbezier-kt--hyperbezierto) in place of
`FLine.cubicTo`, or [`hyperbezierBetween`](graphics.md#flinehyperbezier-kt--hyperbezierbetween) for a whole line from one control polygon and
[`hyperbezierThrough`](graphics.md#flinehyperbezier-kt--hyperbezierthrough) to run a curve through a list of points.

The curve itself, and the control-polygon-to-curve map, are in [`Hyperbezier`](graphics.md#hyperbezier-kt-hyperbezier).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/FLineHyperbezier.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/FLineHyperbezier/)

## FLineInstructionTrajectories.kt { #flineinstructiontrajectories-kt }

Traces how the points of a changing drawing move from frame to frame, as one trajectory line per point.

[`FLineSideways.update`](graphics.md#flineinstructiontrajectories-kt--flinesideways--update) takes each frame's line(s) and matches their anchor points to the previous
frame's; [`FLineSideways.trajectories`](graphics.md#flineinstructiontrajectories-kt--flinesideways--trajectories) and [`FLineSideways.trajectoryMap`](graphics.md#flineinstructiontrajectories-kt--flinesideways--trajectorymap) return the tracks drawn so far.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/FLineInstructionTrajectories.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/FLineInstructionTrajectories/)

## FLineInterpolation.kt { #flineinterpolation-kt }

Morphing one [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) into another: align, match and blend two drawings so any in-between shape can be drawn.

[`interpolatorTo`](graphics.md#flineinterpolation-kt--interpolatorto) builds a reusable [`FLineInterpolator`](graphics.md#flineinterpolation-kt-flineinterpolator) from an [`FLineInterpolationConfig`](graphics.md#flineinterpolation-kt-flineinterpolationconfig)
(alignment, matching and motion settings), and [`FLineInterpolator.lineAt`](graphics.md#flineinterpolation-kt--flineinterpolator--lineat) returns the line at a
given `t`. [`byInterpolatingTo`](graphics.md#flineinterpolation-kt--byinterpolatingto) is the one-shot form for a single evaluation.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/FLineInterpolation.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/FLineInterpolation/)

**Used in:** [FLine examples (Field graphics)](../fline_examples.md)

## FLineMeasure.kt { #flinemeasure-kt }

Measuring, locating, trimming and crossing an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline).

There is one measurer: [`FLine.cursor`](graphics.md#fline-kt--fline--cursor). A cursor walks a line by distance (`setD`) or by node
parameter (`setT`), and everything it reports about the point under it — position, unit tangent,
Frenet frame, curvature — comes from the one segment evaluator in this file: exact cubic first
and second derivatives, straight runs degree-elevated to cubics, degenerate ends handled.
`location()` hands the lot back as an [`FLineLocation`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt-flinelocation).

The FLine-level functions here are front doors onto a cursor for the common one-shot questions:
[`length`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--length), [`locationAt`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--locationat), [`locationAtFraction`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--locationatfraction), [`nearestLocation`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--nearestlocation), [`trim`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--trim), [`splitAt`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--splitat). Use a cursor
yourself when you walk a line step by step.

Two parameterisations run through all of it:

 - **distance** (`d`), in drawing units along the line, from 0 to [`length`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--length). Use it when you want
   things evenly spaced.
 - **`t`**, the node parameter: `t = i + u` is fraction `u` of the way (by curve parameter, not by
   distance) along the segment that ends at node `i + 1`.

Every [`FLineLocation`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt-flinelocation) carries both.

Everything whose answer only exists in the xy plane says so in its name: [`FLineLocation.normal2D`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--flinelocation--normal2d),
[`FLineLocation.signedCurvature2D`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--flinelocation--signedcurvature2d), [`tightBounds2D`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--tightbounds2d), [`area2D`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--area2d), [`isClockwise2D`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--isclockwise2d), [`windingNumber2D`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--windingnumber2d),
[`contains2D`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--contains2d), [`crossings2D`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--crossings2d), [`selfCrossings2D`](graphics.md#flinemeasure-kt--selfcrossings2d). Everything else is 3D.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/FLineMeasure.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/FLineMeasure/)

Use `FLineFillRule.EvenOdd` when a counter should be a hole regardless of its winding direction. |

On Field's canvas (y down) that is to the **left** of the direction of travel; with y up, to the right. It is defined on straight runs too, and is the zero vector only where the line runs straight along z. This is the normal to offset a 2D drawing along. |

## FLineSampling.kt { #flinesampling-kt }

Choosing points along an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline): pluggable samplers that return parameter and position pairs.

[`FLineSamplers`](graphics.md#flinesampling-kt-flinesamplers) holds the built-in [`FLineSampler`](graphics.md#flinesampling-kt-flinesampler)s (uniform, by distance, random, curvature
adaptive, Douglas-Peucker, patterned) and [`FLineSamplers.compose`](graphics.md#flinesampling-kt--flinesamplers--compose) / [`then`](graphics.md#flinesampling-kt--then) chain them.
[`sampleSeries`](graphics.md#flinesampling-kt--sampleseries) returns [`FLineSample`](graphics.md#flinesampling-kt-flinesample)s and [`samplePoints`](graphics.md#flinesampling-kt--samplepoints) returns just the points.

## FLineSerialization.kt { #flineserialization-kt }

Serializes an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) to JSON and back, nodes and properties included, through [`FLineSerializer`](graphics.md#flineserialization-kt-flineserializer).

[`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) names [`FLineSerializer`](graphics.md#flineserialization-kt-flineserializer) in its `@Serializable` annotation, so any `kotlinx.serialization`
format picks it up. Each property value is written with a type tag: numbers, booleans, strings and
`Vec2`/`Vec3`/`Vec4`. A value of any other type throws `SerializationException`; a few runtime-only
properties (`onClick` callbacks, `thicken` strokes) are skipped instead.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/FLineSerialization.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/FLineSerialization/)

## FLineThickening.kt { #flinethickening-kt }

Turning a line into an outline: offsets, ribbons and buffers of an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline), at fixed or varying width.

[`byRibboning`](graphics.md#flinethickening-kt--byribboning) and [`byVariableRibboning`](graphics.md#flinethickening-kt--byvariableribboning) return an [`FLineRibbon`](graphics.md#flinethickening-kt-flineribbon) with left and right edges and a
closed shell. [`byJavaOffsetting`](graphics.md#flinethickening-kt--byjavaoffsetting) uses Java2D strokes; [`byJtsBuffering`](graphics.md#flinethickening-kt--byjtsbuffering), [`byJtsOffsetting`](graphics.md#flinethickening-kt--byjtsoffsetting) and
[`byJtsVariableBuffering`](graphics.md#flinethickening-kt--byjtsvariablebuffering) use JTS, with [`FLineStrokeJoin`](graphics.md#flinethickening-kt-flinestrokejoin) and [`FLineStrokeCap`](graphics.md#flinethickening-kt-flinestrokecap) for the corner and
end style. [`byJtsSplitting`](graphics.md#flinethickening-kt--byjtssplitting) separates a self-intersecting line into an [`FLineSplit`](graphics.md#flinethickening-kt-flinesplit).

## FLineWiggle.kt { #flinewiggle-kt }

Wiggling one line along another, and the moving frames that make it possible.

[`wiggledBy`](graphics.md#flinewiggle-kt--wiggledby) reads a second line's coordinates in a frame travelling along this one, so a small wave
becomes a decoration along a path. [`sweptFrames`](graphics.md#flinewiggle-kt--sweptframes) returns the [`SweptFrames`](graphics.md#flinewiggle-kt-sweptframes) (position, tangent,
normal, binormal) it uses, for placing other things along a line. Tests: `FLineWiggleTest`.

## Hyperbezier.kt { #hyperbezier-kt }

The hyperbezier curve family, ported from Raph Levien's hyperbezier
(linebender.org/blog/hyperbezier/, August 2026); [`fitHyperbezierCubics`](graphics.md#flinehyperbezier-kt--fithyperbeziercubics) is what draws one into an
[`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline).

A hyperbezier is the plane curve traced at unit speed whose curvature is a rational function of
arc length `s`:

```diffstatic {data-lang=text}
    kappa(s) = (a*s + b) / q(s)^1.5,     q(s) = c*s^2 + d*s + 1
```

over `s` in `[0, 1]`, then similarity-transformed so it runs from `(0, 0)` to `(1, 0)`, which is
what the rest of this file calls the **chord frame**. `q` is a dial between two regimes a single
cubic has to compromise between: `q` constant gives circular arcs and Euler spirals *exactly*,
while `q` dipping towards zero gives a corner-like curvature spike. The family also contains the
log-aesthetic curves and the circle involute exactly. Its curvature numerator is linear in `s`, so
it has at most one inflection, and that is what it gives up relative to a cubic: following a cubic
with two inflections takes more than one hyperbezier.

`theta(s)`, the integral of `kappa`, has a closed form. The position integral of `e^(i*theta)`
does not, being Fresnel-like, so that part is done numerically with Gauss-Legendre quadrature.

Construct a curve from a cubic-shaped control polygon with [`hyperbezierFor`](graphics.md#hyperbezier-kt--hyperbezierfor); it is rarely useful
to pick `a`, `b`, `c` and `d` by hand.

## LowSegmentFLineFitting.kt { #lowsegmentflinefitting-kt }

Fits a point sequence with as few line and arc segments as its error budget allows.

[`fitLowSegmentFLine`](graphics.md#lowsegmentflinefitting-kt--fitlowsegmentfline) returns the fitted [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline), and [`fitLowSegmentFLineResult`](graphics.md#lowsegmentflinefitting-kt--fitlowsegmentflineresult) also reports the
error in a [`LowSegmentFLineFitResult`](graphics.md#lowsegmentflinefitting-kt-lowsegmentflinefitresult); [`LowSegmentFLineFitConfig`](graphics.md#lowsegmentflinefitting-kt-lowsegmentflinefitconfig) sets the segment limit and the
improvement a split must earn. Tests: `LowSegmentFLineFittingTest`.

## PlanarTessellation.kt { #planartessellation-kt }

Fills sets of 3D rings, holes included, by grouping them into planes and handing each plane to
[`FloatEarcut`](graphics.md#floatearcut-kt-floatearcut).

[`PlanarTessellation.tessellate`](graphics.md#planartessellation-kt--planartessellation--tessellate) returns [`PlanarTessellation.Polygon`](graphics.md#planartessellation-kt--planartessellation--polygon)s whose triangles refer back
into the input rings, and [`Coplanarity`](graphics.md#planartessellation-kt-coplanarity) sets how close two rings must be to share a plane.
Tessellation commutes with rigid rotation, which `TessellationOrientationOracleTest` checks.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/PlanarTessellation.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/PlanarTessellation/)

## PolynomialTreeFitting.kt { #polynomialtreefitting-kt }

Fits a `List<Vec3>` or an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) with a tree of 3D polynomial curves, splitting a
span until each leaf meets its error targets.

The `fitPolynomialTree3D` extensions take a [`PolynomialTreeFitConfig`](graphics.md#polynomialtreefitting-kt-polynomialtreefitconfig) (polynomial order, depth and leaf limits,
RMS and max-error targets) and returns a [`PolynomialTreeFitResult`](graphics.md#polynomialtreefitting-kt-polynomialtreefitresult). Split, stop and claim rules
are pluggable through [`PolynomialTreeSplitStrategies`](graphics.md#polynomialtreefitting-kt-polynomialtreesplitstrategies), [`PolynomialTreeStopCriteria`](graphics.md#polynomialtreefitting-kt-polynomialtreestopcriteria) and
[`PolynomialTreeClaimCriteria`](graphics.md#polynomialtreefitting-kt-polynomialtreeclaimcriteria); [`PolynomialLeafFLineStyles`](graphics.md#polynomialtreefitting-kt-polynomialleafflinestyles) holds preset styles for
drawing the fitted leaves as FLines.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/PolynomialTreeFitting.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/PolynomialTreeFitting/)

## contours.kt { #contours-kt }

Marching-squares iso-contours for 2D scalar fields, plus the scalar field most callers want to
contour.

A field is just a [`ScalarField2D`](graphics.md#contours-kt-scalarfield2d), `(Double, Double) -> Double`. [`pointEdgeScalarField2D`](graphics.md#contours-kt--pointedgescalarfield2d) builds
one from points and edges — or from a 2D `FLine` — as the union of weighted discs and capsules,
signed so that `iso = 0.0` is the tube boundary; it re-reads the supplied point list on every
sample, so mutating those `Vec2`s moves the field live. [`generateIsoContours`](graphics.md#contours-kt--generateisocontours) samples a field on
an `nx` by `ny` grid and returns stitched polylines, [`generateIsoContoursWithStep`](graphics.md#contours-kt--generateisocontourswithstep) takes a target
cell size instead, and the `FLine` overloads choose the sampling window from the line's 2D bounds
grown by the tube radius.

[`smoothIsoContours`](graphics.md#contours-kt--smoothisocontours) and [`generateSmoothIsoContours`](graphics.md#contours-kt--generatesmoothisocontours) fit cubic splines through the polylines,
treating a contour that ends on the sampling bounds as open and the rest as closed loops.

### Varying the radius along the line — weights

A tube of one radius is `pointRadius`/`edgeRadius`. To make it *taper*, weight the primitives:
every function that builds a point/edge field takes a **weight callback** rather than a list of
weights. On an explicit graph that is [`PointEdgeWeight`](graphics.md#contours-kt-pointedgeweight), `(index, point) -> Double`, indexed the
same way as the `points` you passed in. On an `FLine` it is [`FLinePointWeight`](graphics.md#contours-kt-flinepointweight),
`(nodeIndex, point) -> Double`, where `nodeIndex` is the *fractional* drawing-instruction index of
the flattened point — integral at a `moveTo`/`lineTo`, and interpolated across a `cubicTo`, which
is the same quantity `FLine.uniform_linearize` hands its callback and `linesOut` uses to look up
per-node colour. [`FLine.isoWeights`](graphics.md#contours-kt--isoweights) is the stock implementation: it reads a per-node property and
interpolates between the nodes that set it.

It is a callback rather than a list of weights because on the `FLine` overloads there is no count
a caller could size a list against: the points and edges belong to [`pointEdgeGraph2D`](graphics.md#contours-kt--pointedgegraph2d)'s internal
flattening, and its edge count depends on the line's geometry as well as its instructions.

An edge's weight is always the **minimum** of its two endpoints'. A capsule has one radius for its
whole length and so cannot taper: the taper comes from the union of densely sampled discs, and the
edges only bridge the gaps between them. Taking the *maximum* would let a capsule bulge past the
disc envelope exactly where the weight changes fastest; the minimum fills the gap without ever
fattening it.

### The sign convention

A grid corner is *inside* iff its sample is **strictly below** `iso`; a sample exactly *at* `iso`
counts as outside. The test is two-valued rather than three-way, because under a three-way test —
`below` at one end of an edge, `above` at the other, so "equal" is neither — a sample sitting
exactly on `iso` suppresses the crossing on every edge out of its corner, and the contour
vanishes or shatters into arcs. Samples land exactly on `iso` for ordinary input: any grid that
samples a linear field at its own zero level puts a whole column there, and a unit circle
contoured at `iso = 0` passes through a grid corner at plenty of resolutions, `nx = ny = 16` over
`[-2, 2]` among them.

A crossing that lands on a corner is pushed off it by `ISO_CROSSING_EPSILON`, which moves it by
at most a thousandth of the cell edge it lies on — an analytic bound, since it is a `coerceIn` on
the interpolation parameter. `marchingCubes` in `mesh_sdf.kt` is the 3D marcher and uses the same
convention for the same reason.

### The saddle cell

A cell with four crossings is resolved by the *asymptotic decider*: the sign of the cell's
bilinear saddle value decides which diagonal pair of corners the centre of the cell belongs to.
It is a pure function of the cell's own four corner values, so two cells sharing an edge cannot
disagree about the crossing on it, which is what the stitcher needs. The ambiguity itself does
not go away: when the saddle value is exactly `iso` the two pairings are equally correct and the
decider has nothing to go on. `SADDLE_TIE_RELATIVE_EPSILON` settles that case in the code rather
than leaving it to the direction a multiplication rounded — which matters because every bilinear
field lands there exactly.

### Stitching and winding

Each crossing is computed once and keyed by its grid edge, as `marchingCubes` keys its shared
vertices, so segments are chained by key in time linear in their number. Every segment is
oriented with the inside on its left, so a closed contour comes back counter-clockwise around an
inside region and clockwise around a hole in one: summed signed areas give the inside's true area.

## FLinesAndJavaShapes.kt { #flinesandjavashapes-kt }

Converts [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline)s to and from `java.awt.geom` shapes, and walks them by distance with
[`FLinesAndJavaShapes.Cursor`](graphics.md#flinesandjavashapes-kt--flinesandjavashapes--cursor).

The round trip through `java.awt.geom` (geometry only, not attributes) gives 2D FLines
Java2D's flattening, stroking, insetting and outsetting. `Cursor` moves along a
line by arc length or by node parameter, reports the position, tangent and curvature there, and
splits the line. `CubicSegment2` and `CubicSegment3` hold the per-segment cubic maths: roots,
inflections, bounding boxes and intersections.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/java2d/FLinesAndJavaShapes.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/java2d/FLinesAndJavaShapes/)

## ManifoldHeaderCheck.kt { #manifoldheadercheck-kt }

Checks every FFM descriptor `ManifoldNative` binds against the prototypes in the installed
`manifoldc.h`, and against the structs and enums in its `types.h`. A descriptor has to declare the
same number of arguments, and at every position, and for the return, the same kind of value:
pointer, `double`, `float`, 32- or 64-bit integer (`size_t` is 64), `void`, or a struct passed by
value of the same size.

A descriptor that disagrees with the header still links and still returns a number, so this is
the only thing that notices one. `ManifoldSmokeTest` runs it first.

Pointer *types* are not compared, since FFM has one `ADDRESS`. The two places where the pointee
matters are handled once in the wrapper rather than at each call: [`Solid.slice`](graphics.md#solid-kt--solid--slice) and
[`Solid.project`](graphics.md#solid-kt--solid--project) convert the `ManifoldPolygons` that `manifold_slice` and `manifold_project`
return into a `Section` in one place, and [`Solid.raycast`](graphics.md#solid-kt--solid--raycast) turns the C API's segment fraction
into a distance in the solid's units.

## PlanarContact.kt { #planarcontact-kt }

Finds where two parts touch on a shared plane, and audits apertures cut through that contact, in double precision.

[`planarContact`](graphics.md#planarcontact-kt--planarcontact) intersects the boundary triangles of two [`SolidPlanarMesh`](graphics.md#solidplanarmesh-kt-solidplanarmesh)es lying on a [`ContactPlane`](graphics.md#planarcontact-kt-contactplane) and
returns a [`ContactPatch`](graphics.md#planarcontact-kt-contactpatch); [`planarContacts`](graphics.md#planarcontact-kt--planarcontacts) discovers the shared planes itself. [`auditApertures`](graphics.md#planarcontact-kt--auditapertures) compares
removed regions against an expected boundary and reports mismatch areas against [`GeometryTolerances`](graphics.md#planarcontact-kt-geometrytolerances).
[`polylineTube`](graphics.md#planarcontact-kt--polylinetube) builds a [`Solid`](graphics.md#solid-kt-solid) tube of cylinders and spheres along a polyline.

## Section.kt { #section-kt }

2D regions with holes, from Manifold's `CrossSection`: boolean operations, offsetting with a choice of
[`JoinType`](internal.md#manifoldnative-kt-jointype), and extrusion into a [`Solid`](graphics.md#solid-kt-solid).

## Solid.kt { #solid-kt }

Closed 3D volumes from the Manifold library: primitives, transforms, union, difference and intersection,
with results that stay closed manifolds.

[`Solid`](graphics.md#solid-kt-solid) is the type a box uses; [`TriMesh.toSolid`](graphics.md#solid-kt--tosolid) brings an existing mesh in, and [`Solid.toTriMesh`](graphics.md#solid-kt--solid--totrimesh)
hands the result to Field's mesh display. The native library is optional: [`ManifoldLibrary`](internal.md#manifoldnative-kt-manifoldlibrary) reports
whether it is installed.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/solid/manifold/Solid.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/solid/manifold/Solid/)

**Used in:** [Solids that cannot fail: Manifold in Field](../manifold.md)

## SolidPlanarMesh.kt { #solidplanarmesh-kt }

A double-precision export of a [`Solid`](graphics.md#solid-kt-solid)'s boundary that keeps Manifold's planar-face provenance.

[`Solid.toPlanarMesh`](graphics.md#solid-kt--solid--toplanarmesh) produces a [`SolidPlanarMesh`](graphics.md#solidplanarmesh-kt-solidplanarmesh); each [`SolidPlanarFace`](graphics.md#solidplanarmesh-kt-solidplanarface) groups the triangles of one planar
face. [`SolidPlanarMesh.toSolid`](graphics.md#solidplanarmesh-kt--tosolid) rebuilds a [`Solid`](graphics.md#solid-kt-solid) from it, and [`SolidPlanarMesh.toTriMesh`](graphics.md#solidplanarmesh-kt--solidplanarmesh--totrimesh) is the lossy
float conversion for rendering.

## SolidCraft.kt { #solidcraft-kt }

An optional bridge to the SolidCraft B-rep document engine, whose model stays in native Rust code.

[`SolidCraftLibrary`](graphics.md#solidcraft-kt-solidcraftlibrary) locates the native library and reports whether it is available. `SolidCraftDesign.open`
loads a design, [`SolidCraftDesign.setParameter`](graphics.md#solidcraft-kt--solidcraftdesign--setparameter) edits it, and [`SolidCraftDesign.mesh`](graphics.md#solidcraft-kt--solidcraftdesign--mesh) copies a body out as a
[`SolidCraftMesh`](graphics.md#solidcraft-kt-solidcraftmesh) for display.

## SolidCraftBuilder.kt { #solidcraftbuilder-kt }

Writing a SolidCraft part in Kotlin instead of drawing it: sketches, the features that turn them
into solids and surfaces, and named parameters that stay editable afterwards.

[`solidCraft`](graphics.md#solidcraftbuilder-kt--solidcraft) opens a [`SolidCraftBuilder`](graphics.md#solidcraftbuilder-kt-solidcraftbuilder), whose calls accumulate into SolidCraft's own design
document, the same JSON a saved design holds. So a part written here is evaluated by the engine
that opens one from disk, and everything downstream treats the two alike.
[`SolidCraftBuilder.json`](graphics.md#solidcraftbuilder-kt--solidcraftbuilder--json) is that document and [`SolidCraftBuilder.open`](graphics.md#solidcraftbuilder-kt--solidcraftbuilder--open) evaluates it, giving back
a [`SolidCraftDesign`](graphics.md#solidcraft-kt-solidcraftdesign) to mesh, re-parameterise or export.

Only the evaluation needs the native bridge, since the document is assembled as plain JSON. A
box can therefore build and inspect a design on a machine where SolidCraft was never compiled,
and [`SolidCraftLibrary`](graphics.md#solidcraft-kt-solidcraftlibrary) says whether this one has it.

Lengths and angles are SolidCraft expressions rather than numbers: `"12"` in the design's units,
a quantity such as `"30 deg"`, or a formula over the design's parameters such as `"width/2"`.
That is what keeps a finished part adjustable, through [`SolidCraftDesign.setParameter`](graphics.md#solidcraft-kt--solidcraftdesign--setparameter), without
rebuilding it here.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/solid/solidcraft/SolidCraftBuilder.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/solid/solidcraft/SolidCraftBuilder/)

## bspot.kt { #bspot-kt }

One-to-one matching between two equally sized 2D point clouds, at a million points a side, using
BSP-OT: every source point gets exactly one target and every target is used exactly once, with the
total squared travel distance kept small.

The exact answer to that problem is an assignment problem, and the Hungarian method that
[`assignment`](graphics.md#transport-kt--assignment) in `transport.kt` solves it with is `O(n³)` time over an `n × n` cost matrix. At a
thousand points that is fine. At a million the matrix alone is four terabytes. BSP-OT gives up
provable optimality to get to `O(n log n)`:

1. Choose a direction. Split *each* cloud at its own median along it, so both left halves hold
   the same number of points, and so do both right halves.
2. Recurse, left with left and right with right, with a new direction each time. A leaf of one
   point pairs its source with its target; a leaf of two picks the cheaper of the two pairings.
3. That is one candidate bijection. Make several and merge each new one into the best so far: the
   union of two permutations falls apart into disjoint alternating cycles, and on each cycle you
   keep whichever orientation is cheaper. Then try two-point swaps along the candidate's edges.

The direction in step 1 is what [`BspOt2D.Splits`](graphics.md#bspot-kt--bspot2d--splits) chooses. The default, as in the reference
implementation, fits a Gaussian to each of the two subsets and splits along an eigenvector of the
linear map that carries one Gaussian onto the other, picking one of the two at random per node.
When the subsets differ in shape that axis is the one along which they need to move, and it
about halves the excess cost of random directions at eight trees. Below 50 points it stops fitting and splits
perpendicular to the parent.

The counts are equal by construction, not because the two clouds occupy the same cells, so clouds
of very different density still match completely.

    val result = matchPoints(from, to)            // two List<Vec2> of the same size
    val destination = result.reorder(to)          // destination[`i`](workspace.md#stdlib-kt--i) is where from[`i`](workspace.md#stdlib-kt--i) goes
    val halfway = from.indices.map { from`it` + (destination`it` - from`it`) * 0.5f }

For raw `FloatArray`s, call [`BspOt2D.match`](graphics.md#bspot-kt--bspot2d--match) directly. A previous permutation can be passed as
`initial` and is improved rather than replaced, which suits matching successive frames of a
simulation.

### Cost, measured

On an M1 Max with the default four workers and eight trees, a million points a side takes 3 to
4.5 s for two uniform clouds, and 5.7 s from a uniform square onto three discs (7.4 s with random
splits, which reach a 5% higher cost). Merging is sequential. Array storage is about `69 + 60 P`
bytes a point for `P` workers, roughly 309 MB at a million points and four workers. The SIMD
paths (projection, and cost evaluation through a gather) gave no measurable end-to-end gain over
`simd = false` when this was first measured; partitioning, cycle walking and the swaps are
scalar.

### What it does not give you

- **No optimality guarantee, and further from optimal than the paper.** From a uniform square
  onto three discs, 1000 points, the total cost is 5.5% above the exact Hungarian answer with 8
  trees and 2.9% with 32. Two independent uniform clouds are the hard case: every node's two
  subsets have nearly the same Gaussian, so the transport map is close to the identity and its
  eigenvectors are noise. At 400 points that lands 26% above exact with 64 trees, where random
  splits reach 16%. Leaving those clouds unmatched is 120 times worse. The paper reports
  typically under 1% with 64 candidates; it ranks all candidates before merging, which this
  version, merging as it goes in bounded memory, does not. The bijection is good enough for a
  morph to read as a morph; it is not a solver for the exact assignment.
- **2D only, equal sizes only, uniform weights only.** No partial or unbalanced transport.
- **Deterministic for a given seed and options, across worker counts.** Not promised bit-identical
  across JDKs or CPUs.

Algorithm from Baptiste Genest, Nicolas Bonneel, Vincent Nivoliers and David Coeurjolly,
"BSP-OT: Sparse transport plans between discrete measures in loglinear time", ACM Transactions on
Graphics (SIGGRAPH Asia 2025), https://perso.liris.cnrs.fr/david.coeurjolly/publication/bspot-25/.
The Gaussian split follows `gaussianPartialBSPOT` and the merge `MergePlansNoPar` and
`BijectiveMatching::swapIfUpgrade` in their MIT-licensed
reference implementation, https://github.com/baptiste-genest/BSP-OT, Copyright (c) 2025 the same
authors.

## lp_fan_map.kt { #lp-fan-map-kt }

The central-path fan as a map from the (θ, log μ) plane into a polygon.

For an objective direction c(θ) = (cos θ, sin θ) and barrier weight μ, the barrier maximiser
x(θ, μ) solves  c(θ) = μ Σ wᵢ nᵢ / sᵢ(x). Write g(x) = Σ wᵢ nᵢ / sᵢ(x): the gradient of the
(negated) barrier, a diffeomorphism from the polygon's interior onto the whole plane. Then
g(x) = c(θ)/μ, so (θ, 1/μ) are polar coordinates of g(x) and the fan is the polar grid pulled
back through g⁻¹: one-to-one onto the interior minus the weighted analytic centre (g = 0).

Differentiating the optimality condition with M = μ Σ wᵢ nᵢnᵢᵀ / sᵢ² (the negated Hessian):

```diffstatic {data-lang=text}
∂x/∂θ     =  M⁻¹ c'(θ)
∂x/∂log μ = −M⁻¹ c(θ)
```

and det[∂x/∂θ, ∂x/∂log μ] = det(M⁻¹) · det[c', −c] = 1 / det M > 0. The map never folds; it only
pinches, at both ends of the log μ axis.

## lp_polytope.kt { #lp-polytope-kt }

The three-dimensional companion of lp_trajectories.kt: the same linear-programming methods, as
curve generators, on a convex polytope `{ x : nᵢ·x ≤ bᵢ }` in space. The methods are the 2-D ones
with 3×3 linear algebra in place of 2×2 (the ellipsoid method's constants change with the
dimension: centre step 1/(n+1) = 1/4, expansion n²/(n²−1) = 9/8). The simplex walk follows the
polytope's edges, which the constructor finds by enumerating vertices.

Pure math, independent of Box; doubles throughout, Vec3 only for drawing.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/spatial/lp_polytope.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/spatial/lp_polytope/)

**Used in:** [Linear programs as curves](../lp_curves.md)

It starts from a ball of `initialRadius` (default: the polytope's diameter) around `start`, cuts on the most violated half-space at an infeasible centre and on the objective at a feasible one. In `n = 3` dimensions each cut moves the centre by `−Pg / (4√(gᵀPg))` and replaces `P` by `9/8 · (P − ½ (Pg)(Pg)ᵀ / gᵀPg)` (`n²/(n²−1)` and `2/(n+1)`), which multiplies the volume by `27/32 ≈ 0.84` every step: slower than the 2-D method's 0.77, as the method is in higher dimensions. [`LpSample3.tag`](graphics.md#lp-polytope-kt--lpsample3--tag) and [`LpSample3.scale`](graphics.md#lp-polytope-kt--lpsample3--scale) (`√det P`) are as in [`LpPolygon.ellipsoid`](graphics.md#lp-trajectories-kt--ellipsoid). |

A convex polytope has no local optimum that is not global, so it ends at the optimal vertex. [`LpSample3.scale`](graphics.md#lp-polytope-kt--lpsample3--scale) is `NaN`. |
| <a id="lp-polytope-kt--cuttingplanes"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">LpPolytope</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">cuttingPlanes</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">direction</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec3</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">iterations</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">20</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">center</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">LpCenter</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">LpCenter</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">ANALYTIC</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">minVolume</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1e</span><span class="p">-</span><span class="mi">9</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">LpCuttingPlaneTrace3</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/spatial/lp_polytope/#L912) | A cutting-plane walk in 3-D: find a centre of the region still in play, cut it with the objective (`c·x ≥ c·centre`), repeat. `center` is `LpCenter.ANALYTIC` (the analytic centre of every constraint so far, cuts included), `LpCenter.CENTROID` (the centre of gravity, which removes at least `1 − (3/4)³ ≈ 58%` of the volume each step) or `LpCenter.CHEBYSHEV` (the centre of the largest inscribed ball) or `LpCenter.VOLUMETRIC` (Vaidya's volumetric centre of every constraint so far, started from the analytic centre). Stops when the remaining volume falls below `minVolume` or after `iterations`. [`LpSample3.scale`](graphics.md#lp-polytope-kt--lpsample3--scale) is the remaining volume, and `LpCuttingPlaneTrace3.regions` holds each region. |

## lp_trajectories.kt { #lp-trajectories-kt }

Linear-programming algorithms on a convex polygon, used as curve generators.

A 2-D linear program is "maximise c·x over a convex polygon". Every classical method for it walks
from somewhere to the same optimal vertex, and each walks differently: the barrier method's central
path is a smooth arc from the analytic centre, the primal-dual method takes a few long Newton
strides, PDHG spirals in, the ellipsoid method shrinks a sequence of ellipses, the simplex method
hops along the boundary and cutting planes carve the region away. Here those walks are the product.
Every method returns its whole trajectory with per-step metadata ([`LpSample`](graphics.md#lp-trajectories-kt-lpsample)), and each result type
has a `toFLine` that draws it, with `toFLines` for a whole fan of them.

The pure math is independent of Box and of FLine: an [`LpPolygon`](graphics.md#lp-trajectories-kt-lppolygon) is a list of half-planes and the
methods are plain functions on it. Doubles throughout; [`LpSample.position`](graphics.md#lp-trajectories-kt--lpsample--position) is the Vec2 for drawing.
The visual reference for all of this is https://lpviz.net.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/spatial/lp_trajectories.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/spatial/lp_trajectories/)

It starts from a disc of `initialRadius` (default: the polygon's diameter) around `start`. At an infeasible centre it cuts on the most violated edge; at a feasible one it cuts on the objective, keeping the half where `c·x` is at least its current value. Each central cut in two dimensions moves the centre by `−Pg / (3√(gᵀPg))` and replaces `P` by `4/3 · (P − 2/3 · (Pg)(Pg)ᵀ / gᵀPg)`, which multiplies the area by `√(16/27) ≈ 0.77` every step. [`LpSample.tag`](graphics.md#lp-trajectories-kt--lpsample--tag) is `"feasibility-cut"` or `"objective-cut"` for the cut taken at that centre (`"final"` for the last), and [`LpSample.scale`](graphics.md#lp-trajectories-kt--lpsample--scale) is `√det P`. |

It ends at the optimal vertex, having visited at most half the polygon. [`LpSample.scale`](graphics.md#lp-trajectories-kt--lpsample--scale) is `NaN`. |
| <a id="lp-trajectories-kt--cuttingplanes"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">LpPolygon</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">cuttingPlanes</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">direction</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">iterations</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">40</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">center</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">LpCenter</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">LpCenter</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">ANALYTIC</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">minArea</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1e</span><span class="p">-</span><span class="mi">10</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">LpCuttingPlaneTrace</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/spatial/lp_trajectories/#L929) | A cutting-plane walk: find a centre of the region still in play, cut the region with the objective (`c·x ≥ c·centre`), and repeat. With `LpCenter.ANALYTIC` the centre is the analytic centre of every constraint so far, cuts included, so earlier cuts keep pushing on the path just as extra constraints push a central path; with `LpCenter.CENTROID` it is the centre of gravity, which removes at least `1 − (2/3)²` of the area each step; with `LpCenter.CHEBYSHEV` it is the centre of the largest inscribed disc, and with `LpCenter.VOLUMETRIC` Vaidya's volumetric centre of every constraint so far. The trajectory approaches the optimal vertex from inside; it stops when the remaining area falls below `minArea` or after `iterations`. [`LpSample.scale`](graphics.md#lp-trajectories-kt--lpsample--scale) is the remaining area, and `LpCuttingPlaneTrace.regions` holds the region at every step. |

### LpContinuation { #lp-trajectories-kt-lpcontinuation }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">LpContinuation</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/spatial/lp_trajectories/#L502)

A warm-started [`centralPath`](graphics.md#lp-trajectories-kt--centralpath) for a polygon, direction or weights that move smoothly between calls — an animation's frames. From the third call on it extrapolates each sample linearly from the previous two paths (`2·last − before`, a secant predictor) and passes that as [`centralPath`](graphics.md#lp-trajectories-kt--centralpath)'s `warm`; on the second call it passes the previous path itself. Newton then starts next to the answer and needs fewer steps than following the path cold, for the same path. `last` is the latest path and [`lastSteps`](graphics.md#lp-trajectories-kt--lpcontinuation--laststeps) its Newton step count; [`reset`](graphics.md#lp-trajectories-kt--lpcontinuation--reset) forgets the history, which a jump should do. A prediction that does not fit (a different sample count, or a sample Newton judges further off than the path's own previous sample) is ignored, so a jump costs a cold start and nothing else.

| --- | --- |

| <a id="lp-trajectories-kt--lpcontinuation--centralpath"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">centralPath</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">polygon</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">LpPolygon</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">direction</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">weights</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">samples</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">160</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">muHigh</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1000.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">muLow</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1e</span><span class="p">-</span><span class="mi">5</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">LpTrajectory</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/spatial/lp_trajectories/#L513) | `polygon`'s central path for `direction`, warm-started from the previous calls'. |

## spatial_field.kt { #spatial-field-kt }

The bridges out of Field's plane-geometry results and into the things Field already draws.

Every partitioner in `graph_connectivity.kt`, `dirichlet.kt`, `contours.kt` and `clustering.kt`
answers with *structure* — cell vertex rings, circular arcs, triangle index triples, cluster
labels — and none of them answers with geometry. This file converts each of them: one `toFLines`
per result type, so a Voronoi diagram, an Apollonius cell, a Delaunay triangulation or a k-medoids
partition lands in the same drawing, animation and export machinery as anything drawn by hand.
It is the plane counterpart of `mesh_field.kt`, which does the same job for `TriMesh`.

Two layers:

 1. **Structure → [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline).** [`PointGraph.toFLine`](graphics.md#spatial-field-kt--tofline), [`delaunayTrianglesToFLine`](graphics.md#spatial-field-kt--delaunaytrianglestofline),
    [`VoronoiDiagram.toFLines`](graphics.md#spatial-field-kt--toflines), [`CircularDirichlet.Diagram.toFLines`](graphics.md#spatial-field-kt--toflines),
    [`CircularDirichlet.CellBoundary.toFLines`](graphics.md#spatial-field-kt--toflines), [`ClusterLayer.toFLines`](graphics.md#spatial-field-kt--toflines) and
    [`pointCloudFLine`](graphics.md#spatial-field-kt--pointcloudfline). Each returns styled, drawable lines and nothing else — no `Box`, no
    output, so they are usable from a test or a renderer as readily as from a box.
 2. **[`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) → a captioned figure.** [`Box.showPlane`](graphics.md#spatial-field-kt--showplane) and [`Box.showPlaneGrid`](graphics.md#spatial-field-kt--showplanegrid) rasterise lines to
    inline SVG with `drawToSVG` and push a titled card — live and pannable for one figure, frozen
    for a grid of them — to a box output channel: the fastest way to see a whole pipeline at once,
    and the 2D twin of `Box.showMeshGrid`. [`planeFigureHtml`](graphics.md#spatial-field-kt--planefigurehtml) is the markup on its own.

The figure helpers are AWT-free (Skia's SVG canvas, same as `Box.lines`), so they work headless,
including inside the docs build.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/spatial/spatial_field.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/spatial/spatial_field/)

**Used in:** [Points into structure — Voronoi, Apollonius, contours and clusters](../spatial_geometry_examples.md), [Linear programs as curves](../lp_curves.md), [Evolving Creatures](../evolving_creatures.md)

## stippling.kt { #stippling-kt }

Stippling: place exactly N points so that they follow an image's brightness *and* keep an even,
low-correlation ("blue-noise-ish") spacing from one another.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val dots = imgFromFile("face.png").stipple(5000)        // List<Vec2>, pixel coordinates
```

Sampling the brightness as a probability distribution gets the density right but clumps: two
independent samples are as likely to land on top of each other as anywhere else. This file instead
computes a **weighted centroidal Voronoi tessellation** (Secord's stippling) by Lloyd relaxation on
the CPU. Each iteration

1. rasterises the points into the pixel grid,
2. finds every pixel's nearest point with a separable exact Euclidean distance transform
   (a two-scan nearest-seed pass along each row, then Felzenszwalb–Huttenlocher's lower envelope of
   parabolas down each column), which yields the Voronoi cells as a label raster in `O(pixels)`
   regardless of the point count,
3. moves each point to the density-weighted centroid of its cell.

The rows and columns are split across a fork-join pool of their own, and nothing on the per-iteration
path allocates: the label rasters, the column scratch and the per-worker centroid accumulators are
all allocated once, in the constructor.

### Where the points go, and what relaxation does not change

The *number* of points in a region is decided by the starting sample. Relaxation evens out the
spacing between neighbours and moves hardly any points from one region to another, so the point
density is whatever the start gave, `brightness^densityPower`. With the default of 1, points follow
brightness, and a larger power exaggerates contrast.

That makes the start matter. An independent weighted random sample has the right density on
average and random clumps everywhere, and relaxation keeps the clumps' counts: on a flat field the
count variance in 48-pixel windows is 0.60 of a random scatter's after relaxing, which reads as
blotches in a mid tone. So the start is stratified along a Hilbert curve instead. The curve visits
the image in a way that keeps nearby pixels nearby, it is cut into `count` stretches of equal
density, and each stretch gets one point. Every region the curve covers then starts with its exact
share, and the same measurement after relaxing is 0.028.

Theory predicts a different density: the *optimal* centroidal tessellation of a density `ρ` in 2-D
has point density `ρ^(1/2)`. Lloyd iteration from a weighted start does not travel there. On a
field half at brightness 1 and half at 0.5 the bright/dim count ratio stays at 2 through hundreds of
iterations, against an optimum of 1.41, until the iteration reaches a fixed point on the raster
where [`Stippler.step`](graphics.md#stippling-kt--stippler--step) returns 0. `StipplingTest` pins both powers, the drift and the lumpiness.

### Memory

Besides five rasters of `supersample² * width * height` pixels, each worker keeps its own three
`DoubleArray(count)` centroid accumulators so that workers never contend. That is cheap at ten or a hundred thousand
points, and 384 MB at a million points on 16 workers — pass a smaller `threads` there.

## transport.kt { #transport-kt }

Optimal transport between point sets: which source goes to which target, or how much of each source
goes to each target, at the least total cost. Three solvers, from exact and small to approximate and
large:

- [`assignment`](graphics.md#transport-kt--assignment) (the Hungarian method) answers the one-to-one question exactly, for two equally
  sized sets. It is `O(n³)` over an `n × n` cost matrix, so it is for hundreds of points, maybe a
  few thousand. Flow matching's minibatch coupling and the FLine trajectory matcher use it.
- [`matchPoints`](graphics.md#bspot-kt--matchpoints) (BSP-OT, in `bspot.kt`) answers the same one-to-one question approximately, for 2D
  clouds of a million points a side.
- [`sinkhorn`](graphics.md#transport-kt--sinkhorn) answers a softer question exactly: it transports *mass*, so the sets may differ in
  size and carry weights, and every source may split between several targets. The answer is a
  transport plan rather than a pairing. A small [`sinkhorn`](graphics.md#transport-kt--sinkhorn) `epsilon` makes the plan nearly a
  permutation and its cost nearly the [`assignment`](graphics.md#transport-kt--assignment) cost; a large one blurs it.

### Entropic transport

[`sinkhorn`](graphics.md#transport-kt--sinkhorn) solves the entropy-regularised problem: minimise `Σ πᵢⱼ Cᵢⱼ + ε Σ πᵢⱼ (ln πᵢⱼ − 1)` over
plans `π` whose rows sum to the source weights `a` and whose columns sum to the target weights `b`.
The entropy term makes the problem strictly convex, so the answer is unique, smooth in the inputs,
and found by alternately rescaling rows and columns (Cuturi 2013). This implementation keeps the
scalings as log-domain dual potentials `f`, `g`, so a small `ε` does not underflow, and
`πᵢⱼ = exp((fᵢ + gⱼ − Cᵢⱼ) / ε)`.

`ε` is in the units of the cost. With squared-distance costs it is an area: `ε = 0.01` on points in
a unit square blurs over roughly `√0.01 = 0.1`. Each iteration is `O(n·m)`, and smaller `ε` needs
more of them; [`multiscaleSinkhorn`](graphics.md#transport-kt--multiscalesinkhorn) solves a coarse version first and starts the fine one from it.

## voronoi.kt { #voronoi-kt }

Practical 3D Voronoi and approximate 3D multiplicatively weighted Voronoi
("CircularDirichlet") for Kotlin + Field linalg.

- [`voronoi3d`](graphics.md#voronoi-kt--voronoi3d) builds convex polyhedral cells by intersecting pairwise bisector half-spaces. Six
  clip-box planes are added to **every** cell, not only to the unbounded ones, so a cell always
  comes back as a bounded polyhedron; [`VoronoiCell3.bounded`](graphics.md#voronoi-kt--voronoicell3--bounded) is how you tell whether the answer is
  the site's own cell or an artefact of the box. The box is the sites' bounding box grown on every
  side by `clipPadding * scale + 1`, where `scale` is the cloud's own diagonal (floored at 1).
- [`CircularDirichlet3d.build`](graphics.md#voronoi-kt--circulardirichlet3d--build) extracts approximate support patches on bisector spheres / planes by
  clipping a sampled surface mesh with the weighted score predicate.

The weighted contourer is renderer-oriented: it prefers stable, wound
boundary loops over exact symbolic patch topology.

### How the unweighted clipper assigns a corner to a face

**Combinatorially**: a corner records the planes that produced it, and a face's polygon is exactly
the corners recording that plane. Not by a distance test against a tolerance — a tolerance scaled
off the point cloud lets faces near a near-cospherical site cluster claim corners that are not on
them, and then the cells do not close, which is a T-junction and a hairline crack in any mesh
built from the faces. The `collectCorners` KDoc in [`Voronoi3d`](graphics.md#voronoi-kt-voronoi3d) has the detail.

Closure is not total, because the clipper works in `Float`: **4 of 465 bounded cells** and **12 of
447 clipped cells** fail the strict check that every edge is walked by exactly two faces in
opposite directions. `VoronoiFaceTopologyTest` pins both counts with `<=`, so they can improve but
cannot regress silently. Cell volumes tile the clip box to 1e-4 relative, and a cubic lattice of
sites gives exact unit cubes.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/spatial/voronoi.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/spatial/voronoi/)

**Used in:** [Points into structure — Voronoi, Apollonius, contours and clusters](../spatial_geometry_examples.md), [Meshes and 3D geometry](../mesh_examples.md)

## Mapper.kt { #mapper-kt }

Mapper: a graph that summarises the shape of a point cloud, in any number of dimensions.

[`Mapper.compute`](graphics.md#mapper-kt--mapper--compute) gives every point a *lens* value, cuts the range of the lens into overlapping
bins, clusters the points within each bin, and joins clusters in neighbouring bins that share
points. The [`MapperGraph`](graphics.md#mapper-kt-mappergraph) that comes back has a [`MapperNode`](graphics.md#mapper-kt-mappernode) per cluster and a [`MapperEdge`](graphics.md#mapper-kt-mapperedge)
wherever two clusters share points, so a cloud with branches, loops or separate pieces produces
a graph with branches, loops or separate pieces; [`MapperGraph.components`](graphics.md#mapper-kt--mappergraph--components) and `MapperGraph.loops`
count those directly.

The lens decides what the graph can see. [`Mapper.coordinate`](graphics.md#mapper-kt--mapper--coordinate) slices the cloud along one axis,
[`Mapper.eccentricity`](graphics.md#mapper-kt--mapper--eccentricity) measures how far each point is from the rest and so picks out the ends of
branches whatever direction they run in, and [`Mapper.density`](graphics.md#mapper-kt--mapper--density) measures how crowded a point's
neighbourhood is. Any array with one value per point will do.

[`MapperGraph.toFLines`](graphics.md#mapper-kt--mappergraph--toflines) draws the graph over the cloud's first two coordinates, each node sized by
how many points it holds and coloured by its mean lens value; [`MapperGraph.pointsFLine`](graphics.md#mapper-kt--mappergraph--pointsfline) draws the
points themselves; and [`MapperGraph.network`](graphics.md#mapper-kt--mappergraph--network) hands the graph on as a [`GeometryNetwork`](graphics.md#geometrynetwork-kt-geometrynetwork). The
worked account is `public/docs/mapper.md`.

## MorseSmale.kt { #morsesmale-kt }

The Morse–Smale complex of a 2-D scalar field: where its peaks, pits and passes are, how they
are joined, and which of them are significant.

[`MorseSmale`](graphics.md#morsesmale-kt-morsesmale) is the entry point. It builds a [`MorseSmaleComplex`](graphics.md#morsesmale-kt-morsesmalecomplex) once, from an image channel or
a float grid, and the complex then answers for any persistence threshold without being rebuilt,
which is what makes a persistence slider cheap. Each threshold gives a [`MorseSmaleResult`](graphics.md#morsesmale-kt-morsesmaleresult): the
surviving [`CriticalPoint`](graphics.md#morsesmale-kt-criticalpoint)s, the separatrices between them as a `GeometryNetwork`, and the basin
and peak segmentation as one id per pixel. The whole hierarchy is readable from the complex as
[`PersistencePair`](graphics.md#morsesmale-kt-persistencepair)s and [`Cancellation`](graphics.md#morsesmale-kt-cancellation)s, and [`MorseSmaleTimings`](graphics.md#morsesmale-kt-morsesmaletimings) splits the build by stage.

Persistence is in the field's own units and removes features by significance, so it is a
different thing from blurring the field or smoothing the drawn separatrices. What the threshold
does to a picture, and what the complex is good for once you have it, are in
`public/docs/morse_smale.md`; following the critical points through time or scale is
`afield.geometry.topology.tracking`.

The complex is computed by the optional native library `field_morse_smale`
([`MorseSmaleLibrary`](graphics.md#morsesmalenative-kt-morsesmalelibrary)), so it holds native memory and is closed by the box's next run.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/topology/morsesmale/MorseSmale.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/topology/morsesmale/MorseSmale/)

**Used in:** [Morse–Smale complexes: the shape of a scalar field](../morse_smale.md), [Tracking features through time and scale](../topology_tracking.md)

### PersistencePair { #morsesmale-kt-persistencepair }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">PersistencePair</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">birth</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">death</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dimension</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">persistence</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/topology/morsesmale/MorseSmale/#L65)

One pair of the persistence diagram. `dimension` 0 pairs a minimum (`birth`) with the saddle that merges its basin away (`death`); dimension 1 pairs a saddle with the maximum that fills its cycle. The global minimum's `death` is null and its `persistence` infinite.

## MorseSmaleNative.kt { #morsesmalenative-kt }

Finding `field_morse_smale` on this machine, and calling into it once found.

[`MorseSmaleLibrary`](graphics.md#morsesmalenative-kt-morsesmalelibrary) is the half that answers without loading anything: the library's file name on
this OS, the paths it is looked for in, whether one of them exists, and the Gradle task and
per-OS shell commands that build it. `NativeGeometry` registers it as a
[`NativeGeometryCapability`](graphics.md#nativegeometry-kt-nativegeometrycapability), so the welcome page's Geometry extensions panel can report on the
library whether or not it is installed. The path is resolved afresh on every read, so a library
built during a live session is picked up by the next box run.

The other half, internal to the package, binds the C ABI declared in
`native/field-morse-smale/src/field_morse_smale.h` with java.lang.foreign: one lazy downcall
handle per `fms_` entry point, and a 512-byte buffer that building a complex and simplifying one
carry down and read a message out of when they hand back nothing. The counts and read-outs take
no error buffer. The first symbol lookup checks `fms_abi_version` against the version this
binding expects and refuses a library that disagrees, naming the task that rebuilds it.

Two kinds of native object pass through here, and only one of them is the caller's to free.
Building a complex hands back an address that must be freed exactly once, and reading it copies
the critical points, the cancellation order, the persistence pairs and the stage timings out
into Kotlin arrays in one pass. Simplifying at a threshold builds a second native object, a view;
that call copies the surviving nodes, the separatrix arcs with their traced paths, and the basin
and peak segmentation out of it, then frees the view before returning.

[`MorseSmale`](graphics.md#morsesmale-kt-morsesmale) is the API over it, and its only caller.

## FeatureTracking.kt { #featuretracking-kt }

Following the topological features of a 2-D field from one moment to the next, so that a peak
keeps its identity while it moves, and comparing two fields by their topology alone.

A Morse–Smale complex says where the peaks, pits and passes of one field are; it says nothing
about which peak of this frame is which peak of the last. That correspondence is an assignment
problem, and [`FeatureMatching`](graphics.md#featuretracking-kt-featurematching) solves it exactly for each moment, with a cost per match and a
fixed price for leaving a feature unmatched ([`MatchingWeights`](graphics.md#featuretracking-kt-matchingweights)), so births and deaths are priced
in the same optimisation as the matches. [`FeatureTracker`](graphics.md#featuretracking-kt-featuretracker) drives it frame by
frame and accumulates [`Track`](graphics.md#featuretracking-kt-track)s; [`ScaleSpace`](graphics.md#featuretracking-kt-scalespace) runs the same matching over a blur series instead of
over time, where the scale a feature survives to is a measure of its size.

The input is a list of [`Feature`](graphics.md#featuretracking-kt-feature)s, which [`MorseSmaleResult.features`](graphics.md#featuretracking-kt--features) reads off a Morse–Smale
result and `VectorFieldTopology` supplies from a vector field's critical points, so the tracker
itself is indifferent to where the features came from.

[`persistenceDiagramDistance`](graphics.md#featuretracking-kt--persistencediagramdistance) answers the other question, about whole fields rather than single
features: how far apart two persistence diagrams are, exactly for diagrams of up to a few
thousand pairs and entropically for larger ones. Everything here is plain Kotlin and needs no
native library, though its usual source does. The worked account is
`public/docs/topology_tracking.md`.

## ContourTrees.kt { #contourtrees-kt }

Merge trees and contour trees of a scalar field on a regular grid.

[`ContourTrees.joinTree`](graphics.md#contourtrees-kt--contourtrees--jointree) follows the components of the sublevel sets as the threshold rises,
[`ContourTrees.splitTree`](graphics.md#contourtrees-kt--contourtrees--splittree) does the same from the top down, and [`ContourTrees.contourTree`](graphics.md#contourtrees-kt--contourtrees--contourtree) follows
every component of every level set, so joins and splits are both recorded. Each hands back a
[`ScalarTree`](graphics.md#contourtrees-kt-scalartree) of [`TreeNode`](graphics.md#contourtrees-kt-treenode)s typed by [`TreeNodeType`](graphics.md#contourtrees-kt-treenodetype) and [`TreeArc`](graphics.md#contourtrees-kt-treearc)s between them, and every arc
owns the pixels of the level-set component it stands for, readable per pixel through
[`ScalarTree.arcOfPixel`](graphics.md#contourtrees-kt--scalartree--arcofpixel).

[`ScalarTree.simplify`](graphics.md#contourtrees-kt--scalartree--simplify) is what makes a tree readable: it repeatedly removes leaf arcs whose value
span is under a persistence threshold, so small bumps and dips go first. [`ScalarTree.plot`](graphics.md#contourtrees-kt--scalartree--plot) draws
the tree with height for value, [`ScalarTree.segmentationImage`](graphics.md#contourtrees-kt--scalartree--segmentationimage) paints each pixel by the arc that
owns it, and [`ScalarTree.network`](graphics.md#contourtrees-kt--scalartree--network) hands the tree on as a [`GeometryNetwork`](graphics.md#geometrynetwork-kt-geometrynetwork).

The field is read as the same piecewise-linear surface Field's Morse–Smale complexes use: the
grid cut into triangles along one diagonal, with ties between equal samples broken by pixel
index. The worked account is `public/docs/contour_trees.md`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/topology/trees/ContourTrees.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/topology/trees/ContourTrees/)

**Used in:** [Merge trees and contour trees](../contour_trees.md)

### TreeNodeType { #contourtrees-kt-treenodetype }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">TreeNodeType</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/topology/trees/ContourTrees/#L36)

The kind of a tree node: where a component of the level set begins or ends (`MINIMUM`, `MAXIMUM`), where two components join or one splits (`SADDLE`), or where the tree is rooted (`ROOT`, the global extremum a merge tree ends at).

Constants: `MINIMUM`, `MAXIMUM`, `SADDLE`, `ROOT`.

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">TreeNode</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">vertex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">type</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">TreeNodeType</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/topology/trees/ContourTrees/#L39)

## VectorFieldTopology.kt { #vectorfieldtopology-kt }

The topology of a 2-D flow field: where it stands still, and the curves that divide it up.

`VectorFieldTopology.compute` reads the flow either as two images, u and v in their first
channel, or as one RGB image with u in channel 0 and v in channel 1. It finds the field's zeros
as [`FlowCriticalPoint`](graphics.md#vectorfieldtopology-kt-flowcriticalpoint)s, classified by [`FlowCriticalType`](graphics.md#vectorfieldtopology-kt-flowcriticaltype) into sources, sinks, saddles, the two
kinds of focus and centres, together with the [`Separatrix`](graphics.md#vectorfieldtopology-kt-separatrix) curves that leave each saddle along
its eigen-directions.
Those curves cut the frame into regions inside which every streamline starts at the same place
and ends at the same place, so they summarise the whole field rather than sampling it.

What comes back is ready to draw: [`VectorFieldTopology.streamlines`](graphics.md#vectorfieldtopology-kt--vectorfieldtopology--streamlines) for a grid-seeded picture of
the flow, [`VectorFieldTopology.toFLines`](graphics.md#vectorfieldtopology-kt--vectorfieldtopology--toflines) for the separatrices and
[`VectorFieldTopology.criticalPointsFLine`](graphics.md#vectorfieldtopology-kt--vectorfieldtopology--criticalpointsfline) for the points, coloured by type.
[`VectorFieldTopology.features`](graphics.md#vectorfieldtopology-kt--vectorfieldtopology--features) hands the critical points to
[`afield.geometry.topology.tracking.FeatureTracker`](graphics.md#featuretracking-kt-featuretracker), so a flow that changes can be followed frame
by frame, and [`VectorFieldTopology.network`](graphics.md#vectorfieldtopology-kt--vectorfieldtopology--network) gives the same topology as a [`GeometryNetwork`](graphics.md#geometrynetwork-kt-geometrynetwork),
which is what the other geometry modules read.

Everything here is Kotlin, with no optional native library behind it. A scalar field can be read
the same way through `VectorFieldTopology.gradientOf`, which turns one into its gradient, or into
the flow along its contours. The worked account is `public/docs/vector_field_topology.md`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/topology/vectorfield/VectorFieldTopology.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/topology/vectorfield/VectorFieldTopology/)

**Used in:** [Vector field topology](../vector_field_topology.md)

### FlowCriticalType { #vectorfieldtopology-kt-flowcriticaltype }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">FlowCriticalType</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/topology/vectorfield/VectorFieldTopology/#L46)

What a flow does near a critical point: flows out (`SOURCE`), in (`SINK`), spirals out or in (`REPELLING_FOCUS`, `ATTRACTING_FOCUS`), circles (`CENTER`), or comes in along one direction and leaves along another (`SADDLE`).

Constants: `SOURCE`, `SINK`, `SADDLE`, `REPELLING_FOCUS`, `ATTRACTING_FOCUS`, `CENTER`.

### FlowCriticalPoint { #vectorfieldtopology-kt-flowcriticalpoint }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">FlowCriticalPoint</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">id</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">type</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FlowCriticalType</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">jacobian</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/topology/vectorfield/VectorFieldTopology/#L53)

A zero of the flow, at ([`x`](graphics.md#vectorfieldtopology-kt--flowcriticalpoint--x), [`y`](graphics.md#vectorfieldtopology-kt--flowcriticalpoint--y)) in pixels. [`jacobian`](graphics.md#vectorfieldtopology-kt--flowcriticalpoint--jacobian) is the flow's derivative there, row-major (`du/dx, du/dy, dv/dx, dv/dy`); `divergence` and `curl` are its trace and rotation, and `strength` `sqrt(|det J|)`, how fast the flow moves away from the point (in units of the field per pixel).

### Separatrix { #vectorfieldtopology-kt-separatrix }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Separatrix</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">saddle</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">unstable</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">points</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">end</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/topology/vectorfield/VectorFieldTopology/#L75)

A separatrix: the streamline that leaves a saddle along one of its four eigen-directions. An `unstable` one flows out of the saddle (forward in time); a stable one flows into it (traced backward). `points` are pixel positions starting at the saddle; `end` is the critical point it reached, or null if it left the frame, ran out of length, or stopped at a point weaker than `minStrength`.

## Polyvector.kt { #polyvector-kt }

Turning a raster line drawing into curves, by the polyvector-field method of Bessmeltsev and
Solomon (2019).

The problem this solves is the junction: where two strokes cross, a tracer that follows ink alone
has no way to tell which outgoing branch continues which incoming one. A [`PolyvectorField`](graphics.md#polyvector-kt-polyvectorfield) gives
every ink pixel *two* unsigned directions rather than one, so a crossing is a pixel where both
strokes are represented and each can be followed through it. [`Polyvector`](graphics.md#polyvector-kt-polyvector) is the entry point:
[`Polyvector.fitField`](graphics.md#polyvector-kt--polyvector--fitfield) solves for the field, [`PolyvectorField.trace`](graphics.md#polyvector-kt--polyvectorfield--trace) reads curves off it as a
[`PolyvectorDrawing`](graphics.md#polyvector-kt-polyvectordrawing), and [`Polyvector.vectorize`](graphics.md#polyvector-kt--polyvector--vectorize) does both for a dark-on-light scan.

Fitting the field is the expensive step and tracing is not, which is why the controls come in two
parts: [`FrameFieldParameters`](graphics.md#polyvector-kt-framefieldparameters) for the field, [`TraceParameters`](graphics.md#polyvector-kt-traceparameters) for the trace. A drawing can be
re-traced at several prune ratios without the field being solved again.

The input is *evidence*, 0 to 1, for how much each pixel is ink, not a picture:
[`Polyvector.inkOf`](graphics.md#polyvector-kt--polyvector--inkof) gets it from a dark-on-light drawing as `1 - luminance`, and an edge or ridge
detector's output can be passed to [`Polyvector.fitField`](graphics.md#polyvector-kt--polyvector--fitfield) instead. Coordinates throughout are
pixels at pixel centres, x right and y down. The worked account, including which drawings the
method suits, is `public/docs/polyvector.md`.

The solver is the optional native library `field_polyvector` ([`PolyvectorLibrary`](graphics.md#polyvectornative-kt-polyvectorlibrary)), so a field
holds native memory and is closed by the box's next run.
