## textures.kt { #textures-kt }

Sampled textures for Field 4 shaders: images decoded from disk or memory, CPU-streamed frames, and GPU-writable storage images.

[`LoadedTexture`](graphics.md#textures-kt-loadedtexture) decodes a PNG/JPEG (via STB) or an EXR (via tinyexr) into a Vulkan image with a
mip chain and a default [`TextureSampler`](graphics.md#texturesampler-kt-texturesampler); build one with `LoadedTexture.fromFile`,
`LoadedTexture.fromExrFile`, `LoadedTexture.fromEncodedMemory` or `LoadedTexture.fromRawRGBA`.
[`StreamingTexture`](graphics.md#textures-kt-streamingtexture) re-uploads a CPU `ByteBuffer` each frame it is asked to, and
[`MappedMonochromeTexture`](graphics.md#textures-kt-mappedmonochrometexture) uploads a single-channel image from a shared, header-prefixed mapped
buffer only when its frame counter changes. [`StorageImage`](graphics.md#textures-kt-storageimage) is a texture a compute shader writes.

## FrameSetBarrier.kt { #framesetbarrier-kt }

Holds back presentation of a frame set until every member is ready, so several textures switch
frames together.

Ordinary clock ticks cannot replace an unfinished set; a new seek or reconfiguration revision
can. `FrameSetBarrierTest` covers it.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/texture/video/FrameSetBarrier.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/texture/video/FrameSetBarrier/)

### FrameSetBarrier { #framesetbarrier-kt-framesetbarrier }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">FrameSetBarrier</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">K</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/texture/video/FrameSetBarrier/#L16)

Nonblocking two-phase presentation. Ordinary clock ticks cannot supersede an unfinished set (which would starve a slow decoder); an explicit seek/reconfiguration revision can. Call from one render thread. `K` must be an immutable source-frame identity.

It survives ordinary clock ticks, and is cleared by [`presentIfReady`](graphics.md#framesetbarrier-kt--framesetbarrier--presentifready), by [`revise`](graphics.md#framesetbarrier-kt--framesetbarrier--revise) with a new revision, or by [`reset`](graphics.md#framesetbarrier-kt--framesetbarrier--reset). |

[`presentIfReady`](graphics.md#framesetbarrier-kt--framesetbarrier--presentifready) moves [`pending`](graphics.md#framesetbarrier-kt--framesetbarrier--pending) here once its upload callback has returned, so this names images the caller has committed to rather than ones it has asked for. |

## FrameSetPacer.kt { #framesetpacer-kt }

Paces an asynchronous frame set so each frame gets a whole source-frame interval to prepare
before it is due.

A slow preparation stays the pending demand even when the wall clock has moved past it, which
keeps a slow decoder from being starved; seeks and reconfiguration may still replace it.
`FrameSetBarrierTest` exercises it alongside [`FrameSetBarrier`](graphics.md#framesetbarrier-kt-framesetbarrier).

## VideoDecoder.kt { #videodecoder-kt }

Decodes video frames with FFmpeg into P010 or RGBA8 buffers ([`VideoFrame`](graphics.md#videodecoder-kt-videoframe)) for [`VideoTexture`](graphics.md#videotexture-kt-videotexture).

[`VideoDecodeFormat`](graphics.md#videodecoder-kt-videodecodeformat) picks the output: P010 for ordinary display, RGBA8 when the R/G/B channels
are values that 4:2:0 chroma subsampling would destroy. `VideoFrameTest` covers [`VideoFrame`](graphics.md#videodecoder-kt-videoframe)
buffer release.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/texture/video/VideoDecoder.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/texture/video/VideoDecoder/)

### VideoDecoder { #videodecoder-kt-videodecoder }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">VideoDecoder</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">videoPath</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">outputFormat</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">VideoDecodeFormat</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">VideoDecodeFormat</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">P010</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AutoCloseable</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/texture/video/VideoDecoder/#L34)

VideoDecoder wraps FFmpeg functionality to decode video frames. Converts decoded frames either to P010 for ordinary video display or to tightly-packed RGBA8 for data-bearing RGB movies. The latter matters for atlases whose R/G/B channels are values rather than colour: routing those through 4:2:0 YUV would irreversibly subsample the channels.

## VideoFrameIndex.kt { #videoframeindex-kt }

Frame-number arithmetic for constant-frame-rate video, shared by the code that asks for a frame
and the code that reports which frame a decoder produced.

A timeline position belongs to the frame whose interval contains it, so [`VideoFrameIndex.requested`](graphics.md#videoframeindex-kt--videoframeindex--requested)
floors `seconds * fps`. A decoded presentation timestamp marks a frame's own start, which may
carry rounding error in either direction, so [`VideoFrameIndex.decoded`](graphics.md#videoframeindex-kt--videoframeindex--decoded) rounds to the nearest frame.

## VideoTexture.kt { #videotexture-kt }

Plays a video file into Vulkan textures that a shader can sample, with [`VideoTexture.load`](graphics.md#videotexture-kt--videotexture--load),
[`VideoTexture.play`](graphics.md#videotexture-kt--videotexture--play), [`VideoTexture.pause`](graphics.md#videotexture-kt--videotexture--pause), [`VideoTexture.seek`](graphics.md#videotexture-kt--videotexture--seek) and [`VideoTexture.unload`](graphics.md#videotexture-kt--videotexture--unload).

Frames come from [`VideoDecoder`](graphics.md#videodecoder-kt-videodecoder) as P010 (luma and chroma planes) for display video, or as RGBA8
for movies whose channels carry data. Timing comes from a [`PlaybackClock`](graphics.md#playbackclock-kt-playbackclock): an internal
[`SystemClock`](graphics.md#playbackclock-kt-systemclock) by default, or an [`AudioClock`](graphics.md#playbackclock-kt-audioclock) for audio-locked playback.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/texture/video/VideoTexture.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/texture/video/VideoTexture/)

## WebcamTexture.kt { #webcamtexture-kt }

Exposes a webcam as an RGBA Vulkan texture, captured through OpenCV.

The first frame is uploaded on open so [`WebcamTexture.imageView`](graphics.md#webcamtexture-kt--webcamtexture--imageview) is valid immediately; later
frames are grabbed on a background thread and uploaded from the render thread.

## GeometryView.kt { #geometryview-kt }

Showing a `geometry { }` recipe in a studio-lit `three` view, and handing the recipe language to
this document's AI4 chat.

[`Box.geometry`](graphics.md#geometryview-kt--geometry) runs a [`GeometryBuilder`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt-geometrybuilder) block in a box and draws the [`GeometryScene`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt-geometryscene) it builds:
every part as a mesh with its own material, the scene's background and ground, and the toolbox's
three-quarter camera. [`Box.animateGeometry`](graphics.md#geometryview-kt--animategeometry) re-runs the block with [`GeometryBuilder.t`](graphics.md#geometrybuilder-kt--geometrybuilder--t) moving and
returns a [`Frames`](workspace.md#phased-kt-frames) for the box to launch. The camera is a spec rather than a position, so it
survives both a re-run and an animation frame and the model can be orbited while it changes
underneath.

[`geometryAgent`](graphics.md#geometryview-kt--geometryagent) bridges those views to AI4. The chat agent is given [`GEOMETRY_GUIDE`](graphics.md#geometryview-kt--geometry-guide) before every
turn and a `geometry.look` tool that returns a picture of a view as it stands on screen, which is
what lets a model edit a recipe and then see the result. A view that is not open is drawn by the
CPU rasterizer instead, without the studio's lighting, and the agent is told which it got.

## SimplexView.kt { #simplexview-kt }

An orbitable picture of a handful of embeddings and the distances between them, in a box's output.

[`SimplexView`](graphics.md#simplexview-kt-simplexview) wraps one of the `three` viewers and draws what the madp `tetra` page draws: a
coloured sphere per point, an edge per pair, the point numbers and edge lengths written onto the
picture, and a table of the pairs in the corner. [`simplexView`](graphics.md#simplexview-kt--simplexview) opens one and hands it back, so
[`SimplexView.show`](graphics.md#simplexview-kt--simplexview--show) can replace the simplex underneath without resetting the camera you orbited
to; [`showSimplex`](graphics.md#simplexview-kt--showsimplex) is the one-call form, for a picture that is drawn once. Before the first
simplex arrives the view holds a regular tetrahedron with no lengths on it, and [`SimplexView.dim`](graphics.md#simplexview-kt--simplexview--dim)
greys the current picture while a newer one is being worked out.

What is drawn is an [`EmbeddingSimplex`](data.md#embeddingsimplex-kt-embeddingsimplex), which places the vectors in 3D so that the drawn edges
are their pairwise distances: exactly so for four points or fewer, a best fit above that. The
note in the corner says which of the two you are looking at, and quotes the stress when it is
the second.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
showSimplex(embeddingSimplex(listOf(clipEncode("cat"), clipEncode("dog"), clipEncode("car"))))
```

## SolidInspection.kt { #solidinspection-kt }

The three things the solid inspector measures off a part's boundary: which edges are worth
drawing, which triangles belong to the same face, and one string that identifies the whole set of
parts.

A boundary arrives as a [`SolidPlanarMesh`](graphics.md#solidplanarmesh-kt-solidplanarmesh) whose triangles carry the diagonals its triangulator
needed and the coplanar edges its Boolean history left behind, so drawing every edge buries the
shape under both. `solidOutlineEdges` keeps an edge unless exactly two triangles meet along it and
those two are one flat face: normals parallel and facing the same way, and each triangle's
vertices within tolerance of the other's plane. An edge where some other number of triangles meet,
or where a triangle is too degenerate to have a normal, stays visible, so an open surface keeps
its perimeter rather than reading as a closed solid. The tolerance is the mesh's own
`nativeTolerance` or sixty-four ulps of the part's largest coordinate, whichever is larger, so a
part modelled in metres and the same part in millimetres get the same answer.

`solidPartTopology` groups the triangles into faces by merging across every edge that is not one
of those creases. It keeps the canonical double-precision positions and the original triangle
order, because a pick is resolved against this copy rather than against the render mesh, whose
vertices shading has already split.

`solidArtifactDigest` hashes part names, positions, indices and faces in sorted name order, so the
same boundaries hash the same however the parts were collected. That digest is the geometry
identity a review note is pinned to, which is what lets a note outlive a relaunch.

## SolidParts.kt { #solidparts-kt }

A set of named solid parts, shown in a Three.js scene as something to inspect rather than
something to look at. One call inside a `three { … }` block lays out every part as its own
pickable mesh, draws each one's creases and open boundaries over it as dark lines, and installs
the inspector: units, the explode slider, per-part visibility, assembly motions and the paths a
part came from.

A part arrives as a planar mesh whose triangles carry the diagonals the triangulator needed and
the coplanar edges Boolean history left behind, so drawing every edge would bury the shape under
both. What is drawn instead is the geometric outline: creases between faces that meet at a real
angle, and boundaries where a part ends. Edges between separate parts stay visible, since those
are where the assembly is.

Coordinates stay canonical throughout. Positions reach the GPU as `Float`s relative to one shared
render origin, and `upAxis = ThreeUpAxis.Z` is a rigid display rotation applied on the way out, so
neither large coordinates nor a Z-up convention changes the double-precision data the inspector
reports or the digest that identifies the artifact.

## Three.kt { #three-kt }

One 3D output for everything Field can draw: [`Box.three`](graphics.md#three-kt--three) puts meshes and FLines in one orbitable
Three.js scene.

[`Box.three`](graphics.md#three-kt--three) extends [`Box.threeLines`](graphics.md#threejsviewer-kt--threelines) to meshes, and lays several views out side by side when you ask
for a contact sheet:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
three(channel = "car", height = 460) {
    mesh(car, wireframe = false, pickable = true)
    lines(measurements)                       // annotations in the same space as the solid
    inspect(units = "mm")                     // …and a ruler that reaches both
    camera(yaw = 34.0, pitch = 26.0, distance = 2.4)
    title("ToyCar.glb — 108,936 triangles")
}
```

With `pickable = true` a click on a mesh resolves to a vertex, an edge or a triangle
([`ThreeSurfaceHit`](graphics.md#threescene-kt-threesurfacehit)), so the measure tool can span a solid and its annotations.

### Compared with the CPU rasterizer

The CPU rasterizer in [`VisionGeometryPreview`](graphics.md#visiongeometrypreview-kt-visiongeometrypreview) still draws a mesh to a static PNG, and remains the
tool for value-visualizer thumbnails and pixel-exact tests such as `MeshDefectRenderTest`, since it
is deterministic. It cannot orbit, or put a solid and its FLine annotations in one scene.

### Shading differs

The shading models differ. The rasterizer is two-light Lambert over vertex colours; this is
three.js's `MeshStandardMaterial` under the viewer's ambient/key/rim rig. The same mesh will not
come out pixel-identical. The input is held identical (see [`toThreeDrawable`](graphics.md#threescene-kt--tothreedrawable)), as is back-face
culling, so a face wound the wrong way is missing from both.

## ThreeJsInspector.kt { #threejsinspector-kt }

Measure, section and explode controls for the Three.js viewer, so a 3D preview of something to be
built can be inspected without re-running its box.

The inspector answers three questions:

 * **how far apart are these two things**: [`ThreeMeasurement`](graphics.md#threejsinspector-kt-threemeasurement), drawn in the scene as a dimension
   with witness lines and a legible number;
 * **what does this look like in section**: [`ThreeSection`](graphics.md#threejsinspector-kt-threesection), a cut plane with a highlighted cut
   outline, not merely a hidden front half;
 * **how does it come apart**: [`ThreeExplode`](graphics.md#threejsinspector-kt-threeexplode), a parameter with a scrubber, in two modes.

### Where the work happens

The displacement, the cut and the closest approach are computed in the viewer
(`threejs_viewer.html`), so moving a slider costs no websocket round-trip and no box re-run. Each
of the three is a marked `// [viewer-region …]` region of that HTML, which
`ThreeInspectorMeasureDifferentialTest`, `ThreeInspectorExplodeDifferentialTest` and
`ThreeInspectorSectionDifferentialTest` lift out and run on GraalJS against expectations derived
from the figure geometry.

The regions cover the geometry only. The three.js plumbing around them (`localClippingEnabled`,
the canvas-texture sprite the dimension text is drawn into, the HUD sliders) is not under those
tests, so an empty dimension sprite would leave them green.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/three/ThreeJsInspector.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/three/ThreeJsInspector/)

**Used in:** [FLine examples (Field graphics)](../fline_examples.md), [Three.js scenes with `three { … }`](../three_output.md), [Point to geometry, keep the context](../geometry_review.md)

## ThreeJsViewer.kt { #threejsviewer-kt }

The Three.js viewer's server side: the geometry payload it is sent, the live state of each view,
and [`Box.threeLines`](graphics.md#threejsviewer-kt--threelines), which puts a viewer in a box's output area.

A view is an iframe on `/threejs` that orbits, picks and edits the geometry it is given. The
payload types ([`ThreeGeometryPayload`](graphics.md#threejsviewer-kt-threegeometrypayload), [`ThreeGeometryData`](graphics.md#threejsviewer-kt-threegeometrydata), [`ThreeAttribute`](graphics.md#threejsviewer-kt-threeattribute), [`ThreeIndex`](graphics.md#threejsviewer-kt-threeindex),
[`ThreeBounds`](graphics.md#threejsviewer-kt-threebounds)) mirror three.js `BufferGeometry`, plus the editable and interactive records a click
or a drag reports back. Each view has one [`ThreeGeometryViewState`](graphics.md#threejsviewer-kt-threegeometryviewstate): call its `update` to push new
geometry to every connected viewer. [`installThreeJsHandler`](graphics.md#threejsviewer-kt--installthreejshandler) answers the viewers' websocket
messages, and edits, surface clicks and review notes return to the box through it.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/three/ThreeJsViewer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/three/ThreeJsViewer/)

**Used in:** [Three.js scenes with `three { … }`](../three_output.md), [FLine examples (Field graphics)](../fline_examples.md)

## ThreePartAppearance.kt { #threepartappearance-kt }

Presentation overrides for a named part of a three-dimensional view.

Colours are RGB in 0..1, and a part with no x-ray opacity of its own follows the viewer's slider.
None of it changes geometry, picking, assembly groups or review identity: the styles travel beside
the geometry rather than baked into it, so restyling a part leaves every note on it attached.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/three/ThreePartAppearance.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/three/ThreePartAppearance/)

## ThreeReview.kt { #threereview-kt }

Geometry identity for a three-dimensional view: what a review note is pinned to.

A note survives anything that is only presentation. Callback and session IDs, hover colour, style
and label are left out of the digest, so orbiting, relighting and relaunching identical geometry
all leave a note attached. Canonical solids keep their double-boundary identity, and geometry
displayed alongside them contributes too: a moving ordinary point invalidates a note even when
every solid is unchanged.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/three/ThreeReview.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/three/ThreeReview/)

## ThreeReviewEvidence.kt { #threereviewevidence-kt }

Stores the screenshots a geometry review note carries as PNG files beside the document rather than
as base64 inside it.

The browser sends a context image and a crop of it, each as a data URL, with the viewport and crop
rectangle they were taken from. Kept in the note, those would put megabytes of base64 into a text
property that is saved, versioned and diffed on every edit. `store` writes each image into the
document's `.geometry-review` directory under its own SHA-256 and returns the note's metadata with
a `/three-review-image` URL in place of the bytes, so a second note of the same pixels adds a
reference and no file.

The validation is what makes those files safe to serve back. The images have to agree with the
note about geometry digest, view and panel; the payload has to be a PNG by signature and by
decoding, at the dimensions the browser declared, within 1600 px for the context image and 1024 px
for the crop; no image may exceed two million bytes and the directory may not exceed sixty-four
million. `read` answers only for a 64-character hex name that one of the notes it was handed
actually cites, so the route cannot be talked into returning a path of the caller's choosing or an
image belonging to another view.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/three/ThreeReviewEvidence.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/three/ThreeReviewEvidence/)

## ThreeScene.kt { #threescene-kt }

The intermediate representation the Three.js viewer draws: a [`ThreeDrawable`](graphics.md#threescene-kt-threedrawable) is some geometry plus
how to draw it.

[`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline)s lower to drawables, [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh)es lower to drawables, and anything with a `toTriMesh()`
reaches the viewer that way, so a mesh can be orbited and share a scene with its FLine
annotations. The viewer knows neither source type; it draws drawables.

The geometry is a [`ThreeGeometryData`](graphics.md#threejsviewer-kt-threegeometrydata), a three.js `BufferGeometry` of named attributes and an
index, and [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh)'s positions, indices, normals and colours transcribe into it directly. What a
drawable adds is per-drawable material state, [`ThreeDrawStyle`](graphics.md#threescene-kt-threedrawstyle).

[`ThreeGeometryPayload`](graphics.md#threejsviewer-kt-threegeometrypayload)'s `lines`, `fills` and `points` are unchanged by drawables: a payload with
an empty [`ThreeGeometryPayload.drawables`](graphics.md#threejsviewer-kt--threegeometrypayload--drawables) serialises as a lines-only payload always has, which the
editable path and the inspector rely on.

## ThreeWire.kt { #threewire-kt }

What a Three.js view puts on the wire, and what it refuses to.

A view's geometry goes out in two parts. The websocket carries a *description*: the payload with
every numeric array replaced by a reference into a buffer table, so the message stays small however
large the scene is. The arrays themselves are one binary response from
`GET /three-buffers?uid=…&generation=…`, written straight out of the payload's own arrays, and only
when a viewer asks for them. Nothing is formatted as decimal text, nothing the size of the scene is
allocated, and the bytes go out on a Ktor IO thread rather than on the runloop.
[`ThreeWireBuffers`](graphics.md#threewire-kt-threewirebuffers) is the table a description carries and [`ThreeWireBuffer`](graphics.md#threewire-kt-threewirebuffer) one entry in it.

A geometry over `AFIELD_THREE_PAYLOAD_LIMIT_MB`, 512 MB by default, is not sent at all:
[`ThreePayloadTooLargeException`](graphics.md#threewire-kt-threepayloadtoolargeexception) names the largest contributors and the view keeps what it was
already showing. That ceiling is for the browser, which has to hold the buffers and then copy them
to the GPU; the server streams arrays it is holding anyway.

A client that does not ask for buffers in its hello, as the native visionOS viewer does not, is
sent the FLine half of the payload as JSON numbers instead, the format it decodes, without the
drawables and solid topology it never reads. That form is encoded only while such a client is
connected. The viewer side of all this is the `wire-payload` region of `threejs_viewer.html`, and
`ThreeGeometryWireTest` holds the two halves against each other.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/three/ThreeWire.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/three/ThreeWire/)

One typed array in a buffer response. Offsets are multiples of eight, so a Float64 view needs no copy.

## VisionGeometryPreview.kt { #visiongeometrypreview-kt }

See a Live Metal box's `geometry { … }` on your desk, without a headset.

### What this proves, and what it does not

A `// {{ visionmetal }}` box has three parts, and only one of them can be checked away from the
device today. This previews **the geometry part, and only that**:

 - The mesh is built by the *real* builder. [`capture`](graphics.md#visiongeometrypreview-kt--visiongeometrypreview--capture-2) resolves the box source through the real
   [`KotlinJsHeadProfiles.visionMetal`](languages.md#kotlinjsheadprofiles-kt--kotlinjsheadprofiles--visionmetal) profile, compiles it with the real [`KotlinToJsCompiler`](languages.md#kotlintojscompiler-kt-kotlintojscompiler), and
   runs the emitted JavaScript under `node` against `hostShim` — a mirror of
   `LiveMetalJavaScript.swift`. What gets captured is the byte-identical packed array the headset's
   Metal vertex buffer would receive. Nothing here reimplements `MeshBuilder`; if the shared
   [`VisionMetalKotlinJs`](graphics.md#visionmetalkotlinjs-kt-visionmetalkotlinjs) builder source changes, this changes with it.
 - The **shader is a stand-in**. The box's MSL is not compiled, not translated and not simulated.
   [`render`](graphics.md#visiongeometrypreview-kt--visiongeometrypreview--render) shades with a fixed two-light lambert over the vertex colours the builder wrote. So a
   preview answers *"is my geometry the shape I meant?"* — the other half of the question the
   **Vision Geometry: Built-in Cube** command answers. It cannot tell you your shader is right.

That boundary is repeated in the caption burnt into every rendered frame.

### Typical use

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val capture = VisionGeometryPreview.capture(box.code)
val png = VisionGeometryPreview.renderPng(capture.mesh())
display(png)
```

or, from a Live Metal box's own commands, the **Preview Vision Geometry** action.

## VisionGeometryPreviewBox.kt { #visiongeometrypreviewbox-kt }

The in-Field half of [`VisionGeometryPreview`](graphics.md#visiongeometrypreview-kt-visiongeometrypreview): turning "my mesh only exists in the headset" into a
picture in the box you wrote it in.

A Live Metal box's Kotlin never runs on the Mac — it compiles to JavaScript for the head — so its
output panel is normally empty of anything but log lines. [`Box.previewVisionGeometry`](graphics.md#visiongeometrypreviewbox-kt--previewvisiongeometry) fills that
gap: it takes the box's own source, runs it for real (see [`VisionGeometryPreview.capture`](graphics.md#visiongeometrypreview-kt--visiongeometrypreview--capture-2)) and
draws the resulting mesh straight into the box's output. One command, and your headset geometry is
on the desktop.

## VisionMetal.kt { #visionmetal-kt }

Live Metal: the channel that pushes a box's Metal program down to a visionOS head, which compiles
and renders it there.

A `// {{ visionmetal }}` box is sent as a [`VisionMetalProgramPayload`](graphics.md#visionmetal-kt-visionmetalprogrampayload) carrying any of four independently
revisioned parts — shader ([`VisionMetalShaderPart`](graphics.md#visionmetal-kt-visionmetalshaderpart)), script ([`VisionMetalScriptPart`](graphics.md#visionmetal-kt-visionmetalscriptpart)), uniform
names ([`VisionMetalUniformsPart`](graphics.md#visionmetal-kt-visionmetaluniformspart)) and geometry ([`VisionMetalGeometryPart`](graphics.md#visionmetal-kt-visionmetalgeometrypart)) — so reloading one part
leaves the others resident on the head. [`VisionMetalProgramState`](graphics.md#visionmetal-kt-visionmetalprogramstate) holds one program's current
parts on this side; [`Box.visionMetalProgramOrCreate`](graphics.md#visionmetal-kt--visionmetalprogramorcreate) finds or makes the one for a box, and
[`installVisionMetalHandler`](graphics.md#visionmetal-kt--installvisionmetalhandler) registers the `/ws` handler that heads subscribe through and report
[`VisionMetalStatus`](graphics.md#visionmetal-kt-visionmetalstatus) back on.

Offline checks of the same program live in [`VisionMetalProgramCheck`](graphics.md#visionmetalprogramcheck-kt-visionmetalprogramcheck) (uniform names) and
[`VisionGeometryPreview`](graphics.md#visiongeometrypreview-kt-visiongeometrypreview) (the geometry part).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/visionos/VisionMetal.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/visionos/VisionMetal/)

## VisionMetalKotlinJs.kt { #visionmetalkotlinjs-kt }

Kotlin/JS declarations for the JavaScriptCore runtime owned by Field4Vision's Live Metal
renderer.

Runtime Kotlin/JS compilation currently accepts one source file, so this surface is appended to
the user's source rather than compiled as a separate library. Appending means compiler
diagnostics keep the user's original line numbers. [`completionDeclarations`](graphics.md#visionmetalkotlinjs-kt--visionmetalkotlinjs--completiondeclarations) mirrors the same
public surface in JVM-analysis-safe Kotlin because the completion sidecar does not
load the Kotlin/JS compiler frontend.

This only describes values that really exist in `LiveMetalJavaScript.swift`. Two things cross that
bridge: named `float4` uniform writes, and whole geometry uploads. Geometry is the head's own —
`geometry { … }` builds an indexed triangle mesh in JavaScriptCore and hands the packed arrays to
Metal in one call, so nothing per-vertex crosses the network or the bridge at frame rate.

MSL source and the declared uniform slot order still travel in the `visionmetal/program` payload:
the shader lives in the box's `msl` property, and slot order comes from the head marker's
`uniforms=` option.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/visionos/VisionMetalKotlinJs.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/visionos/VisionMetalKotlinJs/)

## VisionMetalProgramCheck.kt { #visionmetalprogramcheck-kt }

The offline half of "will this Live Metal program actually run?".

A box names a uniform in three places, and these checks catch them disagreeing on the Mac:

 1. the `// {{ visionmetal uniforms=… }}` marker, which becomes the head's slot order;
 2. the shader, which reads `u_NAME` — the head generates `#define u_NAME frame.user[`i`](workspace.md#stdlib-kt--i)` from that
    list, so an undeclared `u_NAME` is a **Metal compile error on the device**;
 3. the script, whose `uniform("name", …)` writes land in a slot only if the name is declared —
    an undeclared write is dropped without a warning, and the shader just sees zero.

All three failures show up as "it doesn't work in the headset", minutes away from the edit that
caused them. Every one is decidable from the box's own text plus a real run of its script, which is
what this does. It is the uniform-shaped companion to
`VisionGeometryPreview.CapturedMesh.windingAgreement`.

Nothing here compiles MSL. These are the checks that need only the ABI the head documents, so
they run wherever Field runs; the real Metal compile happens on the device.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/visionos/VisionMetalProgramCheck.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/visionos/VisionMetalProgramCheck/)

## VisionPose.kt { #visionpose-kt }

The pose **uplink**: head and per-eye viewing geometry travelling *from* a visionOS head *to* this
Field process, so that the Vulkan renderer on this machine can draw the frame the headset is about
to display.

This runs opposite to Field's other visionOS channels. Live Metal ([`VisionMetalProgramState`](graphics.md#visionmetal-kt-visionmetalprogramstate)) pushes a program down
to the head and the head renders it; the RTT stream pushes encoded pixels down
(`native/field-encode/WIRE_FORMAT.md`). Neither tells this process where the wearer is looking, so
the streamed image can only ever be a world-locked surface — a plane in space. Head-locked,
full-field VR needs the pose to come *up* first, which is what this file receives.

### Wire format (`__visionpose__`, version 1)

JSON over the existing `/ws` bus, device → here. Three message types:

| `type` | when | carries |
|---|---|---|
| `visionpose/hello` | once per connection | `device`, `name`, the head's view count and refresh rate |
| `visionpose/frame` | once per compositor frame | the pose, below |
| `visionpose/bye`   | on a clean immersive-space exit | `device` |

A `visionpose/frame` is:

```diffstatic {data-lang=json}
{"channel":"__visionpose__","type":"visionpose/frame","version":1,
 "device":"<uuid>","frameIndex":1842,
 "predictedDisplayTime":123456.789,"sentAt":123456.778,
 "trackingValid":true,
 "originFromDevice":[16 floats],
 "views":[{"transform":[16 floats],"projection":[16 floats]}, …]}
```

Every matrix is **16 floats, column-major** — `m[column * 4 + row]`, which is both `simd_float4x4`'s
own storage order on the device and `Matrix4f`'s here, so the array crosses the wire untransposed.

`originFromDevice` is ARKit's `DeviceAnchor.originFromAnchorTransform`: the head's pose in the
world origin the head established. `views[`i`](workspace.md#stdlib-kt--i).transform` is CompositorServices'
`LayerRenderer.Drawable.View.transform`, i.e. device→eye, and `views[`i`](workspace.md#stdlib-kt--i).projection` is that
drawable's `computeProjection(viewIndex:)`. Both timestamps are in the head's own clock (seconds,
`LayerRenderer.Clock`), so differences *within* one head are meaningful and comparisons against
this machine's clock are not — see [`VisionPoseFrame.receivedAtNanos`](graphics.md#visionpose-kt--visionposeframe--receivedatnanos).

### Not solved here

- **Prediction.** `predictedDisplayTime` is when the *head's own* next frame displays, which is
  earlier than when a frame rendered here could arrive. Shifting the query forward by the measured
  render→encode→network→decode latency is left to the head; this file carries the timestamp
  unchanged so that shift is a one-line change there.
- **Transport.** JSON over the WebSocket reuses the bus, the dev-certificate trust and the
  reconnect logic the other native clients already have, at the cost of TCP in the tracking path.
  A pose is ~700 bytes; at 90 Hz that is ~60 kB/s, which is not a reason to move it to UDP; a
  measured latency would be.

## VisionPoseLatency.kt { #visionposelatency-kt }

Where the time goes between a head moving and the resulting image reaching it.

This attributes latency to stages rather than reporting one number, because the plausible
explanations for "it feels laggy" are spread across five machines' worth of stages, and two of
those stages hold frames back in order to do their job: the receiver's jitter buffer and the
producer's render fence.

### Two clocks, and why the headline number needs neither reconciled

The head's clock (`LayerRenderer.Clock`) and this process's `System.nanoTime` are unrelated. That
would normally make one-way timings unmeasurable. It does not here, because of a property of the
wire we already have: a pose's `predictedDisplayTime` is in the *head's* clock, and the media wire
carries it back to the head as `poseDisplayTimeNanos`. So the head can subtract two of its own
timestamps and get **motion-to-photon with no clock agreement at all**. That is why the headline
figure is measured on the device and reported here, rather than computed here.

The offset is still wanted, for splitting the remainder into "our side" and "their side". It is
estimated NTP-style from [`PING`](graphics.md#visionposelatency-kt--visionposelatency--ping)/[`PONG`](graphics.md#visionposelatency-kt--visionposelatency--pong) round trips, keeping the sample with the **smallest** round
trip rather than an average: the minimum is the one least polluted by queuing in either direction,
and averaging RTTs on a contended Wi-Fi link estimates the contention, not the offset.

### The two stages that hold frames back

The receiver runs a jitter buffer (`RTTStream.bufferFrames`) that holds frames so that
network jitter does not become dropped frames. It is reported as its own span. Without that split,
the buffer doing exactly its job looks like the network being slow, and the obvious "fix" —
shrinking it — trades smoothness for a better number.

Likewise `SUBMIT_TO_ENCODED` includes the render fence: the producer only signals a surface
once its GPU work has completed, so scene complexity lands in that span rather than anywhere else.

### What this cannot see

The device's last observable moment is the decoded frame reaching the display texture. Actual
photons are the compositor's business, up to one refresh later, and with the present path still on
RealityKit there is no hook for it. So the headline is a **lower bound**, short by up to one
compositor frame. That closes when the present path moves to Compositor Services, which is also
what makes reprojection possible; it is not worth faking before then.

## VisionPoseStereoSource.kt { #visionposestereosource-kt }

Drives Field's stereo rendering from a visionOS head's uplinked pose — the consumer end of
[`VisionPoseStream`](graphics.md#visionpose-kt-visionposestream).

Attach it to a [`afield.graphics.vulkan.targets.SideBySideStereoTarget`](graphics.md#sidebysidestereotarget-kt-sidebysidestereotarget) and the eye passes render from the
headset rather than from a desktop mock:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val sbs = SideBySideStereoTarget(renderer)
sbs.poseSource = VisionPoseStereoSource()
```

The projection is **rebuilt** rather than forwarded. The head sends the matrix its compositor
computed, but that carries the compositor's near/far and depth range; Field's Vulkan pipelines use
[`Options.zNear`](graphics.md#options-kt--options--znear)/[`Options.zFar`](graphics.md#options-kt--options--zfar) with a 0..1 depth range. So this takes the frustum *tangents* — the
convention-free part — and builds a projection exactly the way
[`afield.graphics.vulkan.targets.OpenXRHmdTarget`](graphics.md#openxrhmdtarget-kt-openxrhmdtarget) builds one from `XrFovf`'s angles. That is the whole reason
[`VisionEyeView`](graphics.md#visionpose-kt-visioneyeview) carries tangents at all.

The view matrix, by contrast, is forwarded untouched: the wire already carries world→eye, composed
on arrival the same way the head composes its own, so there is nothing to reinterpret.

## CaptureOrientation.kt { #captureorientation-kt }

The row order a pixel source hands to an encoder, and the paths that are held to it.

Row order is not a property of the encoder, and not a property of the file format: it is a
property of the *readback*. A "flip Y" at a call site says what a line of code does and not what
it is for, so each capture path carries the order its source delivers instead, and a test reads
the source back to check that the two agree.

## ModuleDestinations.kt { #moduledestinations-kt }

Where a module's drawing ends up, and a picture of it there: the window it is added to, or the
render-to-texture that holds it — found by walking what the renderer draws, not by being told.

`renderer += module` puts a module in a window's main pass; `rtt += module` in a render target, which
draws when something reaches it (usually the renderer's `preTargets`). Walking the windows' passes,
everything their `others` and `preTargets` reach, and the headset target finds every place that draws
the module, compared by identity. A target drawn by some other path is not found.

[`ModuleDestinations.capture`](graphics.md#moduledestinations-kt--moduledestinations--capture) reads one of those places back as PNG bytes, and
[`ModuleDestinations.renderDisposable`](graphics.md#moduledestinations-kt--moduledestinations--renderdisposable) draws a module alone into a temporary render target and returns
that picture. StackSL's auto-study uses both to show what a module drew.

## Renderer.kt { #renderer-kt }

The Vulkan renderer: one [`Renderer`](graphics.md#renderer-kt-renderer) owns the instance, device, queues, command pools and the
swapchain of each of its windows, and records, submits and presents a frame per tick.

A box beneath the renderer box reaches it as `renderer` and adds modules with `renderer += module`,
which puts them in the main window's [`Renderer.renderList`](graphics.md#renderer-kt--renderer--renderlist); compute modules go to
[`Renderer.computeList`](graphics.md#renderer-kt--renderer--computelist). Each window has its own [`RenderTarget`](graphics.md#rendertarget-kt-rendertarget), found with [`Renderer.renderTargetFor`](graphics.md#renderer-kt--renderer--rendertargetfor).
[`Renderer.captureWindowToFile`](graphics.md#renderer-kt--renderer--capturewindowtofile) writes a window's next frame to a PNG, and [`Renderer.cleanup`](graphics.md#renderer-kt--renderer--cleanup) shuts the
renderer down, releasing its device, windows and targets.

The file also holds [`Target`](graphics.md#renderer-kt-target), the callback shape for drawing into a command buffer, and [`CPUSpan`](graphics.md#renderer-kt-cpuspan),
the per-span CPU timing statistics the frame loop records.

## DynamicBuffer.kt { #dynamicbuffer-kt }

The cursor a Vulkan buffer is written through: std430 padding, integers packed into float slots,
and a buffer that grows under a write that would run past its end. [`DynamicBuffer`](graphics.md#dynamicbuffer-kt-dynamicbuffer) is all of it.
FLine geometry on its way to the GPU, the fabricated scene's shapes and a box's own
`VulkanBuffer.write { … }` block all put their floats here.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/DynamicBuffer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/DynamicBuffer/)

### DynamicBuffer { #dynamicbuffer-kt-dynamicbuffer }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">DynamicBuffer</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">target</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FloatBuffer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">onOverrun</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">FloatBuffer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">FloatBuffer</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/DynamicBuffer/#L89)

A write cursor over GPU memory that pads as std430 does and grows when it runs out. This is what `VulkanBuffer.write { … }` and `append { … }` hand to their block, so a box streaming geometry or particle state writes `put(…)` calls and never computes an offset.

## FrameBufferGroup.kt { #framebuffergroup-kt }

FrameBufferGroup holds one Vulkan buffer per swapchain image, so data written for the current frame never overwrites a buffer an in-flight frame is still reading.

The [`BufferAccessPattern`](graphics.md#framebuffergroup-kt-bufferaccesspattern) chosen at construction decides where the buffers live: host-visible
memory written directly, device-local memory fed through staging buffers (once or every frame), or
device-local memory with a host-visible copy for reading results back, host-cached memory read
every frame, or device-local memory zero-filled when built. Writes go to the current
image's buffer and are recorded with [`FrameBufferGroup.markAsWritten`](graphics.md#framebuffergroup-kt--framebuffergroup--markaswritten);
[`FrameBufferGroup.getLastWritten`](graphics.md#framebuffergroup-kt--framebuffergroup--getlastwritten) returns the most recently written one.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/FrameBufferGroup.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/FrameBufferGroup/)

### BufferAccessPattern { #framebuffergroup-kt-bufferaccesspattern }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">BufferAccessPattern</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/FrameBufferGroup/#L32)

Where a [`FrameBufferGroup`](graphics.md#framebuffergroup-kt-framebuffergroup)'s buffers live and how data moves between host and device.

Constants: `HOST_VISIBLE`, `STAGED_WRITE_ONCE`, `STAGED_STREAM_WRITE`, `DEVICE_LOCAL_DEBUG_READ`, `HOST_VISIBLE_STREAM_READ`, `DEVICE_LOCAL_ZERO`.

## GpuSchema.kt { #gpuschema-kt }

GpuSchema derives a std430 memory layout from an annotated Kotlin class, packs instances of it into buffers, and emits the matching GLSL struct and `buffer_reference` declarations.

Annotate a class with [`GpuStruct`](graphics.md#gpuschema-kt-gpustruct) (and exclude members with [`GpuIgnore`](graphics.md#gpuschema-kt-gpuignore)), then call
[`gpuSchema`](graphics.md#gpuschema-kt--gpuschema) to get its [`GpuSchema`](graphics.md#gpuschema-kt-gpuschema): field offsets, size and stride, [`GpuSchema.write`](graphics.md#gpuschema-kt--gpuschema--write) and
[`GpuSchema.writeArray`](graphics.md#gpuschema-kt--gpuschema--writearray) for packing, [`GpuSchema.arrayView`](graphics.md#gpuschema-kt--gpuschema--arrayview) for indexed writes into a mapped buffer,
and [`GpuSchema.glslDeclarations`](graphics.md#gpuschema-kt--gpuschema--glsldeclarations) for the shader side. [`bindGpu`](graphics.md#gpuschema-kt--bindgpu) binds a schema-backed value to a
[`Structure`](graphics.md#structure-kt-structure) member. Schemas are cached per class.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/GpuSchema.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/GpuSchema/)

## ParallelGeometryPool.kt { #parallelgeometrypool-kt }

ParallelGeometryPool lets several writers produce geometry for the same frame, each into its own per-swapchain-image buffers, and dispatches a module once per writer that published.

See [`ParallelGeometryPool`](graphics.md#parallelgeometrypool-kt-parallelgeometrypool) for the frame-phase rules, writer publication and how `buffer_reference`
push constants switch a module into fan-out mode.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/ParallelGeometryPool.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/ParallelGeometryPool/)

## Structure.kt { #structure-kt }

Structure maps a shader's introspected uniform block or push-constant block onto named Kotlin members, so a box can set, read and bind values by member name.

A [`Structure`](graphics.md#structure-kt-structure) is built from the `Introspected.Member` list that shader reflection produces, and
writes each value at its reflected offset when the block is uploaded. Values can be set
directly, or bound to a function that is re-evaluated each time the block is written
([`bindPushConstant`](graphics.md#structure-kt--bindpushconstant), [`HasUniform`](graphics.md#structure-kt-hasuniform)); a [`ProgressingUniform`](graphics.md#structure-kt-progressinguniform) keeps being written until it reports
completion. A member that nothing has been assigned to fails with [`unassignedMemberMessage`](graphics.md#structure-kt--unassignedmembermessage).

## StructureTypeCheck.kt { #structuretypecheck-kt }

Decides what a Kotlin value set on a shader's uniform member is written as, or why the shader
cannot be given it.

A [`Structure`](graphics.md#structure-kt-structure) is set by member name, and the member that name refers to is whatever the shader's
[`Introspection`](graphics.md#introspection-kt-introspection) last reported. Value and slot can therefore disagree: a `Vector3f` on a member the
shader now declares `float`, an `Int` on a `float`, a `Float` on a `float16_t`. Judged by the
value's Kotlin type alone, each of those writes the wrong number of bytes, or the right number
meaning something else.

The rule is to convert what converts without loss and to refuse a different shape. Shape is
checked first: a scalar belongs in a scalar, a vector in a vector of the same length, a matrix in
a matrix of the same size, and nothing but a buffer-writing value in a struct. Within one shape
the value is converted to the type the member declares whenever that type can hold it, which
covers any integer into a wider one, a narrower or differently signed integer that is in range, an
integer into `float` while it stays exactly representable, a whole float into an integer, and a
`Double` into a `float`. A float set on a half is rounded to the half's precision, which is what
the member asked for. Anything else is refused, naming the value that would not fit. Array
members, device pointers and values whose width is not knowable here are written as given.

Three callers ask this question. `Structure.set` asks it when the value arrives and declines to
store a value it would not be able to write, so the answer reaches whoever is typing. Writing a
block to its buffer asks it per member, and skips the member rather than writing nonsense into the
slot. `Structure.carryValuesFrom` asks it of every value a shader reload is trying to keep, which
is how a reload reports the uniforms it had to drop. Each distinct refusal is reported once, not
once a frame.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/StructureTypeCheck.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/StructureTypeCheck/)

## VBuffer.kt { #vbuffer-kt }

VertexBuffer is a classic vertex buffer with a host-side staging copy that is transferred to device-local memory before drawing.

Most Field geometry instead pulls vertices in the shader through device addresses set in push
constants, which needs no staging step; [`VertexBuffer`](graphics.md#vbuffer-kt-vertexbuffer) remains for code that binds vertex buffers
directly.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/VBuffer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/VBuffer/)

### VertexBuffer { #vbuffer-kt-vertexbuffer }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">VertexBuffer</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">renderer</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Renderer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">size</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">usage</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">VK10</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">VK&#95;BUFFER&#95;USAGE&#95;VERTEX&#95;BUFFER&#95;BIT</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">createCPU</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">HasBuffer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">BufferWriteable</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/VBuffer/#L30)

this is, as far as I can tell, completely decoy — with resizable BAR (or unified memory on Apple Silicon) this staging buffer thing is just excess engineering _and_ writing shaders that do their own pulling is better _and_ device pointers set through push constants is faster and architecturally skips all of the descriptor nonsense

## VulkanBuffer.kt { #vulkanbuffer-kt }

A block of GPU memory, and the ways to hand one to a shader. [`VulkanBuffer`](graphics.md#vulkanbuffer-kt-vulkanbuffer) is the allocation
itself: VMA-suballocated, kept mapped on the CPU side for its whole life, resizable while frames
are in flight, and released through the renderer's frame-retirement queue rather than on the spot.
Vertex data, uniforms, storage buffers, acceleration-structure scratch and compute input and
output are all this one class under different `usage` flags.

Writing and reading go through three small interfaces, and which you reach for is a question of how
much you want to think about layout. [`BufferWriteable`](graphics.md#vulkanbuffer-kt-bufferwriteable) and [`BufferReadable`](graphics.md#vulkanbuffer-kt-bufferreadable) map the allocation as
a plain `FloatBuffer`, `ByteBuffer` or `IntBuffer` and let you address it yourself.
[`DynamicallyWriteable`](graphics.md#vulkanbuffer-kt-dynamicallywriteable) gives you a [`DynamicBuffer`](graphics.md#dynamicbuffer-kt-dynamicbuffer) instead, which pads to std430 as it goes and
grows the allocation under a write that would overflow it; `write { … }` starts at the beginning
and `append { … }` continues from the cursor.

[`HasBuffer`](graphics.md#vulkanbuffer-kt-hasbuffer) is the handle a shader is bound to, and the useful thing about it is that it composes.
Adding a `Long` to one offsets it. `zeroBefore` on a buffer, and `barrier` or `graphicsBarrier` on
any handle, return a handle that records that work on the way to giving the address up. "This
buffer, cleared first" and "this buffer, once the compute writes to it are visible" then travel
with the buffer, so nothing has to remember where in the frame to put the clear or the barrier.

Render workers read the handle, address and descriptor range while recording a frame, on other
threads than the one that writes them. Every one of those fields is therefore `@Volatile`, and
allocation builds its replacements in locals and publishes them at the end, handle before range. A
worker sees either the old allocation, which is still alive, or the new one, and never a null
handle mid-resize.

## magic.kt { #magic-kt }

The buffer DSL: [`buffer`](graphics.md#magic-kt--buffer) and [`defaultBuffer`](graphics.md#magic-kt--defaultbuffer) build a [`BufferParameters`](graphics.md#magic-kt-bufferparameters) that says how a Vulkan buffer is sized, placed in memory and used.

[`defaultBuffer`](graphics.md#magic-kt--defaultbuffer) starts from host-visible, storage and device-addressable memory, which suits
hardware with resizable BAR or unified memory; [`buffer`](graphics.md#magic-kt--buffer) starts from nothing. Size helpers such as
`10.floats` or `4.vec4s` count std430 bytes (a vec3 takes 16). [`linkBuffer`](graphics.md#magic-kt--linkbuffer) looks for an existing
[`BufferParameters`](graphics.md#magic-kt-bufferparameters) of the same name in the box context and merges new settings into it, so boxes
can share one buffer.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/magic.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/magic/)

[`hosted`](graphics.md#magic-kt--bufferparameters--hosted), [`writeOnce`](graphics.md#magic-kt--bufferparameters--writeonce), [`streamWrites`](graphics.md#magic-kt--bufferparameters--streamwrites), [`streamReads`](graphics.md#magic-kt--bufferparameters--streamreads) and [`zeroInitialized`](graphics.md#magic-kt--bufferparameters--zeroinitialized) each set a coherent combination of this and [`accessPattern`](graphics.md#magic-kt--bufferparameters--accesspattern). |

| <a id="magic-kt--bufferparameters--accesspattern"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">accessPattern</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">BufferAccessPattern</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/buffers/magic/#L115) | How the buffer is written and read over its life. ## Attachment.kt { #attachment-kt }

An image plus image view sized and formatted to be used as a framebuffer attachment.

[`Attachment`](graphics.md#attachment-kt-attachment) picks the view's aspect from the usage flags: a depth-stencil usage makes a depth
view and sets `isDepthAttachment`, a colour usage makes a colour view. `cleanup` destroys the view
and then the image.

## CommandBuffer.kt { #commandbuffer-kt }

A Vulkan command buffer allocated from a [`CommandPool`](graphics.md#commandpool-kt-commandpool): primary or secondary, one-time-submit or reusable, with [`CommandBuffer.beginRecording`](graphics.md#commandbuffer-kt--commandbuffer--beginrecording), [`CommandBuffer.endRecording`](graphics.md#commandbuffer-kt--commandbuffer--endrecording) and [`CommandBuffer.reset`](graphics.md#commandbuffer-kt--commandbuffer--reset).

It tracks whether recording is inside a render pass instance, so transfer commands are not recorded where Vulkan forbids them, and can defer host-read barriers on graphics buffers until a flush.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/device/CommandBuffer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/device/CommandBuffer/)

## CommandPool.kt { #commandpool-kt }

A Vulkan command pool for one queue family, from which Field allocates command buffers.

[`CommandPool`](graphics.md#commandpool-kt-commandpool) is created with `VK_COMMAND_POOL_CREATE_RESET_COMMAND_BUFFER_BIT`, so each command
buffer from it can be reset and re-recorded individually.

## DescriptorSetLayout.kt { #descriptorsetlayout-kt }

Descriptor set layouts for the renderer's shaders: [`DescriptorSetLayout`](graphics.md#descriptorsetlayout-kt-descriptorsetlayout) owns a Vulkan layout handle and releases it with its device, and [`DescriptorSetLayout.SimpleDescriptorSetLayout`](graphics.md#descriptorsetlayout-kt--descriptorsetlayout--simpledescriptorsetlayout) builds one from parallel lists of bindings and descriptor types.

That builder supports partially bound arrays, one variable-count (bindless) binding, and update-after-bind. [`UpdatesDescriptorSet`](graphics.md#descriptorsetlayout-kt-updatesdescriptorset) is the interface a bound resource implements to push its descriptor into a command buffer.

## Device.kt { #device-kt }

The logical Vulkan device: [`Device`](graphics.md#device-kt-device) wraps a [`PhysicalDevice`](graphics.md#physicaldevice-kt-physicaldevice) and enables the extensions and features the renderer uses.

It also reports optional capabilities such as ray tracing limits and Metal object export, and offers [`Device.calibratedHostGpuTimeNS`](graphics.md#device-kt--device--calibratedhostgputimens) for lining GPU timestamps up with host time.

## Fence.kt { #fence-kt }

A Vulkan fence the CPU waits on to learn that submitted GPU work has finished.

[`Fence`](graphics.md#fence-kt-fence) creates the fence, optionally already signalled, and registers it with `AutoDisposer`
under its [`Device`](graphics.md#device-kt-device), so a fence that is never cleaned up is still destroyed. `fenceWait` blocks
without a timeout, `reset` re-arms it, and `isSignaled` polls it.

## ImageLayouts.kt { #imagelayouts-kt }

Maps Field's logical image layouts to the layout handed to Vulkan, collapsing to `GENERAL`
when the driver supports `VK_KHR_unified_image_layouts`.

Every call that passes a layout to Vulkan goes through [`vkLayout`](graphics.md#imagelayouts-kt--vklayout); [`ImageLayouts`](graphics.md#imagelayouts-kt-imagelayouts) holds the switch
that [`Device`](graphics.md#device-kt-device) sets.

## Instance.kt { #instance-kt }

The Vulkan instance: SDK and driver selection, layers, extensions and the debug messenger.

[`Instance`](graphics.md#instance-kt-instance) calls `Options.doVulkanSDK` before anything else, so the loader and driver it gets are
the ones Field chose (KosmicKrisp or MoltenVK on macOS). It enables the validation layer when
validation or shader `debugPrintf` is requested and a layer is installed, adds
`VK_KHR_portability_enumeration` on macOS when the loader offers it, and records what it actually
enabled in `enabledExtensions`. With VR enabled and an OpenXR runtime bootstrapped, the instance is
created through OpenXR's `xrCreateVulkanInstanceKHR`, so the runtime can add the extensions it needs.

## MacHdrActivator.kt { #machdractivator-kt }

Enables Extended Dynamic Range (EDR) on the macOS CAMetalLayer that backs the GLFW/MoltenVK
window.  Without this call the OS compositor clamps output to SDR even when an HDR Vulkan
swap-chain format (e.g. scRGB) is selected.

Implementation: the GLFW window handle is an NSWindow*.  We walk the Objective-C object graph
via the ObjC runtime (`objc_msgSend`) using LWJGL's low-level JNI call helpers, without
pulling in any extra native library or annotation processor:

  NSWindow → contentView (NSView) → layer (CAMetalLayer) → setWantsExtendedDynamicRangeContent: YES

All class and method lookups are done via reflection so this file compiles and loads on
Windows/Linux without modification. It reaches LWJGL through five entry points:
`GLFWNativeCocoa.glfwGetCocoaWindow`, `LibObjC.sel_registerName`, `LibObjC.getLibrary`,
`JNI.callPPP` and `JNI.callPPZV`.

All ObjC messaging is wrapped in a try/catch so a failure degrades gracefully to SDR.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/device/MacHdrActivator.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/device/MacHdrActivator/)

## Queue.kt { #queue-kt }

Vulkan device queues: [`Queue`](graphics.md#queue-kt-queue) fetches a queue from a family and submits command buffers with wait and signal semaphores and an optional fence.

The subclasses [`Queue.GraphicsQueue`](graphics.md#queue-kt--queue--graphicsqueue), [`Queue.ComputeQueue`](graphics.md#queue-kt--queue--computequeue) and [`Queue.PresentQueue`](graphics.md#queue-kt--queue--presentqueue) choose the queue family for graphics, compute and presentation to a surface.

## Semaphore.kt { #semaphore-kt }

A Vulkan semaphore for GPU-to-GPU ordering between queue submissions, timeline by default.

A timeline [`Semaphore`](graphics.md#semaphore-kt-semaphore) keeps its own counter: `nextSignalValue` advances it for the submission
that will signal, `currentValue` is the value to wait on, and `markExternallySignaled` advances it
when something outside Field's submissions (such as image acquisition) signals it. Constructed with
`timeline = false` it is a binary semaphore, and both values are always 0.

## SwapChain.kt { #swapchain-kt }

The window's presentation chain: [`SwapChain`](graphics.md#swapchain-kt-swapchain) creates the swapchain images and their views for a surface, acquires the next image each frame and presents it on a [`Queue.PresentQueue`](graphics.md#queue-kt--queue--presentqueue).

The present mode follows the vsync setting, and [`SwapChain.presentImage`](graphics.md#swapchain-kt--swapchain--presentimage) returns a [`SwapChain.PresentResult`](graphics.md#swapchain-kt--swapchain--presentresult) that says whether the window needs resizing.

## VulkanNames.kt { #vulkannames-kt }

Debug names and command-buffer labels for Vulkan objects, as seen in validation messages and
frame debuggers such as RenderDoc.

[`nameObject`](graphics.md#vulkannames-kt--nameobject) attaches a name to a device handle; [`beginLabel`](graphics.md#vulkannames-kt--beginlabel) and [`endLabel`](graphics.md#vulkannames-kt--endlabel) bracket a region of a
command buffer. All three do nothing unless validation is on (`Options.validate`) and their own
toggle (`Options.debugObjectNames`, `Options.debugLabels`) is set, and when the driver does not
expose the `VK_EXT_debug_utils` entry point. Labels are also skipped on macOS. Name strings are
encoded once and cached, so the same name can be passed every frame without allocating.

## timing.kt { #timing-kt }

GPU-side profiling for the Vulkan renderer: per-frame query pools for timestamps, pipeline statistics and, where the driver offers VK_KHR_performance_query, performance counters.

[`ProfilingOptions`](graphics.md#timing-kt-profilingoptions) switches each kind on and sizes its pool; [`GpuProfiler`](graphics.md#timing-kt-gpuprofiler) owns one set of pools per frame in flight and hands out query slots as commands are recorded.

## ImGuiPanel.kt { #imguipanel-kt }

A world-space rectangle that shows an [`ImGuiRenderToTexture`](graphics.md#imguirendertotexture-kt-imguirendertotexture) in VR and turns controller rays into
ImGui pointer input.

Place the panel with [`ImGuiPanel.place`](graphics.md#imguipanel-kt--imguipanel--place) or [`ImGuiPanel.faceToward`](graphics.md#imguipanel-kt--imguipanel--facetoward), raycast it with
[`ImGuiPanel.raycast`](graphics.md#imguipanel-kt--imguipanel--raycast) or [`ImGuiPanel.interact`](graphics.md#imguipanel-kt--imguipanel--interact), and draw its quad with the per-eye matrix from
[`ImGuiPanel.panelMvp`](graphics.md#imguipanel-kt--imguipanel--panelmvp). `afield.examples.four.ImGuiVrPanelDemo` is a worked example.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/imgui/ImGuiPanel.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/imgui/ImGuiPanel/)

Returns the same [`Hit`](graphics.md#imguipanel-kt--imguipanel--hit) as [`raycast`](graphics.md#imguipanel-kt--imguipanel--raycast). |

## ImGuiRenderToTexture.kt { #imguirendertotexture-kt }

Draws Dear ImGui (through imgui-java) into a Field render-to-texture target, so an ImGui interface
can be shown as a texture on any surface, including a panel in VR.

[`ImGuiRenderToTexture`](graphics.md#imguirendertotexture-kt-imguirendertotexture) owns the ImGui context, the font atlas and the vertex buffers, and records
ImGui's draw lists into its target each frame, honouring clip rects with a dynamic scissor. Only the
font atlas is bound as a texture; other ImGui texture ids are ignored. [`ImGuiPanel`](graphics.md#imguipanel-kt-imguipanel) places such a
texture in world space and feeds controller rays back to it as pointer input.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/imgui/ImGuiRenderToTexture.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/imgui/ImGuiRenderToTexture/)

## BinocularGazeIntersection.kt { #binoculargazeintersection-kt }

Estimates where the two eyes converge from a pair of per-eye gaze rays.

[`BinocularGazeIntersection`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt-binoculargazeintersection) takes the closest approach of the left and right rays and rejects
depths it cannot trust, so a caller can place an object at the point the viewer is looking at.
`BinocularGazeIntersectionTest` covers it.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/BinocularGazeIntersection.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/BinocularGazeIntersection/)

### BinocularGazeIntersection { #binoculargazeintersection-kt-binoculargazeintersection }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">BinocularGazeIntersection</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">minimumAngleDegrees</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.25</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maximumSeparation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.03</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">minimumDistance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.05</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maximumDistance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">8.0</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/BinocularGazeIntersection/#L26)

Closest approach of two forward eye rays, in metres, with explicit rejection of unreliable depth. Real rays can be skew: [`position`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--position) is the midpoint of [`leftPoint`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--leftpoint) and [`rightPoint`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--rightpoint), and [`separation`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--separation) is their gap. Read [`valid`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--valid) before placing an object there.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--minimumangledegrees"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">minimumAngleDegrees</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | The smallest angle between the two rays that still gives a depth, in degrees. Nearer to parallel than this the closest-approach solve is ill-conditioned, so [`status`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--status-2) becomes `Status.PARALLEL` and no point is written. Must be above 0 and below 90. |
| <a id="binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--maximumseparation"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maximumSeparation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | How far [`leftPoint`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--leftpoint) and [`rightPoint`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--rightpoint) may be apart, in metres, before the rays count as missing each other and [`status`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--status-2) becomes `Status.RAYS_MISS`. Skew rays always leave some gap; this is how much of it to forgive. |
| <a id="binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--minimumdistance"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">minimumDistance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Nearest accepted depth along either ray, in metres. Closer gives `Status.OUT_OF_RANGE`. |
| <a id="binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--maximumdistance"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maximumDistance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Farthest accepted depth along either ray, in metres. Beyond it, `Status.OUT_OF_RANGE`. |
| <a id="binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--status"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">Status</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/BinocularGazeIntersection/#L44) |  |
| <a id="binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--status-2"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">status</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/BinocularGazeIntersection/#L54) | Why the last [`update`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--update) or [`solve`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--solve) accepted or rejected a depth. `Status.NO_TRACKING` until the first call. |
| <a id="binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--valid"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">valid</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/BinocularGazeIntersection/#L58) | True only for `Status.VALID` — the one check to make before using [`position`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--position). |
| <a id="binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--raysvalid"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">raysValid</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/BinocularGazeIntersection/#L65) | True when both rays were finite, long enough to normalize and had distinct origins, so [`leftDirection`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--leftdirection) and [`rightDirection`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--rightdirection) are meaningful. The convergence tests come after this, so a pair of usable rays that converge badly leaves this true while [`valid`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--valid) is false. |
| <a id="binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--position"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">position</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/BinocularGazeIntersection/#L69) | Midpoint of [`leftPoint`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--leftpoint) and [`rightPoint`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--rightpoint) — where to put an object the viewer is looking at. |
| <a id="binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--leftpoint"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">leftPoint</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/BinocularGazeIntersection/#L72) | The point on the left eye's ray closest to the right eye's ray. |
| <a id="binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--rightpoint"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">rightPoint</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/BinocularGazeIntersection/#L75) | The point on the right eye's ray closest to the left eye's ray. |

| <a id="binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--rightdirection"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">rightDirection</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/BinocularGazeIntersection/#L81) | Unit forward direction of the right eye's ray, as the last solve normalized it. |

Negative means the convergence is behind the eye. |
| <a id="binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--rightdistance"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">rightDistance</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/BinocularGazeIntersection/#L88) | Distance from the right eye to [`rightPoint`](graphics.md#binoculargazeintersection-kt--binoculargazeintersection--rightpoint), in metres. ## ComputeTarget.kt { #computetarget-kt }

A [`Target`](graphics.md#renderer-kt-target) that records compute and ray-tracing modules into a frame without drawing to a window.

Modules and plain command-recording functions are added with `+=` on a [`ComputeTarget`](graphics.md#computetarget-kt-computetarget) and run each
frame: compute modules first, then ray-tracing modules, then the other targets.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/ComputeTarget.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/ComputeTarget/)

## ExtEyeGazeInteraction.kt { #exteyegazeinteraction-kt }

Combined eye gaze from OpenXR's `XR_EXT_eye_gaze_interaction`, as a single pose action inside the
HMD target's existing gameplay action set.

Creation returns null on a runtime that does not advertise the extension, reports no eye-gaze
support in its system properties, or refuses the action, its suggested binding or its action
space, so a target asks once and then has either gaze or none. It has to happen before the action
sets are attached to the session. Each frame the gaze pose is located against the target's
reference space and written into an [`EyeGazeState`](graphics.md#openxreyetracking-kt-eyegazestate) with the sample time the runtime reports for
it; the state is invalidated first, so a frame in which the action is not active reads as inactive
rather than as the last pose that worked.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/ExtEyeGazeInteraction.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/ExtEyeGazeInteraction/)

## FrameHistory.kt { #framehistory-kt }

Tracks the previous frame's camera for one render target, so temporal passes can reproject pixels
and know when there is no usable history.

[`FrameHistory`](graphics.md#framehistory-kt-framehistory) holds the reprojection matrix and an availability flag that drops whenever the
frame sequence, size or scene epoch breaks.

## HasRenderToTexture.kt { #hasrendertotexture-kt }

A [`RenderToTexture`](graphics.md#rendertotexture-kt-rendertotexture) owner that modules can be attached to as if it were the target itself.

[`ElectronRTTView`](imaging.md#electronrttview-kt-electronrttview) implements [`HasRenderToTexture`](graphics.md#hasrendertotexture-kt-hasrendertotexture) over the target it draws into, and
[`WebRTCSink`](imaging.md#webrtc-kt-webrtcsink) forwards to the view it captures from, so a module reaches either of them the two
ways it reaches a [`RenderToTexture`](graphics.md#rendertotexture-kt-rendertotexture): `+view` inside `moduleHere { }`, or
`view += "name" to module`. The second form is the two operators here; the first is an operator
on `Parameters`, the `moduleHere { }` receiver.

## HtcEyeTracker.kt { #htceyetracker-kt }

Native binding for `XR_HTC_eye_tracker`, which Field's LWJGL version does not generate.

Layouts and signatures follow HTC's ViveEyeTrackerHelper.cs and enum values in OpenXRUtils.cs:
https://github.com/ViveSoftware/VIVE-OpenXR-Unity/tree/25a5fd212420688952ead9deba735357656278ec/com.htc.upm.vive.openxr/Runtime

Only 64-bit ABIs are supported: enum/bool32/float = 4 bytes, pointer/handle/time = 8 bytes, and
`create` returns null on any other pointer width. The per-eye arrays are inline rather than
pointers, and their elements carry no `type`/`next` header.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/HtcEyeTracker.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/HtcEyeTracker/)

## MndxXDevSpace.kt { #mndxxdevspace-kt }

Hand-rolled bindings for `XR_MNDX_xdev_space`.

This is a Monado *vendor* extension: it never made it into the official OpenXR registry, so
LWJGL generates no bindings for it. We resolve the entry points through `xrGetInstanceProcAddr`
and lay the structs out by hand. Definitions transcribed from Monado's
`src/external/openxr_includes/openxr/XR_MNDX_xdev_space.h` (spec version 3, extension 445).

It is the only route to WiVRn's body trackers. The obvious one, `XR_FB_body_tracking`, is a dead
end there; [`OpenXRHmdTarget`](graphics.md#openxrhmdtarget-kt-openxrhmdtarget)'s body-tracking setup says why, and cites the WiVRn source.

The extension enumerates every "xdev" (tracked device) the runtime knows about (HMD, controllers,
body trackers) and hands back an `XrSpace` per device, which the caller then locates with the
ordinary `xrLocateSpace`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/MndxXDevSpace.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/MndxXDevSpace/)

## MotionItems.kt { #motionitems-kt }

Per-item motion for 2D items drawn by stable identity, for passes that need each item's previous
pose.

[`MotionItems`](graphics.md#motionitems-kt-motionitems) keeps this frame's and last frame's [`MotionPose`](graphics.md#motionitems-kt-motionpose) for each key and writes the
difference, falling back to no motion when the item is new, changed revision or was cleared.
`MotionItemsTest` covers it.

## MultiPingPongRenderToTexture.kt { #multipingpongrendertotexture-kt }

Several passes per frame between two images: [`MultiPingPongRenderToTexture`](graphics.md#multipingpongrendertotexture-kt-multipingpongrendertotexture) runs an optional
init pass, a number of middle passes and an optional final pass, each reading what the last one
wrote.

It suits iterated kernels such as blurs or relaxation steps, where one frame needs many passes.
Shaders can tell the passes apart through push constants the target fills in (pass index, pass
count, and whether this is the init or final pass).

## OpenXREyeTracking.kt { #openxreyetracking-kt }

Plain state holders for OpenXR eye tracking: the combined gaze of `XR_EXT_eye_gaze_interaction` and
the per-eye gaze, pupil and geometry streams of `XR_HTC_eye_tracker`.

Each holder is filled in place on the renderer's queue thread and carries its own validity flags,
so read [`EyeGazeState.poseValid`](graphics.md#openxreyetracking-kt--eyegazestate--posevalid) or the per-stream flags of [`HtcEyeState`](graphics.md#openxreyetracking-kt-htceyestate) before using a value.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/OpenXREyeTracking.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/OpenXREyeTracking/)

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">EyeGazeState</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/targets/OpenXREyeTracking/#L22)

Combined gaze from `XR_EXT_eye_gaze_interaction`, in the target's LOCAL reference space (metres, +Y up, -Z forward). Updated in place on the renderer's queue thread. Numeric pose values retain the last valid observation; check [`poseValid`](graphics.md#openxreyetracking-kt--eyegazestate--posevalid) before using them.
