That it is there does not mean it is in use — [`requestedDriver`](graphics.md#vulkanprobe-kt--vulkanstatus--requesteddriver) says which one was asked for. |
| <a id="vulkanprobe-kt--vulkanstatus--error"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">error</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | What went wrong, phrased for the Vulkan panel to show, or null when nothing did. A probe that crashed loading a driver, or ran past its timeout, reports it here rather than throwing, so a failed probe still returns a status. |

## Window.kt { #window-kt }

The GLFW window a Vulkan renderer draws into, with its input listeners and a framebuffer-to-PNG capture.

[`Window`](graphics.md#window-kt-window) creates a client-API-less GLFW window (decorated, or borderless when fullscreen),
tracks its size and the [`Renderer`](graphics.md#renderer-kt-renderer) attached to it, and routes key, character, cursor, mouse
button, scroll and focus events to listeners. [`Window.saveFramebufferToTempFile`](graphics.md#window-kt--window--saveframebuffertotempfile) writes the
framebuffer to a PNG; [`openWindowsSnapshot`](graphics.md#window-kt--openwindowssnapshot) lists the windows currently open.

## WindowPointer.kt { #windowpointer-kt }

The pointer over a renderer window and the window's size, in window points, read once a frame.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/graphics/vulkan/util/WindowPointer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/util/WindowPointer/)

### WindowPointer { #windowpointer-kt-windowpointer }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">WindowPointer</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">window</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Window</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">onPoll</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">WindowPointer</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Unit</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">{</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/graphics/vulkan/util/WindowPointer/#L23)

The pointer and the window's size **in points** (the cursor's units, half the framebuffer's pixels on a Retina display), read on the window's poll, where GLFW allows it, and readable from any thread afterwards. A sketch that works in canvas pixels, origin top left, y down, uses [`width`](graphics.md#windowpointer-kt--windowpointer--width) and [`height`](graphics.md#windowpointer-kt--windowpointer--height) as its world and [`x`](graphics.md#windowpointer-kt--windowpointer--x), [`y`](graphics.md#windowpointer-kt--windowpointer--y) as its mouse.

Registering adds a sequence to its poll map, so nothing is read until the window is polled. |
| <a id="windowpointer-kt--windowpointer--name"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | The key this registration takes in the window's poll map; a second pointer under the same name on the same window replaces the first. |

Until it has, [`width`](graphics.md#windowpointer-kt--windowpointer--width) and [`height`](graphics.md#windowpointer-kt--windowpointer--height) are the framebuffer's pixels, twice the points on a Retina display, so a sketch that places things by the window's size waits for this. |

## fmchirp.kt { #fmchirp-kt }

FM chirp curves: an eight-parameter family of 0..1 remapping curves, packed as half floats, that evaluate the same way in Kotlin and in GLSL.

[`FMChirpCurves`](graphics.md#fmchirp-kt-fmchirpcurves) holds the parameter type, evaluation, sampling, measures such as roughness and foldover, and least-squares fitting to target points. [`FM_CHIRP_GLSL`](graphics.md#fmchirp-kt--fm-chirp-glsl) is the matching shader source, registered as the `fmchirp` shader template by [`registerFMChirpShaderTemplate`](graphics.md#fmchirp-kt--registerfmchirpshadertemplate); [`registerFMChirpVisualizers`](graphics.md#fmchirp-kt--registerfmchirpvisualizers) gives the parameter type an HTML summary when it is printed in a box.

## superpc.kt { #superpc-kt }

Push constants as a Kotlin class, and the GLSL that reads them back. A subclass of
[`PushConstants`](graphics.md#superpc-kt-pushconstants) declares its members as ordinary `var` properties; reflection turns those into a
byte layout with explicit offsets, `glsl()` emits the push-constant block and accessors that match
it, and `writeTo` serialises the current values into a buffer by those same offsets.

The reflection runs once per class and the layout is cached, so the per-frame cost is the write.
Members are laid out in `@PcOrder` order where that annotation is given and alphabetically where
it is not, which is what makes a layout stable from one run to the next.

### What the generated GLSL looks like

One push-constant block, a `layout(offset = …)` on every member, a float register file loaded out
of that block by `loadRegs()`, and then accessors under the names the Kotlin class used:

```diffstatic {data-lang=glsl}
{{ pc.dec }}
void main() {
    loadRegs();
    uFragColor = baseColor();
}
```

A scalar member becomes a macro, so `time` in Kotlin reads as `time` in shader code. A vector
member becomes a function of no arguments under its own name, so `baseColor` reads as
`baseColor()`. To keep those macros clear of the block's own members, a member inside the block
carries a leading underscore: Kotlin's `time` is declared as `_time` and the bare name is the
macro that reads it out of the register file.

### Instruction payloads

A property whose name already begins with an underscore is an instruction payload: it is declared
in the push-constant block under exactly that name and nothing else happens to it. It is not
loaded into the register file and gets no accessor, so a shader reads it from the block itself and
a frame pays nothing for payloads it is not reading.

### Member types

`Float`, `Vector2f`, `Vector3f` and `Vector4f` become a `float`, `vec2`, `vec3` and `vec4`. The
half-precision types travel packed into unsigned integers, to be unpacked in the shader: `Vec2h`
as a `uint`, `Vec3h` and `Vec4h` as a `uvec2`, and the eight-lane `Vector8h` as a `uvec4`. Every
member has to be a `var`, since the layout reads and writes through the property itself, and any
other type fails when the layout is built rather than at draw time. `otherDeclarations` is the way
around all of this: raw GLSL inserted into the block that reflection never sees, which you place
yourself at `nextFreeOffset(…)`.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
class MaterialPC : PushConstants<MaterialPC>() {
    @PcOrder(0) var time: Float = 0f
    @PcOrder(1) var baseColor: Vector4f = Vector4f(1f, 1f, 1f, 1f)
    @PcOrder(2) var uvScale: Vector2f = Vector2f(1f, 1f)
    @PcOrder(100) var _patch0: Vec4h = Vector4f().half
}

val pc = MaterialPC()
pc.time = 1.0f
pc["uvScale"] = Vector2f(2f, 2f)

shaderTemplate["pc"] = mapOf("dec" to Resolver { pc.glsl() })
mesh.push.bindAll { pc }
```

The block reaches the shader through the template engine, as above, and the instance is bound by
handing it to a mesh's push-constant structure, which writes it out each time that mesh's push
constants are assembled for a draw. The buffer it is written into has to be little-endian, and a
`ByteBuffer` is big-endian until it is told otherwise.

## templating.kt { #templating-kt }

The template engine behind `{{ slot }}` in a Field shader: a Jinja-shaped expander written against
the Kotlin standard library alone, which a shader stage's source runs through before shaderc
sees it. `Box.shaderTemplate` is where a box puts the values it resolves against.

A template may contain:

- `{{ expr }}`, replaced by whatever `expr` resolves to.
- `{% if expr %}` … `{% else %}` … `{% endif %}`, nested freely. `not expr` and `!expr` negate.
  An empty string, a zero, an empty map and an empty list are false; a resolver is true.
- `{% property "name" %}`, which expands another named shader property in place and needs an
  include resolver to find it. `{% include "name" %}` is the same tag under its older spelling,
  kept so that saved documents still compile.

Everything a template reads comes from a `Resolver`, one function from a key to a value, and what
comes back is read by value rather than by type. `null` means not resolved, so the next resolver in
the chain is asked. A `String` is the answer, and so is anything else through its `toString`. A
`Resolver`, a `Map` or a list of `Resolver`s is structural instead: the rest of the path is
resolved against it, to a depth of fifty.

`{{ a.b.c }}` is matched longest prefix first, so `a.b.c` is offered to every resolver, then
`a.b`, then `a`, then the empty key. A resolver may therefore own a whole dotted namespace or just
its root, and where `a` answers with something structural, `b.c` is resolved against that. A path
that resolves nowhere stops the shader rather than silently emitting nothing, and says where: the
line and column, the line itself under a caret, and every key that was tried against every
resolver with what each returned.

`runShaderTemplate` is `runTemplate` plus `#line` directives around any expansion that spans
lines, so a compiler error after one still names the shader line that was written rather than the
line it grew into.

## util.kt { #util-kt }

Small helpers shared by the Vulkan renderer: the host OS, memory-type selection and result checking.

[`updateForever`](graphics.md#util-kt--updateforever) builds a sequence for a mesh's `update` map, [`OS`](graphics.md#util-kt--os) reports the platform, [`memoryTypeFromProperties`](graphics.md#util-kt--memorytypefromproperties) picks a device memory type, and [`vkCheck`](graphics.md#util-kt--vkcheck) throws on a failed Vulkan call.

## Syphon.kt { #syphon-kt }

Field's end of [Syphon](https://syphon.info), the macOS standard for sharing GPU frames between
applications: a [`SyphonServer`](graphics.md#syphon-kt-syphonserver) publishes frames that Resolume, TouchDesigner, MadMapper, OBS
(with its Syphon source), VDMX or Max can receive, and a [`SyphonClient`](graphics.md#syphon-kt-syphonclient) receives what they publish.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val out = syphonServer("Field")             // appears in every Syphon client's list
out.publish(image)                          // a BufferedImage, RGBA bytes, or a RenderToTexture

val inp = syphonClient("Resolume Arena")    // a server's name, app name or uuid
display("main", inp.png())                  // the latest frame
```

Field reaches Syphon through a small Objective-C library, `native/field-syphon`, that is optional
and macOS-only — build it once with `./gradlew buildSyphonNative` (needs Xcode).

Every frame crosses the boundary through memory today: a [`RenderToTexture`](graphics.md#rendertotexture-kt-rendertotexture) is read back from the
GPU and copied into Syphon's shared IOSurface, and a received frame is read back into a
`ByteArray`. At 1920 x 1080 that is about 8 MB a frame each way. Publishing an IOSurface that
already exists ([`SyphonServer.publishIOSurface`](graphics.md#syphon-kt--syphonserver--publishiosurface)) skips the CPU entirely.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/io/syphon/Syphon.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/io/syphon/Syphon/)

## SyphonGpu.kt { #syphongpu-kt }

Publishes every frame a [`RenderToTexture`](graphics.md#rendertotexture-kt-rendertotexture) draws to a [`SyphonServer`](graphics.md#syphon-kt-syphonserver) without the CPU touching the
pixels: the frame is copied GPU-side into an IOSurface (on the same command buffer that drew it),
and once that frame's GPU work has completed Syphon blits the IOSurface into its own shared one.

Made by [`SyphonServer.followOnGpu`](graphics.md#syphon-kt--syphonserver--followongpu); a [`Target`](graphics.md#renderer-kt-target) in the renderer's list, placed after the source so
it runs after the source has drawn. The IOSurface reaches Vulkan as host memory
(`VK_EXT_external_memory_host`, see [`IOSurfaceHostBuffer`](graphics.md#iosurfacehostbuffer-kt-iosurfacehostbuffer)), which both KosmicKrisp and MoltenVK
offer on Apple silicon. Two surfaces alternate; if Syphon is still copying the one due next, the
frame is skipped rather than overwritten under it.

## SyphonTexture.kt { #syphontexture-kt }

A [`SyphonClient`](graphics.md#syphon-kt-syphonclient)'s frames as a texture for a shader to sample: bind this object itself as a
`sampler2D` (`prop<SyphonTexture>(name) = client.texture()`). Made by [`SyphonClient.texture`](graphics.md#syphon-kt--syphonclient--texture), and
kept current by the renderer's list, which calls [`render`](graphics.md#syphontexture-kt--syphontexture--render) each frame.

Syphon's frame is an IOSurface that the sending process draws into. Where the driver allows it,
Vulkan samples that IOSurface's own memory, with no copy of any kind ([`path`](graphics.md#syphontexture-kt--syphontexture--path-2) says which route):

- `Path.IMPORTED_IMAGE`: MoltenVK. The IOSurface backs a `VkImage` (`VK_EXT_metal_objects`).
- `Path.HOST_LINEAR_IMAGE`: KosmicKrisp (and MoltenVK if the first is refused). The IOSurface's
  pages are imported as host memory (`VK_EXT_external_memory_host`) and bound to a linearly tiled
  `VkImage` whose row pitch is the surface's own.
- `Path.HOST_BUFFER_COPY`: the pages are imported as a buffer and copied into an image on the GPU,
  once per new frame; used when the driver will not lay a linear image over them.
- `Path.CPU_COPY`: the fallback: a blit into a staging buffer, a swizzle on
  the CPU, and an upload. Also what `texture(zeroCopy = false)` asks for.

The texture is `B8G8R8A8_SRGB` on the zero-copy paths and `R8G8B8A8_SRGB` on the copy path; either
way the shader sees RGBA, top row first (v = 0 is the top of the sender's picture). When the sender
changes size Syphon replaces the IOSurface, and the texture re-imports the new one; the old one is
released only after the frame that last sampled it has completed. (The copy path keeps the first
frame's size and skips frames of another.) Like every Syphon client, the zero-copy paths
read the sender's surface while it may be drawing the next frame into it; Syphon has no cross-process
fence to wait on.

## SolidAgreement.kt { #solidagreement-kt }

The measurement this package exists for: **one written shape, evaluated two completely independent
ways, and the disagreement reported as a number.**

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val bracket = cuboid(4, 3, 1) - cylinder(2, 0.5).at(1, 0, 0)
println(bracket.crossCheck(SolidQuality(edgeLength = 0.02, segments = 256)).report())
```

### Two implementations that share no code

Almost nothing in a graphics codebase gets to do this. The usual options are to assert against a
remembered constant (which pins the current behaviour, not the correct one) or against a closed
form (which only exists for a handful of shapes). Here both sides are *implementations*, and they
share no code whatsoever:

| | side A | side B |
|---|---|---|
| the shape becomes | a distance field over `Double`s | a CSG tree over Manifold handles |
| the surface comes from | `afield.geometry.mesh.marchingCubes`, in Kotlin | Manifold's exact boolean kernel, in C++ |
| the volume comes from | a sum of signed tetrahedra over `Float` triangles | Manifold's own integration, in `double` |
| the genus comes from | edge/vertex adjacency in `mesh_topology.kt` | Manifold's Euler characteristic |

There is no path by which a bug in one produces the same wrong answer in the other. Five-figure
agreement is therefore strong evidence that both are right, in a way that any number of assertions
against constants would not be.

The same argument covers a **third** reading, the differentiable one in
`SolidGradient.kt`, which is `toScalarField`'s arithmetic replaced by
[`afield.math.autodiff.AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) and shares no line of code with it. It is measured by
[`SolidExpr.gradientAgreement`](graphics.md#solidinverse-kt--gradientagreement) rather than folded in here, and the reason is that the two compare
different objects: this file compares **surfaces** — volume, area, genus, Hausdorff deviation —
and the differentiable reading produces a *field*, exactly as `toScalarField` does. Folding it in
would have meant inventing a volume for something that has none. What the two share is the
argument, so each cross-references the other.

### Agreement does not converge to zero

There are two regimes:

 - **Polyhedral shapes** — cuboids, polygon-profile extrusions, and booleans of those. The exact
   lowering *is* the truth, so the marched one converges to it and the residual goes to zero as
   [`SolidQuality.edgeLength`](graphics.md#solidexact-kt--solidquality--edgelength) shrinks. Expect the relative volume error to fall roughly as `h²`.
 - **Curved shapes** — anything with a sphere, a cylinder, a circular profile or a round offset.
   Manifold's circle is an **inscribed n-gon**, whose area falls short of the true one by
   `1 − (n/2π)·sin(2π/n) ≈ 2π²/3n²`. The field lowering describes the true curve. So agreement
   converges to that deficit and not to zero, however fine the march.

[`facetingDeficit`](graphics.md#solidagreement-kt--facetingdeficit) computes the second one from the segment count alone, so a curved shape's
residual can be checked against a *predicted* floor rather than a remembered one. That is the
difference between "these two numbers are close" and "these two numbers are as close as the
geometry permits, and here is the formula".

## SolidExact.kt { #solidexact-kt }

Lowering **(b)**: a [`SolidExpr`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt-solidexpr) as an *exact* Manifold [`Solid`](graphics.md#solid-kt-solid) — or a stated refusal.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
when (val l = (cuboid(2, 2, 1) - cylinder(3, 0.3)).exactSolid()) {
    is SolidLowering.Lowered -> println("volume ${l.value.volume}, genus ${l.value.genus}")
    is SolidLowering.Refused -> println("no exact form: ${l.why}")
}
```

### Refusals are in the type

The discipline is [`afield.lang.rectsl.RectSLFnLowering`](languages.md#rectslfn-kt-rectslfnlowering)'s, wholesale, and for the same reason it gives:
a wrong answer is worse than no answer, so the lowering never guesses. Every node either maps to
the corresponding Manifold call or refuses **with a reason**, and the refusal propagates up.

A `null` would invite a caller to substitute something plausible; a thrown exception loses the
reason at the first `runCatching`. A stated reason survives into a test assertion, a diagnostic and
a docs page — which is why the refusals in this package are enumerable and enumerated:

| node | why there is no exact form | flavour |
|---|---|---|
| [`SolidExpr.SmoothUnion`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--smoothunion) | the fillet surface lies on **neither** operand, so no sequence of unions, intersections and differences of the two can produce it | permanent |
| [`SolidExpr.SmoothDifference`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--smoothdifference) | the same, for the filleted cut | permanent |
| [`SolidExpr.Gyroid`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--gyroid) | a trigonometric field on all of space, not a bounded volume | permanent |
| [`SolidExpr.Round`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--round) | `minkowskiSum` with a sphere exists, but that sphere is an inscribed polyhedron, so the result is strictly *inside* the true offset by up to its sagitta — and refining the march does not close a gap that is not the march's | *would not converge* |
| [`SolidExpr.Shell`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--shell) | `grow − erode` exists as two Minkowski operations, with [`SolidExpr.Round`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--round)'s problem twice over and a concave decomposition between them | *would not converge* |

The last two are the interesting ones. They are not "we did not get to it": an exact-looking answer
is available and is **the wrong answer**, systematically and in a direction that does not shrink.
Filing them beside the smooth blends would flatten a real distinction, so the type carries
`SolidLowering.Refused.closable` and the reason says which kind it is.

Note what is **not** on the list. Every [`Profile`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt-profile) node lowers exactly — including [`Profile.Offset`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--profile--offset),
because `Section.offset(d, JoinType.ROUND)` is definitionally the Minkowski sum with a disc, which
is *exactly* what `sdf − d` means. So a rounded slot has an exact form and a rounded solid does not,
and the asymmetry is real: Clipper offsets a 2D region as a region, where the 3D story has to go
through a polyhedral ball.

## SolidExpr.kt { #solidexpr-kt }

The SolidSL algebra: 3D solids and 2D profiles as immutable data values, with the builder
functions that write them and the bounds that enclose them.

A [`SolidExpr`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt-solidexpr) is a tree of primitives ([`sphere`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--sphere), [`cuboid`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--cuboid), [`cylinder`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--cylinder), [`cone`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--cone), [`torus`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--torus),
[`gyroid`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--gyroid)), transforms ([`at`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--at), [`turned`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--turned), [`sized`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--sized), [`mirrored`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--mirrored)), booleans (`+`, `-`, [`unionOf`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--unionof),
[`differenceOf`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--differenceof), [`intersectionOf`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--intersectionof), [`smoothUnion`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--smoothunion), [`smoothDifference`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--smoothdifference)) and modifiers ([`rounded`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--rounded),
[`shelled`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--shelled)). A [`Profile`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt-profile) is the 2D counterpart, turned into a solid by [`extruded`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--extruded) or [`revolved`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--revolved).

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val bracket = cuboid(60, 40, 8) - Profile.rect(26, 9).offset(4.5).extruded(30).at(0, 0, -15)
val field = bracket.toScalarField()
val exact = bracket.exactSolid()
```

This file only builds and measures the tree. Reading it is done elsewhere in the package:
[`toScalarField`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt--toscalarfield) lowers it to a sampled distance field, [`exactSolid`](graphics.md#solidexact-kt--exactsolid) to Manifold's exact CSG,
[`toGlsl`](graphics.md#solidglsl-kt--toglsl) to a shader function, and [`buildSolid`](graphics.md#solidexact-kt--buildsolid) mixes the first two.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/solidsl/SolidExpr.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/solidsl/SolidExpr/)

**Used in:** [A solid, written down: `afield.lang.solidsl`](../solid_notation.md), [Solids that cannot fail: Manifold in Field](../manifold.md)

### SolidExpr { #solidexpr-kt-solidexpr }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">sealed</span> <span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">SolidExpr</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/solidsl/SolidExpr/#L108)

A 3D solid written down as a **value** instead of as a closure — the symbolic notation that `afield.geometry.mesh`'s signed-distance family and `afield.geometry.solid.manifold`'s exact CSG kernel can *both* evaluate.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |

| <a id="solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--cylinder"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Cylinder</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">height</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">radiusLow</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">radiusHigh</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">radiusLow</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">segments</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">SolidExpr</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/solidsl/SolidExpr/#L134) | A cylinder, cone or truncated cone along **Z**, centred on the origin, so `z` runs from `-height/2` to `+height/2`. |

| <a id="solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--revolve"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Revolve</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">profile</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Profile</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">degrees</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">360.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">segments</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">SolidExpr</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/solidsl/SolidExpr/#L173) | A [`Profile`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt-profile) revolved about **Z**: the profile's `x` becomes the radius in the XY plane and its `y` becomes `z`. ## SolidField.kt { #solidfield-kt }

Lowering **(a)**: a [`SolidExpr`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt-solidexpr) as a signed distance field, so everything `mesh_sdf.kt`,
[`marchingCubes`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt--marchingcubes) and `Solid.levelSetOf` already do keeps working unchanged.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val mesh = (cuboid(2, 2, 1) - cylinder(3, 0.3)).march(resolution = 96)
```

### This lowering always succeeds

Unlike [`exactSolid`](graphics.md#solidexact-kt--exactsolid), this lowering always succeeds. Every node in the algebra has a field form —
that is where the algebra came from. What it does *not* always have is an **exact** distance
function, and the difference matters to a ray marcher (which steps by the field's value and
overshoots if the value is an overestimate) even though it does not matter to a marching cubes
(which only reads signs). [`fieldNotes`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt--fieldnotes) enumerates the places where the field is sign-correct but
not metric-correct, so the gap is a fact rather than a surprise.

### It is thread-safe, where the `sdf…` family is not

`mesh_sdf.kt` is explicit that a [`ScalarField3D`](graphics.md#mesh-sdf-kt-scalarfield3d) "must **read** the vector it is handed and not
write to it", and its own combinators capture a single scratch [`Vec3`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec3) to transform into. That makes
them fast and single-threaded.

This lowering does not do that. Internally it builds a tree of [`Field3`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt-field3) — a `fun interface` over
three primitive `Double`s, so there is no boxing and nothing to alias — and only wraps a [`Vec3`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec3) at
the very top, in [`toScalarField`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt--toscalarfield). So the field is re-entrant and safe to call from any thread.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/solidsl/SolidField.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/solidsl/SolidField/)

**Used in:** [A solid, written down: `afield.lang.solidsl`](../solid_notation.md)

## SolidGlsl.kt { #solidglsl-kt }

Lowering **(c)**: the same [`SolidExpr`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt-solidexpr) as GLSL, so the shape that produces the fabricable mesh can
also be ray-marched on a GPU at sixty frames a second.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val part = cuboid(2, 1.2, 0.4) - cylinder(2, 0.3).at(0.5, 0, 0)
println(part.toGlsl().glsl)          // float sdSolid(vec3 p) { … }
println(part.toRaymarchFragment())   // a complete fragment shader that draws it
```

This is the lowering that only a *symbolic* notation can have. A `(Vec3) -> Float` runs on the JVM
and nowhere else; an expression tree can be walked into whatever language you like. RectSL does
the same in 2D, in `RectSLGlsl.emitSdf`.

### What is emitted, and the unusual shape of it

Straight-line, single-assignment, **entirely scalar** GLSL: no `vec2`, no `vec3` locals, no
swizzles, no loops, no branches except the conditional operator.

```diffstatic {data-lang=glsl}
float sdSolid(vec3 p) {
    float x0 = p.x;
    float y0 = p.y;
    float z0 = p.z;
    float q1 = abs(x0) - 1.0;
    …
    return d7;
}
```

That looks like a strange thing to hand a shader compiler. Any driver will re-vectorise this in
its first pass, so nothing is lost at run time. What is *gained* is that the emitted text falls
inside a grammar small enough to write a reader for — which is what
`SolidSLGlslTest` does. It parses the shader back and evaluates it at tens of thousands of points
against [`SolidExpr.toField3`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt--tofield3), so the claim "the GLSL computes the same field" is **measured**
rather than asserted from the fact that both came from the same tree walk. A dropped negation, a
swapped `min` and `max`, an argument in the wrong position: all of those compile perfectly and all
of them are caught. Compilation alone — which is where the 2D precedent stops — proves only that
the text is *valid*.

### A raymarcher needs to know when the field lies

Sphere tracing steps along the ray by the field's value, which is only safe when that value is a
lower bound on the true distance. Several nodes here return something larger than the true distance
([`SolidExpr.Intersect`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--intersect) and [`SolidExpr.Difference`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--difference) are pointwise maxima; a twisted [`SolidExpr.Extrude`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--extrude)
shears space), and stepping by an over-estimate walks a ray straight through a thin wall.

So [`GlslSolid.stepScale`](graphics.md#solidglsl-kt--glslsolid--stepscale) is part of the result rather than a magic number in the shader: the
emitter reads [`fieldNotes`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt--fieldnotes) and reports the multiplier the march should use. `1.0` means the field
is a true distance function and sphere tracing is exact; anything less says how much this
particular expression has to be slowed down, and [`GlslSolid.notes`](graphics.md#solidglsl-kt--glslsolid--notes) says which node caused it.

## SolidGradient.kt { #solidgradient-kt }

Lowering **(c)**: a [`SolidExpr`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt-solidexpr) as a value *and an exact gradient* — with respect to its own named
parameters, not only to position.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val template = (sphere(0.8) + cylinder(1.6, 0.3))
    .parameterize {
        param("r") { it.node == "Sphere" && it.field == "radius" }
        param("h") { it.node == "Cylinder" && it.field == "height" }
    }
    .orThrow()

template.gradientAt(0.9, 0.0, 0.0, doubleArrayOf(0.8, 1.6))
// SolidGradientSample(value = 0.1, dPosition = [1, 0, 0], dParameters = [-1, 0])
```

### Why a third reading

`SolidField.kt` opens by saying a lambda "cannot be printed, compared, serialized, rewritten, or
emitted as GLSL", and this package answered that with two readings that can:
[`toScalarField`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt--toscalarfield) and [`exactSolid`](graphics.md#solidexact-kt--exactsolid). Both are *evaluations*. Neither changes what you can ask the
notation for.

`afield.lang.rectsl.RectSLFn` made the same argument one step further in 2D and is the model here,
verbatim: "a track that lowers to an `Fn` is a track you can take the derivative of, and therefore
a track you can **solve**: declare where a rect should be at some instant and let a gradient find
the numbers that put it there." That is what is missing in 3D, and this file plus
`SolidInverse.kt` is it.

The 2D answer does not port. `afield.math.functions.Functions.Fn` is `(Double) -> Double` — one input, and
a solid is a function of `(x, y, z)` *and* of however many named parameters the author declared.
The tool that does fit is `afield.math.autodiff.AD`: reverse-mode automatic differentiation over `Double`,
with the whole elementary set `SolidField.kt` needs already present. So this lowering is a
line-for-line transposition of [`SolidExpr.toField3`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt--tofield3) into [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) arithmetic, and the two are meant to
be read side by side.

#### Reverse mode, and not forward

The quantity that matters is one scalar loss over many sample points and a handful of parameters.
Reverse mode gets *every* parameter derivative from one forward pass and one backward sweep;
forward mode costs one pass per parameter, and `autodiff_forward.kt` says so itself — its `Dual2`
is for the opposite shape, one input and many outputs. The position gradient is only three inputs
and falls off the same tape for free, so there was never a reason to run two modes.

### The differentiable reading is total on the algebra

`SolidExact.kt` puts every refusal in the type and enumerates five of them. This file has **none
of that flavour**: the differentiable reading is
total on the algebra for exactly the reason [`toScalarField`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt--toscalarfield) is total on it — it is the same algebra
evaluated in a different arithmetic. Every node that has a field form has a differentiable form,
because `AD` is closed under everything `Field3` uses.

In fact the shape of it *inverts* the exact lowering's:

| node | [`toScalarField`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt--toscalarfield) | [`exactSolid`](graphics.md#solidexact-kt--exactsolid) | this reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`SolidExpr.SmoothUnion`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--smoothunion) | native | **refused** — the fillet lies on neither operand | native, and **C¹**: the one boolean with no kink at all |
| [`SolidExpr.SmoothDifference`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--smoothdifference) | native | **refused** | native, C¹ |
| [`SolidExpr.Gyroid`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--gyroid) | native | **refused** — not a bounded volume | native; one `abs` kink on the mid-sheet |
| [`SolidExpr.Round`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--round) | native | **refused** — would not converge | native, and exactly `f − r`: the cleanest derivative here |
| [`SolidExpr.Union`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--union) | native | native | subgradient on the seam, split 0.5/0.5 |

The constructs the exact kernel refuses hardest are the ones this reading is *best* at. A smooth
blend is differentiable by construction; a hard union is not. If you are going to fit a shape,
[`smoothUnion`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--smoothunion) and [`smoothDifference`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--smoothdifference) are the operators to write it with, and
[`SolidExpr.gradientNotes`](graphics.md#solidgradient-kt--gradientnotes) will tell you so about your own expression.

What *is* refused, always with a stated reason, is **binding a parameter to a slot** — see
[`SolidExpr.parameterize`](graphics.md#solidgradient-kt--parameterize). They fall into three groups: the address is wrong, two names claim one
number, or the seed is singular before the first step — from "that path does not exist, here are
the ones that do" to "`segments` is an integer facet count that [`toScalarField`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt--toscalarfield) ignores entirely,
so there is no derivative to take". Nothing guesses; a wrong derivative is worse than no
derivative.

### Kinks and the 0.5/0.5 tie rule

A distance field is full of kinks. `min` and `max` *are* CSG; `abs` is [`SolidExpr.Shell`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--shell) and
[`SolidExpr.Gyroid`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--gyroid); `sqrt` at zero is every radial primitive's own centre. A derivative at a kink
is a choice, and `autodiff.kt`'s file KDoc has already made it: `abs`, `min` and `max` **split the
derivative 0.5/0.5 at an exact tie**, and it says why — that is "precisely what a central
difference reports at a kink, so the analytic gradient and the finite-difference oracle *agree
there too*".

That matters here. It means the CSG seam does not have to be carved out of the
finite-difference census: a point sitting exactly on the boundary between two united children is a
point where the analytic answer and the numerical oracle still match. The convention is inherited
rather than re-chosen, so there is one place it is written down.

Every remaining place where the gradient is a subgradient, is zero when you might have expected
otherwise, or is genuinely **singular**, is enumerated by [`SolidExpr.gradientNotes`](graphics.md#solidgradient-kt--gradientnotes) — the third
notes function in this package, beside [`SolidExpr.fieldNotes`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt--fieldnotes) and [`SolidExpr.allRefusals`](graphics.md#solidexact-kt--allrefusals). The
singular ones matter: `√(x²+y²+z²)` has an infinite position gradient at the origin, so a
[`SolidExpr.Sphere`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--sphere)'s field is not differentiable at its own centre. Its *parameter* gradient
`∂/∂r = −1` is exact everywhere, which is the asymmetry that makes fitting work anyway.

@see SolidExpr.parameterize to name the numbers you want derivatives with respect to
@see afield.lang.solidsl.fitParameters for the inverse problem this exists to serve
@see SolidExpr.gradientAgreement for this reading measured against [`toScalarField`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt--toscalarfield), which shares
  no code with it — [`SolidAgreement`](graphics.md#solidagreement-kt-solidagreement)'s own argument applied to a third column

### ADField3 { #solidgradient-kt-adfield3 }

## SolidInverse.kt { #solidinverse-kt }

The payoff of lowering **(c)**: **inverse design.** Declare what a solid should look like and let a
gradient find the numbers that make it so.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val truth  = (sphere(0.80) + cylinder(1.60, 0.30)).let { it }
val target = truth.sampleField(count = 3000, seed = 7)

val template = truth.parameterize {
    param("r") { it.node == "Sphere" && it.field == "radius" }
    param("h") { it.node == "Cylinder" && it.field == "height" }
}.orThrow()

val fit = template.fitParameters(target, start = doubleArrayOf(0.35, 2.60))
println(fit.report())
fit.fitted.march(96)      // an ordinary SolidExpr again
```

This is `afield.lang.rectsl.Track.fitParameters` in three dimensions, and it is the reason
`SolidGradient.kt` exists. RectSLFn's KDoc: "a track that lowers to an `Fn` is a track you can take
the derivative of, and therefore a track you can **solve**: declare where a rect should be at some
instant and let a gradient find the numbers that put it there."

### The target is a sampled field, not a mesh

A [`SolidSamples`](graphics.md#solidinverse-kt-solidsamples) is a bag of points with a signed distance at each. Three things recommend it over
fitting against a mesh:

 - **It has a gradient.** A mesh-to-mesh distance goes through a nearest-triangle search whose
   result is a discontinuous function of the parameters — the nearest triangle *changes* — and
   marching cubes has to be re-run at every step. A field residual is `pred − target` at a fixed
   point, and its derivative is exactly what [`SolidTemplate.adFieldWith`](graphics.md#solidgradient-kt--solidtemplate--adfieldwith) hands over.
 - **The target need not be a solid at all.** [`sampleField`](graphics.md#solidinverse-kt--samplefield) builds one from another [`SolidExpr`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt-solidexpr),
   which is what a recovery test wants; but a scan, a level set from somewhere else, or a hand-
   written list of "this point must be 2mm outside" constraints is the same type.
 - **It is cheap and fixed.** Sample once; every iteration reads the same array. A 3000-point
   target costs one march-free forward pass and one backward sweep per step.

The cost is that it fits the *field* and not the *surface*, and those are different objectives. Two
shapes can have the same zero set and different fields — [`SolidExpr.Intersect`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--intersect)'s own
[`SolidExpr.fieldNotes`](graphics.md#solidfield-kt--fieldnotes) entry says it over-estimates distance outside a concave corner — so a field
residual is a stricter target than "look the same". Strictly speaking that is a feature for
recovery (there is one right answer and the loss knows it) and a hazard for design (you may not
care about the field away from the surface). [`SolidFitOptions.band`](graphics.md#solidinverse-kt--solidfitoptions--band) is the dial: clamp both sides
into a narrow band around zero and the objective becomes almost purely about the surface.

### What makes a parameter refuse to move

This is the failure mode of inverse design and it is worth naming before it happens, because it
presents as a *converged* optimisation:

 - A hard [`SolidExpr.Union`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--union) gives the whole derivative to whichever child is nearest. A child that
   is nowhere nearest — swallowed inside another — receives exactly zero from every sample, and its
   parameters have a zero gradient. Write the shape with [`smoothUnion`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--smoothunion) and every child contributes
   within `k` of the seam.
 - A [`SolidExpr.Difference`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--difference) cutter entirely inside the body is the same story.
 - A [`SolidExpr.Empty`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--empty) subtree, or an `Extrude` sample past the end of the sweep, is a structural
   zero.

[`SolidFit.deadParameters`](graphics.md#solidinverse-kt--solidfit--deadparameters) reports exactly which parameters had a zero gradient at the *start*, so
that reads as a diagnosis rather than as a mysteriously immediate convergence. And
[`SolidExpr.gradientNotes`](graphics.md#solidgradient-kt--gradientnotes) says the same things about an expression before it is ever fitted.

## SolidPointCloudFit.kt { #solidpointcloudfit-kt }

Fitting a parametric solid to a **point cloud** — unoriented samples on a surface, with no signed
distances, no normals and no correspondence.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val cloud = someTarget.samplePointCloud(count = 3000, seed = 4, noise = 0.004)
val fit = template.fitToPointCloud(cloud, start = doubleArrayOf(0.3, 1.1, 0.4))
```

### Why a point cloud is a different problem from [`fitParameters`](graphics.md#solidinverse-kt--fitparameters)

[`fitParameters`](graphics.md#solidinverse-kt--fitparameters) regresses against a [`SolidSamples`](graphics.md#solidinverse-kt-solidsamples) — a bag of points *with a signed distance at
each*. That is a rich target and it is also a slightly circular one: the distances come from
`toScalarField`, so the oracle already knows the answer in the same representation the model
speaks. It is the right test of whether the gradient works. It is not the problem anybody has.

The problem anybody has is a **point cloud**: a `.psub` plane subdivision rendered as points, a
compressed-splat PLY, a depth scan. Points on a boundary. No sign, no inside/outside, no normals
you trust, no correspondence to anything, some noise, and — nearly always — only the part of the
surface that faced the sensor.

The loss is the obvious one, and the three failure modes below all follow from what it does
*not* contain:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
L(θ) = (1/N) · Σ f(pᵢ; θ)²
```

The model's own field, squared, at each cloud point. A surface point should be *on* the surface, so
`f` should be zero there. That is the whole objective.

#### The missing interior term

There is **no term that wants the interior filled**. `L` is minimised by putting the model's
zero level set through the points, and a shape that puts *some* surface through them scores as well
as the shape that generated them. Three consequences, each measured in `SolidSLPointCloudTest`:

 - **A full cloud recovers well.** Points all round a closed surface pin it from every side, and
   the missing interior term does not get a chance to matter.
 - **A partial view does not, and it fails in a specific direction.** Crop the cloud to one
   hemisphere and every parameter that only shows itself on the missing side is unconstrained. The
   loss does not go up when they wander, because there are no points there to notice. This is not
   a solver failure — the solver finds a genuine minimum of the objective it was given — and no
   amount of restarting fixes it. It is the objective that is wrong for that data.
 - **`Shell` and `Round` are dangerous under this loss** in a way they are not under
   [`fitParameters`](graphics.md#solidinverse-kt--fitparameters). `abs(f) − t` is zero on *two* surfaces, so a shell can satisfy a cloud with the
   wrong one of them.

[`SolidCloudFit.unconstrainedParameters`](graphics.md#solidpointcloudfit-kt--solidcloudfit--unconstrainedparameters) reports the first-order version of the second bullet: a
parameter whose gradient stays near zero **across the whole cloud** is a parameter the data does
not see. It is the point-cloud analogue of [`SolidFit.deadParameters`](graphics.md#solidinverse-kt--solidfit--deadparameters) and it exists for the same
reason — the failure presents as a *converged* optimisation.

#### The target generation shares no code with the model

[`SolidExpr.samplePointCloud`](graphics.md#solidpointcloudfit-kt--samplepointcloud) marches the shape with `afield.geometry.mesh.marchingCubes` and samples its
triangles by area. That path touches nothing in `SolidGradient.kt`: no [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad), no tape, no
`toADField`. So a recovery here is two independent implementations agreeing, in the same sense
[`SolidAgreement`](graphics.md#solidagreement-kt-solidagreement) means it, rather than one implementation checking its own arithmetic.

It is also what a real cloud is like. Triangle-area sampling is uniform over the *surface*, so
(unlike vertex sampling) a coarsely marched flat face is not under-represented relative to a
finely marched curved one.

## SolidSimplify.kt { #solidsimplify-kt }

Rewriting a [`SolidExpr`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt-solidexpr) into a smaller one that means the same thing — the other half of what
making the 3D family symbolic bought, beside a second and third backend.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val messy = unionOf(listOf(sphere(1), sphere(1))).at(0, 0, 0).at(1, 0, 0) - SolidExpr.Empty
println(messy.simplified())        // Translate(child=Sphere(radius=1.0, segments=0), x=1.0, …)
```

None of these rewrites is available to a closure. Two `sdfSphere(1.0)` lambdas are different
objects and always will be; two `SolidExpr.Sphere(1.0)` are `==`. Nothing can ask a `(Vec3) -> Float`
whether it is ever non-zero, or where; a node knows its own [`SolidExpr.bounds`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--bounds) without sampling.
This file is what those two facts are worth.

### The rules

The dull ones first, because a notation accumulates them the moment anyone generates code into it:
identity transforms drop out, adjacent [`SolidExpr.Translate`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--translate)s and [`SolidExpr.Scale`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--scale)s fold, nested
booleans of the same kind flatten into one n-ary node (which matters more here than in most
algebras, because n-ary is exactly what reaches Manifold's *batch* boolean rather than a fold), and
[`SolidExpr.Empty`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--empty) is absorbed.

Two of them are worth more than that:

 - **Disjoint operands.** `a ∩ b` where the two bounds do not overlap is [`SolidExpr.Empty`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--empty); `a − b`
   where `b` is nowhere near `a` is just `a`. That is a fact about the *expression*, decided from
   symbolic bounds with nothing sampled and nothing built. On a generated assembly — a hundred
   bores drilled through one plate of which twelve actually meet it — this is the difference
   between a shader that runs and one that does not.

 - **A vanishing blend removes a refusal.** `SmoothUnion(a, b, k)` with `k` at or below zero *is*
   a plain union, and a plain union has an exact CSG form where a smooth blend never will. So
   simplification can move an expression from the level-set fallback onto the exact path, which is
   a strange and rather nice thing for a peephole optimiser to be able to do. [`simplified`](graphics.md#solidsimplify-kt--simplified) is
   therefore worth calling before [`buildSolid`](graphics.md#solidexact-kt--buildsolid) and not only before [`toGlsl`](graphics.md#solidglsl-kt--toglsl).

### What it does not do

It does not compose two [`SolidExpr.Rotate`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--rotate)s unless they turn about the same single axis. Two
general Euler rotations compose to a matrix, and a matrix does not always come back out as three
Euler angles without a gimbal case to get wrong — and the whole discipline of this package is that
a rewrite which is *nearly* right is worse than no rewrite. It also does not reassociate
[`SolidExpr.SmoothUnion`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--smoothunion), which is genuinely non-associative, or reorder a
[`SolidExpr.Difference`](graphics.md#solidexpr-kt--solidexpr--difference)'s operands, which is genuinely non-commutative.

Every rule is checked by sampling: `SolidSLSimplifyTest` asserts that the simplified expression's
field agrees with the original's at thousands of points, for every rule and every combination it
has. A rewrite that changes the shape is the failure this file exists to rule out, so it is the
most heavily sampled.

## StackSLBox.kt { #stackslbox-kt }

Host-side entry points for StackSL: compiling the stack language to GLSL, and evaluating it on
the GPU sample by sample. The language, its compiler and its diagnostics live in
`afield.lang.stacksl`; this file is the Kotlin surface a box calls.

[`stackSL`](graphics.md#stackslbox-kt--stacksl) holds a box's StackSL source, falling back to a parent box's. [`compileStackSL`](graphics.md#stackslbox-kt--compilestacksl),
[`stackSLToGlsl`](graphics.md#stackslbox-kt--stacksltoglsl) and the standalone [`slGlsl`](graphics.md#stackslbox-kt--slglsl) are pure compilation and need no device. [`slEval`](graphics.md#stackslbox-kt--sleval) and
[`slSweep`](graphics.md#stackslbox-kt--slsweep) actually run the compiled function: they wrap it in a small compute shader and dispatch
it through a `Renderer` that defaults to `fromContext()`, so they need a live graphics context.
Neither binds any texture sampler, so a source that needs one is rejected.

[`slSweep`](graphics.md#stackslbox-kt--slsweep) returns a [`StackSLSweep`](graphics.md#stackslbox-kt-stackslsweep), which implements `ToHTML` and draws itself as an inline SVG
plot of the four output channels with per-channel min/median/max; [`StackSLSweep.h`](graphics.md#stackslbox-kt--h) is that HTML.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLBox.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLBox/)

**Used in:** [StackSL cheatsheet](../stacksl_cheatsheet.md), [StackSL examples](../stacksl_examples.md)

## StackSLFeedback.kt { #stackslfeedback-kt }

StackSL with its own previous frame: [`Box.stackFeedback`](graphics.md#stackslfeedback-kt--stackfeedback) draws a box's `stackSL` program
fullscreen every frame into a float ping-pong target, with the last frame bound as
`sampler2D state`, so `prev`, `sample`, `gather` and the store words (`0->` … `3->`) read what the
program drew a frame ago. [`StackSLFeedback`](graphics.md#stackslfeedback-kt-stackslfeedback) is the running host; [`StackSLLowering`](graphics.md#stackslfeedback-kt-stacksllowering) is the panel it
shows in the box's output — the lowered GLSL, its helpers, wires, stack depth and diagnostics.
`StackSLFeedbackTest` covers the shader it builds and the panel.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/)

| <a id="stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbacksettings--timescale"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">timeScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/#L63) | Seconds of program time per second of wall time — what `time` and `0.1t` count in. |
| <a id="stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbacksettings--paused"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">paused</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/#L66) | Hold the picture: no frame is drawn and time stops until this is false again. |
| <a id="stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbacksettings--displaygamma"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">displayGamma</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/#L73) | The exponent the window applies to what the program drew. A browser shows a WebGL canvas's numbers as sRGB, and Field's window expects linear light, so 2.2 shows a program the way the StackTrinket page and the StackSL gallery show it. The state itself is never changed by this. |
| <a id="stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbacksettings--showlowering"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">showLowering</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/#L76) | Show the [`StackSLLowering`](graphics.md#stackslfeedback-kt-stacksllowering) panel in the box's `lowering` output channel. |
| <a id="stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbacksettings--viewport"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">viewport</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Rect</span><span class="o">?</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/#L79) | Where in the window the picture goes; null fills it. |
| <a id="stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbacksettings--inputs"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">inputs</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MutableMap</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">HasImageView</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/#L88) | More pictures the program can read beside `state`, in order: the first is `sample1` / `gather1` / `texelSize1`, the second `sample2`, up to three. Any texture will do — a classmate's WebRTC stream (`webrtcSource`), a camera, another render target. Each is copied, the right way up and at the state's size, once per step, so `0 sample1` reads it at this pixel with y up, exactly as `prev` reads the last frame. See [`input`](graphics.md#stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbacksettings--input). |
| <a id="stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbacksettings--input"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">input</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">texture</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">HasImageView</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/#L91) | Add `texture` as the next input, read by `sample1`, `sample2`, …; `name` is its GLSL sampler name. |

| <a id="stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbackshader--picture-vertex"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="nc">PICTURE&#95;VERTEX</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/#L414) | The fullscreen triangle as Field draws one elsewhere: `fragUV.y = 1` lands in row 0. |
| <a id="stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbackshader--picture-fragment"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="nc">PICTURE&#95;FRAGMENT</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/#L426) | Reads the state at `fragUV`; drawn with [`PICTURE_VERTEX`](graphics.md#stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbackshader--picture-vertex) it comes out top row first. |
| <a id="stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbackshader--copy-fragment"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="nc">COPY&#95;FRAGMENT</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/#L444) | Copies an input texture into an image stored like the state: drawn with [`VERTEX`](graphics.md#stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbackshader--vertex), it reads `source` with v flipped, because Field's textures keep their top row first. With `encode` set (an sRGB source, such as a WebRTC stream's browser paints) it re-encodes what sampling decoded, so the program reads the numbers the picture holds — the values a browser ShaderTrinket's `iChannel` gives, and the space `state` is in. Without it a stream reads darker, by the gamma. |
| <a id="stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbackshader--vertex"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="nc">VERTEX</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/#L470) | The fullscreen-triangle vertex shader: `fragUV` runs 0..1 with y up, and the image is written so that image row 0 holds `uv.y = 0`. That is the row `texture(state, vec2(u, 0))` reads, so `prev` reads back this pixel. Field's render targets put clip `y = +1` in row 0, so the usual `gl_Position = pos * 2 - 1` would store the picture upside down relative to its own sampling and every feedback step would flip it; [`StackSLFeedback.show`](graphics.md#stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedback--show) flips it back for the window. |
| <a id="stackslfeedback-kt--stackslfeedbackshader--fragment"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">fragment</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">lowered</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">inputs</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">emptyList</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/#L486) | The fragment shader around `lowered`, the GLSL the compiler made for a program. `params` is `(seconds, frame, width, height)`; a negative frame draws black, which is how the state is cleared. The hash is StackTrinket's, so a program's grain looks as it does there. |

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">StackSLLowering</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">source</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">result</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">StackSLCompileResult</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">glslError</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">running</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ToHTML</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSLFeedback/#L516)

What one compile of a feedback program came to, as StackTrinket's lowering panel shows it: whether it is drawing, the stack depth with the leftover values under the returned top, the helpers it pulled in, how many dangling wires (tunable numbers) it has, each diagnostic at its line and column; [`glslHtml`](graphics.md#stackslfeedback-kt--stacksllowering--glslhtml) is the lowered GLSL line by line. It is a [`ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml), so `display("lowering", it)` draws the summary.

## stackAutoNumbers.kt { #stackautonumbers-kt }

Live numbers for a `{{ stack.auto.foo }}` slot: every literal in the StackSL becomes a member of a
uniform block, `foo_numbers`, that sliders, Kotlin or a keyframe can turn without a recompile.

[`StackAutoNumbers`](graphics.md#stackautonumbers-kt-stackautonumbers) holds the block's layout and the calls that seed it and switch it live.
`StackAutoNumbersTest` covers it.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/stackAutoNumbers.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/stackAutoNumbers/)

## modelling.kt { #modelling-kt }

A self-tuning controller for pushing the *distribution* of a scalar signal towards a target
shape. You hand [`AdaptiveDistributionController.pushSamples`](graphics.md#modelling-kt--adaptivedistributioncontroller--pushsamples) a batch of samples each frame and it
returns a [`ControlOutput`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-controloutput) whose `appliedParams` are the next parameter values to send to whatever
produced them — a shader, a simulation, a tone curve.

The error signal comes from a [`FeatureExtractor`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-featureextractor); [`UniformQuantileFeatureExtractor`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-uniformquantilefeatureextractor) is the
built-in one and measures how far a set of sample quantiles sit from their targets. Internally
each feature gets a recursive-least-squares row (with forgetting) that learns a local Jacobian,
the step is a Tikhonov-regularised Gauss-Newton solve scaled by a confidence estimate, then
softened near the parameter bounds, rate-limited by `maxStep`, clipped, and finally offset by a
per-parameter sinusoidal dither so the estimator keeps seeing excitation.

[`ControllerConfig.observationDelayFrames`](graphics.md#modelling-kt--controllerconfig--observationdelayframes) is the important knob: it models pipeline latency
explicitly by pairing each observation with the command issued that many pushes earlier, so the
loop does not have to be slowed down to learn correctly. Use [`AdaptiveDistributionControllerBank`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-adaptivedistributioncontrollerbank)
for one controller per scene, and [`AdaptiveDistributionLoop`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-adaptivedistributionloop) to drive `observe`/`apply` from a
`Runloop` hook.

This is plain `DoubleArray` math with no GPU or `Box` dependency; every array in
[`ControllerConfig`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-controllerconfig) must be `parameterNames.size` long. [`main`](graphics.md#modelling-kt--main) runs a synthetic drifting-Gaussian
plant against the controller and prints a trace.

## quantilewarp.kt { #quantilewarp-kt }

Reshapes a scalar signal's distribution by fitting a monotone 8-knot PCHIP curve from the
measured quantiles of recent samples onto the quantiles of a chosen target distribution —
[`TargetDistributions.UnitNormal`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt--targetdistributions--unitnormal) by default, or any [`QuantileFunction`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt-quantilefunction).

[`AdaptiveQuantileWarp.update`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt--adaptivequantilewarp--update) takes a batch of samples, merges it with the last
`historyFrames` batches, and returns a [`QuantileWarpState`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt-quantilewarpstate): the knot pairs, an
[`QuantileWarpState.evaluate`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt--quantilewarpstate--evaluate) for CPU-side use, and the same 16 knots packed into four `vec4`s
ready for push constants via [`QuantileWarpState.applyToPushConstants`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt--quantilewarpstate--applytopushconstants). Successive states are
smoothed towards each other by `smoothingAlpha` and forced strictly increasing, so the curve
stays invertible even when the input degenerates.

`fieldQuantileWarpIncludeSource` is the matching GLSL — `fieldQuantileWarp8` and
`fieldQuantileWarpMix` evaluate the identical PCHIP curve on the GPU — and is reachable from
shader source as the built-in include named by [`FIELD_QUANTILE_WARP_INCLUDE_NAME`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt--field-quantile-warp-include-name).
[`Box.fieldProbeQuantileWarp`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt--fieldprobequantilewarp) closes the loop: it installs a runloop hook that drains a
`ShaderFieldProbe`, updates the warp, calls your `apply` callback and renders a knot table into a
box display channel.

Two constraints: exactly eight strictly increasing probabilities inside `(0, 1)`, and
[`Box.fieldProbeQuantileWarp`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt--fieldprobequantilewarp) needs a live `Box` plus a probe configured for continuous snapshot
reads.

## FLineInspect.kt { #flineinspect-kt }

Make a figure answerable: [`inspect`](graphics.md#flineinspect-kt--inspect) draws FLines the way `lines` does and then *names* whatever you
click on, in the figure's own coordinates.

The problem it solves is the one the panel documents ran into — a figure was drawn, and then the
numbers about it were fished back out with `println` because there was no way to ask the picture
"which edge is this, and how far along it am I?". `inspect` wires [`FLine.onClick`](graphics.md#standarddrawing-kt--onclick) and
[`FLine.hoverColor`](graphics.md#standarddrawing-kt--hovercolor) for every line it is given, so a click reports the element under the pointer
(see [`FLineIntersection`](graphics.md#standarddrawing-kt-flineintersection)) and writes a readable card into a second output channel.

## pointing_render.kt { #pointing-render-kt }

Seeing what the pointer found: the picked part lit, a crosshair where the pointer was aimed, and a
caption that names what it hit.

### Why this is in the layer and not left to the caller

Because "it compiles" and "a hit record came back non-null" are both worthless as evidence for
something whose whole job is to tell a person what they are touching. The failure mode is not a
crash; it is *the wrong part lit*, or a pointer that is confidently off by the height of a caption
band. Neither shows up in a unit test's return value, and both are obvious in a picture.

So the layer ships its own way of drawing itself, `SpatialPointerPixelTest` decodes the PNG back
out and reads samples from it, and the demo transcript uses the same call a person would.

### What the picture is

[`TriMesh.renderPng`](graphics.md#mesh-field-kt--renderpng)'s rasterizer, over a mesh whose per-vertex colours have been repainted by part
([`TriMesh.coloredByPart`](graphics.md#pointing-render-kt--coloredbypart)), with a crosshair composited on afterwards at the pointer's pixel. All of
it CPU: no GPU, no window, no AWT — so it runs inside a live Field box, inside a test, and inside a
headless docs capture, identically.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val scene = pickScene { add("model", mesh, parts = builder.groups()) }
val camera = MeshView().rayCamera(scene.mergedMesh())
val at = Vec2(360f, 270f)
display(scene.pointerFigureHtml(camera, at))
```
